Zod's `.email()` does not normalize case. As a result `Blocked@Example.com` passes the blacklist, and `John@x.com` creates a second attendee row next to an existing `john@x.com` (who then receives a duplicate invitation). Both comparisons should be done on lowercased values.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner permission check uses `&&` instead of `||`

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`, so a user must satisfy both predicates at once. A team member who is only an admin (not the owner) is therefore rejected with FORBIDDEN, even though the UI exposes the "additional_guests" action and other checks in the codebase use `booking.isUserTeamAdminOrOwner` (an OR). In practice only the organizer (or an attendee) can add guests; team admins/owners operating on someone else's team booking get a confusing permission error. The two calls should be combined with `||`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Emails sent with unfiltered `guests` instead of `uniqueGuests`

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the raw request payload, but the DB write only used `uniqueGuests`. Inside `sendAddGuestsEmails` the check `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` decides whether someone gets a full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (new guest) or the `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` (existing attendee). Because already-existing attendees appear in `guests` whenever the caller resubmits them, those attendees get a full duplicate booking confirmation with a `METHOD:REQUEST` ICS instead of the "guests added" notice. Pass `uniqueGuests` here.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores host/attendee email opt-outs

Every other helper in this file consults `eventTypeDisableHostEmail(eventTypeMetadata)` / `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail(eventTypeMetadata)` before enqueuing emails, but `sendAddGuestsEmails` has no `eventTypeMetadata` parameter and unconditionally sends the organizer email (plus team members) and attendee emails. Event types configured with `disableStandardEmails.all.host` or `.attendee` will still send mail when guests are added, violating the organizer's explicit preference. The handler already loads `eventType`; its metadata should be passed through and checked here.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add unlimited arbitrary email addresses

The authorization check grants access to anyone whose email is in `booking.attendees`, and guests added by this same endpoint become attendees too. There is no cap on the number of addresses in `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` (`z.array(z.string().email())`) and no rate limiting, so a booker (or a guest they previously added) can repeatedly POST arbitrary addresses and cause cal.com to send them calendar invites and attendee emails from the organizer's identity — a spam/open-relay vector against arbitrary third parties. If attendees are meant to invite others, this needs at least a per-booking count limit and rate limiting, and probably a config flag.

Calendar sync uses the acting user's credentials, not the booking organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` builds the EventManager with the credentials of whoever called the mutation. The event being updated belongs to `booking.userId`. When a team admin/owner or an attendee (explicitly allowed by the permission check above) adds guests, the EventManager either has no calendar credentials at all (plain attendees) or only the actor's (admins), so `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` does not update the organizer's calendar event — guests are persisted in the DB and emailed, but never actually added to the calendar invite. Credentials for the booking's organizer/host should be used.

Error toast always shows raw tRPC code; fallback message is unreachable

`const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`` always evaluates to a non-empty template string (e.g. `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR: <english text>`), so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` never falls back and users are shown internal error codes instead of the localized "Unable to add guests" text. Additionally `t(err.message)` only produces a translation when the server message happens to be a key; other messages are leaked verbatim.

Hardcoded "Remove email" tooltip is not translated

The remove button tooltip uses the literal string `content="Remove email"` instead of `t("remove_email")` / an existing locale key, while every other user-facing string in this component goes through `useLocale()`. In a fully localized product this surfaces English text in all non-English locales.

No tests for the new addGuests endpoint or dialog

The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that mutates attendee records, talks to calendar integrations and sends emails, plus a new dialog and a new form component, but contains no tests. The permission matrix (organizer / team admin / team owner / attendee / unrelated user), the dedupe and blacklist filtering, and the case where `updateCalendarAttendees` throws are exactly the kind of logic that regresses silently; at minimum a unit test for the handler's authorization and filtering would be expected.

No validation of booking status before mutating attendees

The handler loads the booking by id and only checks existence and permissions; it never checks `booking.status`. A direct API call can therefore add guests (and trigger calendar invites and emails) to a CANCELLED or REJECTED booking, resurrecting attendee records and sending invitations for an event that no longer takes place. The booking status should be validated (e.g. ACCEPTED/PENDING) before modifying attendees.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Read-modify-write of retryCount loses increments under overlapping cron runs

Both increment sites (the `else` branch here and the one at line 195) compute `reminder.retryCount + 1` in application code from the value returned by the earlier `findMany`. If two cron invocations overlap — plausible because the per-reminder loop awaits a `profile.findFirst` and `getBookerBaseUrl` call for every reminder, so a run can exceed the cron interval — both read the same retryCount and write the same value. Failures are then under-counted and a persistently failing reminder may never reach the `> 1` threshold, so it is retried indefinitely and the PR's retry cap never takes effect. Use Prisma's atomic `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount cleanup clause is not scoped to SMS/unscheduled reminders

The new deletion branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` inside the `OR` is not restricted by `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` or `scheduled: false`, unlike the pre-existing branch next to it. As written, any WorkflowReminder row (email, WhatsApp, or an already-scheduled reminder) whose retryCount is greater than 1 is hard-deleted on each cron run. Today only this handler increments retryCount, but the column lives on the shared model, so as soon as another scheduler writes retryCount — or a concurrent run manages to schedule a reminder after it has already been bumped twice — unrelated reminders are silently purged, and an already-scheduled reminder is deleted without cancelling its provider-side scheduled message (referenceId), leaving an orphaned SMS/email job that will still fire. The clause should be constrained to the same rows this handler owns, e.g. `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduled: false, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment no longer describes the delete query

The comment says "delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date", but the query now also deletes unscheduled SMS (and, due to the unscoped OR branch, non-SMS) reminders that have exceeded the retry limit. The comment should be updated to reflect both deletion conditions so future readers understand that the cleanup is not limited to past-due reminders.

Generated Prisma artifacts for retryCount were not regenerated

The schema's `zod` and `kysely` generators write committed outputs (`packages/prisma/zod/*`, `packages/prisma/kysely/types.ts`). This PR adds `retryCount` to `WorkflowReminder` and the migration, but does not update those generated files, so the WorkflowReminder zod schema and the Kysely `WorkflowReminder` interface still lack the new column. Any code that validates a reminder via the generated zod schema will silently drop retryCount, and Kysely-typed queries cannot reference it; the repository's prisma-generate check will also fail or produce a dirty diff. Regenerate and commit the zod/kysely outputs alongside the schema change.

New retryCount predicate has no supporting index

The `retryCount > 1` condition has no index, and mixing it in an `OR` with the indexed `(method, scheduledDate)` predicate means Postgres cannot satisfy the whole query from the existing composite index. WorkflowReminder is a high-volume table (one row per reminder per booking), so every cron invocation can fall back to a sequential scan of the whole table. Consider a partial index such as `CREATE INDEX ... ON "WorkflowReminder"(retryCount) WHERE retryCount > 0`, or restructuring the cleanup so the unindexed predicate is not part of the main scan.

Reminders that cannot be attempted never increment retryCount and are retried forever

retryCount is only incremented when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy or throws. When `sendTo` is missing (e.g. an SMS_ATTENDEE reminder for a booking with no `smsReminderNumber`, or an SMS_NUMBER step with an empty `sendTo`) or the computed `message` is empty, the `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` guard simply skips the reminder. Those rows stay `scheduled: false` forever, are re-fetched on every cron run, and are skipped again — exactly the unbounded-rescheduling behavior this PR is meant to stop. A missing phone number is one of the common failure modes, so this path needs to bump retryCount (or delete the reminder) when the reminder cannot be attempted.

Unguarded update inside catch can abort the whole batch

The `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` added inside the catch block is not itself protected. If it throws (row deleted concurrently by the cleanup query, or a transient DB error), the exception escapes the `catch` and the `for` loop, so all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are left unprocessed and the endpoint returns a 500. Additionally, this catch also runs when `twilio.scheduleSMS` succeeded but the subsequent `update({ scheduled: true, referenceId })` threw; in that case retryCount is bumped even though a Twilio message is already scheduled, so the reminder is re-sent on the next run (duplicate SMS) and then eventually deleted while the Twilio job remains live. The increment should be guarded with its own try/catch and should not be applied when the failure occurred after a successful provider call.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Composite `Prisma.Sql` expectations are not structurally equal to reduce-built fragments

The service builds org/team and combined-filter conditions through `reduce` using nested fragments like `Prisma.sql`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` and `Prisma.sql`(${acc}) AND (${condition})`. The expectations at lines 295, 332, and 429 are single flat `Prisma.sql` templates. `Prisma.Sql` equality is structural over its internal `strings` and `values`, not based on the rendered SQL text, so a nested fragment built with `reduce` will not deep-equal a flat template even when the SQL renders identically. These assertions will fail; compare rendered SQL or execute the query instead of using `toEqual` on `Prisma.Sql` objects.

Exact SQL array order depends on unordered repository results

The expected SQL hard-codes the order of `teamIds` and user IDs inside `ANY([...])`. `teamIds` comes from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId` and user IDs come from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`; neither call specifies an `orderBy`. If Postgres returns those rows in a different order, the `ANY` arrays differ even though the authorization semantics are identical, and the exact `Prisma.sql` comparison fails intermittently. Sort the IDs before asserting or compare semantically.

No database execution coverage for org/team `ANY` conditions

The only test that actually executes the generated conditions against Postgres uses `scope: "user"`. The org/team authorization paths, which are the only places that emit `ANY(${array})`, are only compared as `Prisma.sql` strings and never run against the database. A real parameter-binding/type-inference problem in those paths (for example around array parameters) would therefore pass the test suite while failing in production. Add a `$queryRaw` execution test for at least one org/team scope.

Removing `findMany` breaks existing consumers

This PR deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, but the diff updates no call sites. `InsightsBookingService` is exported and was previously responsible for executing the denormalized query; any consumer still calling `findMany` will fail TypeScript compilation or runtime. Either migrate every call site in this PR or keep a `findMany` wrapper that executes a raw query using `getBaseConditions()`.

Unparenthesized OR authorization condition can be miscombined by callers

When scope is `team` or `org` and no filter conditions are supplied, `getBaseConditions()` returns `authConditions` directly. For those scopes `authConditions` is a top-level `OR` such as `(team booking) OR (user booking)`. If a caller appends another predicate, e.g. `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" >= ...`, SQL precedence makes it `(team booking) OR ((user booking) AND date filter)`, so the extra predicate is applied only to one branch. The returned fragment should always be wrapped in parentheses, otherwise date/security predicates can be silently skipped for part of the dataset.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`sed -i ''` is macOS-only, so the script silently fails to update .env on Linux

`sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD/macOS in-place invocation. With GNU sed (Linux), the empty `''` argument is not consumed as an in-place suffix, so the command errors out and the file is never modified, yet the script still prints "✅ Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL in $ENV_FILE to $TUNNEL_URL", leaving developers with a stale webhook URL while believing it was updated. Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"` or write to a temp file) and check the command's exit status before printing success. `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is also cwd-dependent and only correct when the script is run from `scripts/`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded en-US locale

The "cache_last_updated" value uses `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` while the component already uses `useLocale()` for translations. Non-US users therefore see US-formatted dates (M/D/YY, 12-hour clock) in an otherwise translated UI. Use the active user locale (e.g. from the locale context / `useLocale().i18n.language`) so the timestamp follows the user's locale settings.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache deletion always fails for credentials not owned by the session user (delegation/team credentials)

The authorization check is `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`, i.e. it only accepts credentials whose `userId` equals the logged in user. Team/service-account delegation credentials are not user-owned (they are stored with `userId = null` and belong to a team / DelegationCredential), and in-memory delegation credentials even have negative ids, so the query never matches and the mutation throws "Credential not found or access denied". The UI does not guard against this: `canDisconnect` is computed from `delegationCredentialId`, but `hasCache` only checks the integration type, so the "Delete cached data" item is rendered for delegation-connected Google calendars and then always fails with the generic "Error deleting cache" toast. Either authorize team/delegation ownership in the handler or hide the action when `delegationCredentialId` is set. Note also that for in-memory delegation credentials, cache lookups are keyed by `userId` (see `getCachedAvailability`), so a delete-by-`credentialId` would not clear those rows even if it succeeded.

Cache status reports expired cache rows as a live cache

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups over all CalendarCache rows for a credential without filtering on `expiresAt`. Expired rows are not removed from the table (availability reads just ignore rows with `expiresAt < now` and the row is only replaced on the next upsert), so a user whose Google cache expired weeks ago is shown "Cache Status — Last updated: <old date>" and offered "Delete cached data" even though the cache is effectively dead and the next availability request will miss. Add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` to the `where` clause so the indicator reflects a usable cache. Relatedly, the migration backfills `updatedAt = NOW()` for all pre-existing rows, so after deploy every legacy cache row will display the deploy timestamp as its "last updated" time rather than when it was actually written.

Cache status stays stale after deleting cached data

The deleteCacheMutation only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop; it never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. In the apps-installed calendar page `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` is rendered without an `onChanged` prop, so `onSuccess` is undefined. As a result the dropdown keeps showing "Cache Status / Last updated: …" and the "Delete cached data" entry after the rows were already deleted, until a full page reload. The sibling `disconnectMutation` in the same component does invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (and `viewer.apps.integrations`) in `onSettled`, so the omission looks accidental. Add the same invalidation to the deleteCache mutation.

Cache-status query bypasses the CalendarCache factory and runs on every connectedCalendars call

The handler instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of going through `CalendarCache.init()` (the factory that returns the mock when calendar-cache is disabled / not enabled for the user's teams). Consequence: every `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` request — including onboarding, apps pages, and users/orgs where the calendar-cache feature is off — performs an extra `groupBy` aggregate over CalendarCache, even though the mock exists specifically to avoid that work when the feature is disabled. Scope the query (e.g. only for Google credentials, and via the repository factory) so non-cache users don't pay for it.

Removal of the `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` assertion drops type-checking of the hand-written where clause

`findMany` previously validated the hand-rolled `FindManyArgs` (whose `where` is a narrowed custom shape with e.g. `googleChannelId?: string | null | { not: null }`) against Prisma's generated `SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` via `satisfies`. The new code passes the raw object to `prisma.selectedCalendar.findMany` without that assertion, so a future edit to the custom `FindManyArgs` type can now silently produce a filter Prisma will reject at runtime instead of failing the build. This change is also unrelated to the feature. Restore the `satisfies` assertion (or explain why it had to go) so the type contract keeps being enforced.

Unconditional bulk update of all SelectedCalendar rows on every cache refresh

`fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` now ends with `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, whose only effect is to bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` via the Prisma `@updatedAt` attribute (the data object is empty). This runs on every cache population, which is triggered by the Google push webhook — i.e. potentially many times per minute for busy calendars — and issues an UPDATE touching every SelectedCalendar row of the credential, adding write load and row-lock contention. The PR description itself notes that SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is not shown in the frontend (the UI uses CalendarCache.updatedAt), so this write has no consumer. Remove it, or make it conditional on an actual reader existing.

Unrelated dev:cron change introduces an undeclared `tsx` dependency invoked via npx

Changing `dev:cron` from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts` is unrelated to calendar cache status/actions and means the script depends on `tsx`, which is not declared anywhere in this package's devDependencies. On a clean checkout `npx` will download `tsx` from the network at run time (failing in offline sandboxes/CI) and pins nothing, so different developers may run different versions. Either revert this line or add `tsx` as a devDependency and call it through the package manager (`yarn tsx`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation calls are fire-and-forget

The calls to `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` inside `forEach` are not awaited. For email reminders the actual cancellation work is now the async DB update that sets `cancelled`; if the serverless invocation ends before that update completes, the reminder is never marked and the cron will not cancel the SendGrid email. This is the core regression path for cancelled bookings. Collect these promises and await them before returning. The same fire-and-forget pattern also appears in the reschedule and workflow handlers.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Immediate cancellation does not delete or mark the WorkflowReminder row

When `immediateDelete` is true, the function returns after the SendGrid request without deleting the row or setting `cancelled`. In the reschedule path this leaves the old booking's reminder with `scheduled: true` and the old `referenceId` until the cron's past-date cleanup. It also means a failed SendGrid call is invisible to the cron retry mechanism. The immediate path should delete the row or set a persisted state so failed cancellations can be retried.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
No index supports the new cron cancellation query

The cron now repeatedly queries `WorkflowReminder` with `cancelled = true` and a `scheduledDate` range, but the migration only adds the column. On a large `WorkflowReminder` table this is a full scan every 15 minutes. Add an index, preferably a partial index for cancelled reminders, or document why it is intentionally omitted.

One SendGrid cancellation failure aborts all reminder cancellations

The whole cancellation loop is inside one `try/catch`, and the collected `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` promises are only awaited after the loop. If a single `client.request` fails (invalid/already-cancelled batch, rate limit, etc.), the code jumps to `catch`, skips every remaining `remindersToCancel`, and never executes the delete promises already collected. Those reminders stay in the DB, and the same failing reminder can block every subsequent cron run, so cancelled emails are still sent. Handle each reminder independently and delete/flag it per reminder.

Rescheduled reminders still use immediate SendGrid cancellation

This passes `true` for `immediateDelete`, so rescheduling still POSTs cancellations directly to SendGrid instead of marking the reminder `cancelled` and letting `scheduleEmailReminders` cancel it close to the send time. That reintroduces the pending-cancellation limit that this PR is meant to fix: after enough reschedules, SendGrid cancellations fail and the old reminders are still sent. Because this immediate path also does not set `cancelled`, a failed cancellation has no DB marker for the cron to retry. Use the deferred cancellation path for reschedules, or otherwise persist the cancellation for retry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring-cancellation calendar deletes are no longer awaited before Promise.all

In the `allRemainingBookings` + `credentialId` branch, calendar deletions are collected by pushing into `apiDeletes` from inside `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })`. Because the callback is async and now contains an `await` before the first push, the callback yields immediately and `apiDeletes` is still empty when `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs later in the handler (line 652). The recurring-booking calendar events are therefore never awaited before the request returns, and any rejection from `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent` escapes as an unhandled rejection (which terminates Node by default). The sibling branch just below (lines 476-484) was correctly converted to a `for...of` loop with `await`; this branch needs the same conversion.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Commented-out example points at a non-existent path

The template comment `// example: import("./example"),` references `./example`, but the example app directory in this package is `_example` (the previous comment was `// import * as example from "./_example";`). A developer copying/uncommenting this template will get a module-resolution error. It should read `// example: import("./_example"),`.

`!calendar` early return skips cleanIntegrationKeys and sends raw credentials to the client

In `getConnectedCalendars`, when `getCalendar` returns null the function returns `{ integration, credentialId }` with the raw `integration` object. `integration` comes from `getApps(credentials)`, i.e. the app object that carries `credentials` (including the user's OAuth `key`) and `credential` — see how this same object is used at lines 27-30 of this file. The other two return paths correctly call `cleanIntegrationKeys(integration)` precisely to avoid leaking credentials to the client (there is even a comment "Don't leak credentials to the client"), but this path returns them verbatim, so any credential whose calendar implementation is missing/keyless will ship the user's secrets to the browser via the connectedCalendars endpoint. Pre-existing, but it is inside the function this PR modifies; the return should also be `{ integration: cleanIntegrationKeys(integration), credentialId }`.

async forEach makes reschedule cancellations fire-and-forget and defeats the try/catch

Same defect as in the vital reschedule file: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` returns immediately because `forEach` ignores the promises returned by the async callback. The outer `try/catch` around the loop therefore no longer catches errors from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`, those errors surface as unhandled rejections, and the function resolves before the calendar/video deletions complete, so the old event may remain on the user's calendar after a reschedule. Replace the `forEach` with `await Promise.all(...map(...))` or a `for...of` loop with `await`.

getCalendar is called for non-calendar-variant apps and its promise is dropped

In `getCalendarCredentials`, `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` runs for every credential, but the result is only kept when `app.variant === "calendar"`; for other variants the promise is created and discarded. Now that `getCalendar` is async this is (a) a wasted dynamic `import()` of the app's calendar module for every non-calendar-variant app on every call, and (b) a floating promise whose rejection (e.g. the lazy import failing, or `calendarType.split` on a malformed credential type) becomes an unhandled rejection. Move the `getCalendar` call inside the `app.variant === "calendar"` branch.

requestReschedule deletions are started asynchronously and never awaited

The `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` block in the `requestReschedule` mutation discards every returned promise. Before this change the callback was synchronous, so the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls were at least initiated synchronously in the handler; now they are deferred until after the surrounding synchronous code runs (i.e. potentially after `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` and after the mutation returns), and no failure from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` is observed or logged (unhandled rejection, fatal by default in Node). The old calendar/video event for the rescheduled booking can silently survive. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` or a `for...of` loop with `await`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end uses the slot start minute instead of the slot end minute

`const end` is computed from `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`, exactly the same value as `start`. For a 60-minute slot starting 12:00 when a fixed host's working hours end at 12:30, `end > workingHour.endTime` is `720 > 750`, so the slot is not rejected even though it ends at 13:00. This lets round-robin fixed hosts be booked outside their working hours. Compute `end` from `slotEndTime` (or compare timestamps) and reject slots whose end exceeds the working-hour end.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length date override comparison uses object identity

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two distinct Dayjs object references, so it is always false. If a date override with equal start and end is used to represent an unavailable day, that case is never detected; only slots before the override are rejected, and the slot at the override start can be treated as available. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare timestamps.

false_positives.candidate:
Active date overrides are filtered by wall-clock date, not actual UTC/invitee date

`activeOverrides` compares `dayjs.utc(override.start)`—where `override.start` is the organizer's wall-clock date/time stored as UTC—against the invitee day boundaries. The new conversion below explicitly treats it as wall time by subtracting the organizer offset, but this filter does not. For example, with an organizer in UTC+14, an override at local D 01:00 is stored as D 01:00Z but actually occurs at D-1 11:00Z; when an invitee in UTC views day D-1, the stored value is outside that invitee day, so the override is ignored and normal working hours are used. Convert the override to actual UTC (or to the invitee timezone) before deciding whether it belongs to the invitee day.

Date override date comparison mixes server-local and UTC dates

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` formats in the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime` is a `.utc()` Dayjs. On self-hosted servers not running in UTC, the shifted override date is compared to a UTC slot date, so date overrides can be missed or matched to the wrong day. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` (and end) for the date/range calculations so both sides use UTC.

Date override short-circuits the busy-time check

When a slot falls inside a user's date override, `dateOverrideExist` is true and `checkIfIsAvailable` returns true before reaching the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom. A date override replaces working hours, not existing bookings/calendar busy time, so a fixed host with an override 10:00-14:00 and an existing booking 11:00-12:00 will still make the 11:00 round-robin slot pass. That can lead to double booking the fixed host. Only bypass the normal working-hours check for an override; the busy check must still run.

No test covers the fixed-host round-robin date override behavior or the new availability branches

The only added test changes the invitee timezone for a personal event. It does not exercise the PR's main claim: a round-robin event with a fixed host whose date override should constrain available slots. There are also no tests for a fixed host with busy time inside an override, slots partially overlapping an override, or split working hours. These missing cases would have caught the early return that skips busy checks and the working-hours containment bugs.

Working-hours check tests only the first matching day and ignores days with no hours

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true as soon as it sees the first entry whose `days` includes the slot's UTC day and the slot is outside that one interval. With split availability (09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00), a 13:30 slot is outside the first interval, so the host is marked unavailable even though the second interval contains it. Conversely, if no working-hour entry includes the slot's day, `find` returns undefined and the function falls through to the busy check, treating the fixed host as available on a day they do not work. The check should test whether the slot is inside any matching interval and reject it when no interval matches.

An attacker who starts an install with their own installation_id while the victim completes OAuth as a different GitHub account is not caught, which defeats the stated security fix. `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the module is imported, not when each instance is created. Dataclasses only reject clearly mutable defaults (list/dict/set), so a datetime default is accepted, but every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit `queued` — including every call to `from_integration()` — will share the exact same timestamp equal to the process/module import time. The field therefore never records when an assignment was actually queued, so any future staleness, debounce, or ordering logic reading it will be wrong. true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Error-handling test is timing-dependent and asserts the wrong outcome

The test makes the first result processor call raise and the second succeed, then asserts that no offset was committed for the partition. In the implementation, OrderedQueueWorker completes the offset in its finally block even when processing raised, so both offsets become complete and the background commit loop should eventually commit the partition. The test only sleeps 0.2 seconds after processing finishes, while the commit loop wakes every 1 second, so it usually passes before the commit happens and will flake when setup or processing takes slightly longer. It therefore does not reliably verify the intended error semantics; it should either assert the actual expected commit behavior or the production code should keep failed offsets outstanding.

Failed work items are still marked offset-complete

OrderedQueueWorker.run has a finally block that unconditionally calls complete_offset(), including when result_processor raises and the exception is merely logged by the generic except. Once the offset is removed from outstanding, OffsetTracker will treat it as processed and the commit loop will commit past it, so the failed result is acknowledged to Kafka and will not be retried. This also contradicts the strategy docstring that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Failed offsets should remain outstanding or be sent through an explicit retry/DLQ path, not completed as if the work succeeded.

Queues are unbounded, so submit applies no backpressure

Each queue is created as queue.Queue() with the default maxsize of 0, which is infinite, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always enqueues immediately. poll() only emits a metric and never blocks or rejects based on queue depth. A single slow subscription can therefore grow its queue without bound while the consumer keeps polling and decoding messages, increasing memory use and accumulating an uncommitted Kafka backlog until the process is OOM-killed. This contradicts the class docstring's claim of natural backpressure; use a bounded queue and block or apply another explicit backpressure policy.

Shared queue pool is permanently shut down and then reused

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and reuses it for every create_with_partitions call, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down all queues and workers. On a Kafka rebalance Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again with the same factory, so the new strategy gets an already shut-down pool. With queue shutdown available, put() raises ShutDown, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches it, marks the offset complete, and the background commit loop commits it, silently dropping messages. Without queue shutdown, the workers are gone and the offsets may never complete. The pool should be owned by the strategy or recreated for each strategy instance, not shut down from close() while the factory still holds it.

Shutdown stops workers before draining queued items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False), but each worker checks while not self.shutdown before calling get() again. A worker that finishes its current item therefore exits immediately, leaving any remaining items in the queue even though immediate=False was requested. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close also joins the commit thread before shutting the pool down, so work processed during shutdown is not committed. The net effect is that graceful shutdown abandons buffered results and relies on Kafka redelivery, contrary to the graceful-drain behavior implied by the code and docstrings.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs

FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown. Both APIs were added in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs, q.shutdown raises AttributeError, which the broad except swallows, so blocked worker threads are never woken. Each worker.join(timeout=5.0) then waits the full 5 seconds, meaning shutdown takes 100 seconds with the default 20 queues and leaves the threads alive. Separately, if a worker ever hits the except queue.ShutDown clause, evaluating the missing attribute raises another AttributeError and kills that worker. Use an Event/sentinel-based shutdown compatible with the supported Python version.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache has no invalidation and can override fresh allows

`Check` returns immediately from `permDenialCache` before consulting `permCache` or the DB, and `permDenialCache.Set` is called after any DB-backed denial. Nothing invalidates these entries when permissions are granted or when a new dashboard/folder is created. A denied check (for example, before a just-created dashboard's creator permission is visible, or before an admin grants a role) therefore keeps returning Allowed=false for the 30s shortCacheTTL even after the DB grants access. This also means a stale denial overrides a later-refreshed allow in permCache, which directly undermines the PR goal of making newly created resources accessible. Deny entries need invalidation, or must not override a fresh cached allow, and likely deserve a shorter TTL.

Denial cache key uses raw subject ID and omits identity type

The denial-cache key is built from the raw subject ID (`checkReq.UserUID`) before `GetUserIdentifiers` resolves the canonical UID, and it does not include the identity type. The permission cache, in contrast, is keyed by the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID`. The same user can therefore have separate denial entries for `user:123` and `user:<uid>`, so the denial cache is bypassed when the subject form changes. Conversely, identities such as `user:123`, `service-account:123`, or `anonymous:123` share the same denial key even though they can represent different principals; a denial for one can be served for another until TTL expiry. Resolve the subject first and include the identity type plus canonical UID, and escape or hash the key components.

No test that Check populates the denial cache

The new test for the denial cache only seeds `permDenialCache` manually; it does not exercise a normal denied `Check` and verify that the denial entry is written. A bug in the key used by `s.permDenialCache.Set` or a missed Set call would pass the current tests. Add a case with a denying fake permission store that asserts a second identical `Check` is served from the denial cache without incrementing `store.calls` and still returns Allowed=false.
