Add `key={key}` to the `GrafanaRuleListItem` branch.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is shown in the list view but clicking it does nothing because the drawer requires a rulerRule

AlertRuleMenu now decides whether to show "Silence notifications" from the prom-rule abilities, so in the new prom-only list view (GrafanaGroupLoader / FilterView) the item is rendered when the user has silence permission. However the drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`, where `rule` is the optional rulerRule prop. In the list view that prop is undefined, so `handleSilence` sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true but no drawer ever mounts and the click is a no-op. Either the menu item must be hidden when no ruler rule is available, or `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` must be able to build the silence from the prom rule. The GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts the Silence item is present but never clicks it, so this dead action is not caught.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment and variable name still describe ruler-rule preloading that was removed

The ruler prefetch (`alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)`) was removed from `useGrafanaGroupsGenerator`, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX..." and the local variable is still called `cacheAndRulerPreload`. Both now describe behaviour that no longer exists and will mislead future readers into thinking ruler rules are still fetched here; update the comment and rename the variable (e.g. `cachePreload`).

Delete (and Pause) menu items are gated on rulerRule, so they disappear from the prom-only list view

AlertRuleMenu still renders the Delete item only when `canDelete && rulerRule`, and the Pause item only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123). This PR changes the alert list view so that `GrafanaRuleListItem` -> `RuleActionsButtons.V2` passes only `promRule` and never a ruler rule (the ruler API calls were removed on purpose). `canDelete`/`canPause` are now correctly computed from `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, but the extra `rulerRule` guard means they are never used: Delete is no longer available anywhere in the alert list view even for users with delete permission, whereas before this PR the ruler rule was fetched and the action was shown. `handleDelete` only needs the identifier (`RuleActionsButtons.V2` passes `() => showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)`), so requiring a ruler rule is unnecessary. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test actually grants AlertingRuleDelete and asserts exactly 4 menu items (no Delete), codifying the regression.

Federation detection is lost: useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to a hook that hardcodes isFederated = false

Before this change `useAllAlertRuleAbilities(rule: CombinedRule)` computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which made Update/Delete/Pause/Restore unsupported for federated Mimir/Metrics Enterprise rule groups (they are immutable from Grafana). It now just delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, where `const isFederated = false;` is hardcoded (with a TODO). As a result `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAlertRuleAbilities` (still used by the rules table and other rule-based components) will report these actions as supported for federated groups, showing Edit/Delete/Pause controls that the backend rejects. The `CombinedRule` still carries `rule.group`, so federation can still be detected; the delegation loses it.

No test covers Delete/Silence in the prom-only list; the new test asserts the broken behaviour

The new "should render correct menu actions" test grants AlertingRuleDelete and per-folder delete permissions but then asserts `expect(menuItems.length).toBe(4)` (Silence, Copy link, Duplicate, Export), i.e. it locks in the fact that Delete is missing from the prom-only list view; it also never clicks Silence even though the drawer cannot render without a ruler rule. Additionally, `RulesTable.test.tsx` mocks `useRulerRuleAbilities`/`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` wholesale, so the `(ruler ability) || (prom ability)` combination logic is never exercised with real hooks, and the newly added `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`/`useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` have no direct unit tests for provisioned rules or folder-loading states. Add at least one test that grants delete/silence and verifies the actions actually work in the prom-only list.

Prom-rule abilities restrict ModifyExport and Pause to alerting rules, dropping them for Grafana recording rules

`useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` sets `[AlertRuleAction.ModifyExport]: [isAlertingRule, exportAllowed]` and gates `Pause`/`Restore`/`DeletePermanently` on `isAlertingRule`, i.e. `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule`. The ruler-based equivalent gates these on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule`, which is also true for Grafana-managed recording rules, and Grafana recording rules can be paused and exported. In the new list view (where only the prom-based ability is available) the Export item therefore disappears for Grafana recording rules, and Pause would be reported unsupported (currently masked by the separate `rulerRule` guard in AlertRuleMenu). Use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule` for the actions that apply to recording rules, and keep `alertingRule` only for Silence.

Rule view links no longer carry returnTo, losing back-navigation from the rule viewer

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader.GrafanaRuleListItem` built the view link with `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })`, where `returnTo = createReturnTo()`. The new component uses `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` without the `returnTo` query parameter. The rule view page uses `returnTo` to render its back link to the page the user came from (e.g. a filtered/paginated list); without it users are sent to the default destination instead of the list they navigated from. Restore the `returnTo` parameter (the AlertRuleMenu export item still relies on this mechanism).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Empty-after-interpolation targets are not filtered out

The expr filter runs before applyTemplateVariables. A query whose whole expression is a variable (for example $query) passes the filter even when interpolation produces an empty string, so runSplitQuery can execute datasource.runQuery with an empty expr. On the shard path the same ordering in shardQuerySplitting.ts:50 lets such an empty target reach groupTargetsByQueryType; when it is later passed to runSplitQuery it is filtered out and can leave the grouped request list empty, causing the Math.max/undefined access in runSplitGroupedQueries to fail. Filter again after mapping, as the old shard code did, or map before filtering.

Interpolation before querySupportsSplitting bypasses the $__range guard

runSplitQuery applies template variables to every target at line 299 before partitioning with querySupportsSplitting. applyTemplateVariables resolves $__range against the full request range and removes the token, so isQueryWithRangeVariable in querySupportsSplitting no longer detects these queries and they are split. Each time chunk then keeps the full-range duration (for example rate({...}[$__range]) becomes rate({...}[2d]) in every 1-day chunk), producing overlapping or double-counted results; these queries were previously left unsplit specifically to avoid that. Check the range variable on the raw expression before interpolation, or carry the original expression through to the guard.

Targets are interpolated twice on the shard-splitting path

runShardSplitQuery maps every target through applyTemplateVariables here, and then each shard group calls runSplitQuery, which applies applyTemplateVariables again (querySplitting.ts:299). Template interpolation is not idempotent: a literal escaped dollar such as $$__range becomes $__range after the first pass and is substituted on the second, and variable values containing $ are re-expanded. The new test expecting 5 applyTemplateVariables calls (one initial plus four shard groups) asserts this double interpolation. Pass already-interpolated targets to the nested splitting call or add an option to skip interpolation there.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID dropped from 'Plugin Request Completed' logs

The diff removes the explicit trace correlation from logRequest (`traceID := tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` plus its append to logParams) and now relies on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` to populate the log record. However, the contextual attributes installed by the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext` are only endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname; they do not include a trace ID. Unless `ConcreteLogger.FromContext` independently extracts the trace ID from the OTel span, the 'Plugin Request Completed' lines lose their traceID field, breaking the log/trace correlation these logs had before this PR. Verify traceID still appears and add a test that asserts it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards the injected logger, making FromContext-based logs unassertable

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns a brand-new `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver (or a logger sharing the same `Logs`). `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now emits its log via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. When a `TestLogger` is injected into the middleware, the Info call is recorded on the throwaway logger returned by FromContext, so `testLogger.InfoLogs.Calls` stays 0. Any test (existing or newly added) that asserts the middleware logged a request cannot observe it, and the moved contextual-logging behavior is effectively untestable with this fake. `FromContext` should return a logger that records into the same `Logs` as the receiver.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
FromContext silently drops contextual attributes on type-assertion failure

`grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` type-asserts the value returned by `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` to `*log.ConcreteLogger`; if the infra logger ever returns a different concrete type (for example a future wrapper around the concrete logger), the assertion fails and the method returns `d.New()`, a plain logger without the contextual attributes. Because this wrapper is now the only path by which pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname reach the backend request logs, a failed assertion would silently drop every one of those fields. Wrap the returned `log.Logger` directly (assign it to an interface-typed field) rather than asserting a concrete type, or at minimum surface the failure.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and moved log fields are untested

Responsibility for endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname was moved out of LoggerMiddleware's explicit logParams into the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and the middleware ordering in pluginsintegration.go was changed (Metrics -> ContextualLogger -> Logger). There is no test for the new middleware and no test asserting those fields still appear in 'Plugin Request Completed' logs after the move. A regression in the middleware ordering or in `log.WithContextualAttributes`/`FromContext` would silently drop all these fields with no failing test. Add coverage that exercises the full chain and asserts the emitted log record contains the expected fields.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert device limiting is not atomic and allows exceeding the limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` first calls `CountDevices` and, only if `count < deviceLimit`, runs a separate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. The count and the insert are independent statements with no transaction, lock, or conditional insert. Under concurrency, two first-time requests from different new devices can both observe `count < deviceLimit` and both insert, so the number of tracked devices exceeds the configured `device_limit`. Because tagging now runs synchronously on the authentication path, this race is easy to trigger with parallel browser sessions. The limit needs to be enforced atomically (e.g. a single conditional insert that also checks the count, or serialization via a lock), otherwise the configured limit is only advisory.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero affected rows is conflated with 'device limit reached', producing false limit errors

`updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever the UPDATE affects 0 rows. Zero rows means 'no row matched the WHERE clause', which also happens for legitimate cases that are not a limit breach: (a) a device that already exists but has not been updated in the last 30 days is excluded from `CountDevices` but its old `updated_at` is outside the `BETWEEN now-30d AND now+1m` window, so it can never be re-activated while the store is at capacity and is incorrectly reported as 'limit reached'; (b) on MySQL, `RowsAffected` reports *changed* rows, so if client_ip/user_agent are unchanged and `updated_at` is truncated to the same value the row matches but 0 rows are reported, yielding a false limit error. The error means 'could not refresh this device', not specifically 'limit reached', so callers and users are misled.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed because the local cache is populated before the DB write succeeds

In `tagDeviceUI` the device's cache key is written (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`, line 87) *before* `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs (line 93). With the new `return err` at line 147, `ErrDeviceLimitReached` now propagates through `TagDevice` into `Anonymous.Authenticate`, which returns `nil, err` and fails the request. But the cache entry set on line 87 is never removed on failure. On the next request from the same device (within the 29-minute cache TTL) `tagDeviceUI` hits the cache and returns nil without touching the DB, so `Authenticate` succeeds. Net effect: the limit only fails the very first request per device per 29 minutes and is trivially bypassed by reloading the page; furthermore, an expired device that `updateDevice` refuses to update still reaches the app on retry without ever being recorded, so it never counts toward the limit. The cache must only be populated after a successful write, and `ErrDeviceLimitReached` must not be masked by a cache hit.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous authentication now performs a synchronous DB call using the request context

The previous implementation tagged the device in a detached goroutine (`context.Background()` with a 2-minute timeout and a panic recovery). The new code calls `TagDevice(ctx, ...)` inline in `Authenticate` with the inbound request context. This adds a DB round-trip (a count plus an upsert) to the anonymous auth path, makes tagging fail if the inbound request context is cancelled or short-lived, and removes the panic recovery so a panic in tagging now propagates into authentication. If synchronous enforcement is required, at least keep panic recovery and use a bounded/detached context rather than the raw request context.

Device-limit rejection is returned as a raw error and surfaces as an internal server error

When `TagDevice` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, `Authenticate` returns `nil, err`. That error is a plain `fmt.Errorf` with no HTTP status mapping, so the authn middleware has no way to translate it and the client over the limit receives an internal-server (500) response rather than a defined status such as 403/429. The raw 'device limit reached' string is also exposed. A dedicated typed/status error should be returned so the caller can respond with a meaningful status and message.

Frontend type allows undefined but backend always sends 0

`anonymousDeviceLimit` is typed `number | undefined` here (and defaulted to `undefined` in `GrafanaBootConfig`), but the backend DTO field `FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` has no `omitempty`, so the JSON always contains the key and it is `0` when the feature is unlimited. Consumers that test `=== undefined` to detect 'not configured' will never match; they must treat `0` (or `<= 0`) as unlimited. Either make the DTO field a pointer with `omitempty` or type it as `number` and document that 0 means unlimited.

No test covers the primary enforcement path or the cache-driven bypass

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a brand-new device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached` a single time; it does not assert that an existing, in-window device can still be successfully re-tagged while the store is at capacity (the main reason for `updateDevice`), nor does it exercise the end-to-end rejection through `Anonymous.Authenticate`. `impl_test.go` only runs with the default limit of 0. As a result, neither the retry-after-error bypass (cache set before write, see impl.go) nor the false-limit cases in `updateDevice` are caught by the tests.

Provider signature changed without regenerating wire_gen.go

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` changed its dependency from `anonstore.AnonStore` to `db.DB`, and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an extra `int64` argument for which there is no wire provider. `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` is registered through Grafana's wire dependency graph, and `pkg/server/wire_gen.go` is generated but committed. That file is not part of this PR, so it still calls the old signature and the build will fail to compile unless `wire_gen.go` (and any wire set referencing `ProvideAnonDBStore`) is regenerated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup progress logged at Error level with full ID list

All the new progress/success log statements use `r.log.Error` instead of `r.log.Debug`/`Info`: 'Annotations to clean by time' (line 534), 'cleaned annotations by time' (537), 'Annotations to clean by count' (554), 'cleaned annotations by count' (557), 'Tags to clean' (576) and 'cleaned tags' (579). These fire on every successful batch of every cleanup cycle (and the cycle now runs every minute), so normal operation will continuously emit error-level logs that trigger alerting/noise. Worse, each call logs the entire `ids` slice, which can contain up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` IDs (the new test uses a batch size of 32767), producing enormous log lines and substantial log-storage pressure. These should log at Debug level and log only `len(ids)`, not the full slice. This looks like debugging output left in by accident.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The cleanup job interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, making the entire cleanup suite (temporary files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) run ten times more often. This change is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (avoiding annotation cleanup deadlocks), is not mentioned in the description, and does the opposite of helping: running the annotation deletes far more frequently increases write/lock contention on the annotation tables rather than reducing it. It should be reverted (or, if intentional, justified and validated separately), otherwise production DB load and contention increase by an order of magnitude.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete stores the wrong logger in the context

Delete does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` (line 97) using the base logger instead of the per-request `log` that carries name/kind/method fields, unlike Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection. Downstream storage.Delete error logs therefore lose the request-scoped fields, making them harder to correlate. Use `log` here as the other methods do.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Storage failures are recorded into the legacy metric and legacy writes into the storage metric

On the Storage error-return path, Create calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ..., startStorage)` (line 45) and Update does the same (line 129) instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Conversely the DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records its result via `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` (line 166). As a result storage errors/latency are attributed to the legacy store and legacy-write errors to unified storage, making the per-backend error and latency metrics/dashboards wrong. Use `recordStorageDuration` for the Storage call and `recordLegacyDuration` for the Legacy call on every path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name as the resource `kind` metric label

In the Delete success path the storage duration is recorded with the object name passed as the `kind` argument: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` (line 106). The third parameter of `recordStorageDuration` is the resource kind, so every deleted object adds a new label value, exploding metric cardinality and mislabeling the series. It should pass `options.Kind`, as all the other calls do.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes use the request context and get cancelled when the handler returns

Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection launch the legacy write in a goroutine that derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51 `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`; same pattern at lines 110, 135, 163). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which is immediately after the goroutine is spawned. The legacy backup write is therefore usually aborted with `context canceled` before it runs, so mode 3's safety-net write to legacy silently does not happen and the legacy-store metrics record spurious failures/timeouts. Detach the goroutine's context from the request (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` to keep values, or a fresh background context) so it survives handler completion.

Async legacy-write failures are never logged

The legacy-write goroutines capture the legacy error but only feed it to a metric and never log it (e.g. Create lines 55-56 `_, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...)` then `d.recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`; same in Delete, Update and DeleteCollection). The previous synchronous implementation logged these failures with `log.Error`. Now a failed legacy backup write is invisible in logs, so operators cannot diagnose why the legacy copy is missing. Log the error inside the goroutine (using a logger not tied to the soon-to-be-cancelled request context).

Unit tests never assert the legacy (async) write and don't wait for the goroutine

TestMode3_Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection set up expectations on the legacy store but never verify the legacy write occurred (no `AssertCalled`/`AssertExpectations`) and never wait for the goroutine. Because the legacy write is fire-and-forget, the tests pass even if the legacy path never runs, so the defining behavior of mode 3 (dual write to legacy) is not actually tested. The goroutine can also still be invoking the shared `*mock.Mock` and metrics registry after the subtest returns, which can cause data races/flaky failures under `-race`. Wait for the goroutine (channel/WaitGroup) and assert the legacy call was made.

mode 3 integration tests race the asynchronous legacy write

The new mode 3 subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which after writing through the k8s API immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoint and asserts the same UIDs are present (line 529), and `getFromBothAPIs` does a legacy GET right after each k8s write. Mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, so these assertions race the background write and can fail intermittently (and will fail deterministically while the request-context cancellation bug exists). The test needs to wait/poll for the legacy copy to appear (e.g. `require.Eventually`) rather than asserting immediately.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check after acquiring the write lock causes duplicate manifest loads

After reading the cache under RLock and releasing it, the function takes the write lock at line 48 but never re-checks whether the cache was filled by another goroutine in the meantime. On a cold start (or any time the cache is nil in non-Dev env), N concurrent callers all observe `ret == nil` at line 45 and then queue on the write lock; each one runs the full read path (lines 51-67, including reading and JSON-decoding assets-manifest.json, and its error paths) and overwrites the cache. The final value is still correct, but N concurrent requests produce N serialized disk reads/parses instead of one, and every queued request is blocked for the whole duration of the I/O. This is the classic double-checked-locking omission: re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and return the cached value early.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No test exercises concurrent GetWebAssets calls

The PR's sole purpose is to eliminate a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache, but it adds no test. A race like this is only reliably caught by running concurrent GetWebAssets invocations under `go test -race`; without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce an unguarded read/write without CI noticing. Add a test that spawns multiple goroutines calling GetWebAssets against a temp manifest and asserts they all get a non-nil, consistent result (run with -race).

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false and ignores the feature flag

enableSqlExpressions always returns false: if the flag is enabled, the !flag expression yields false so the if is skipped and it returns false; if the flag is disabled, the if is entered and it also returns false. The feature flag FlagSqlExpressions therefore has no effect, and SQL expressions are rejected even for operators who explicitly enable the flag. The enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(...) computation plus the branch is dead code, and the function name and flag read imply the flag is supposed to control availability. If the flag is intended to keep an opt-in path (the PR description says the flag still exists), the final statement should return true; otherwise it should simply return false and drop the flag read so it is not mistaken for a working security control. As written it is a latent trap: restoring the DB implementation later would still leave the feature permanently disabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Behavior change disabling SQL expressions is untested; existing SQL tests likely break

The change makes TablesList, NewSQLCommand, SQLCommand.Execute and the QueryTypeSQL branch of ReadQuery always fail, but no test files are included in the diff. The new pkg/expr/sql/db.go stubs return errors from RunCommands/QueryFramesInto, so existing tests that call TablesList/NewSQLCommand (for example pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go and pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go) or that exercise the SQL branch of ReadQuery will now fail with 'not implemented'. There is also no new regression test asserting that a SQL expression is rejected. Add or update tests for the reader rejecting QueryTypeSQL and for the stub behavior so the security fix is covered and CI stays green.

false_positives.candidate:
Misleading error message: 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'

When SQL is disabled the reader returns fmt.Errorf('sqlExpressions is not implemented'). The feature is not unimplemented - it is deliberately disabled for security - so this user-facing error is misleading. Likewise the new stubs in pkg/expr/sql/db.go make TablesList fail, and NewSQLCommand maps that failure to 'error reading SQL command', hiding the real reason a query is rejected. Use a message that states SQL expressions are disabled/unsupported.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No longer serialized: concurrent BuildIndex for the same key races and leaks the losing index

Removing the function-wide cacheMu means two BuildIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource can now run simultaneously (e.g. two Search RPCs that both miss the cache for a key, which is exactly the case the TODO in getOrCreateIndex warns about). Both build a full index, both assign to b.cache[key], and the index that loses the assignment is never closed, leaking file handles/disk (bleve file-backed indexes) or memory. The old coarse lock at least serialized the two builds; if per-key concurrency is now intended, add per-key single-flight and close the replaced index before overwriting the cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu.RLock, while BuildIndex now writes to the same map from multiple concurrent goroutines (the coarse lock that previously serialized all builds is gone and only the final `b.cache[key] = idx` is locked). A concurrent TotalDocs call — e.g. from a metric collector or while the index for another namespace is being built — can trigger the unrecoverable runtime error "concurrent map iteration and map write" and crash the process. Guard the loop with RLock.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed inside search index init errgroup

In searchSupport.init, every goroutine launched into the errgroup does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and assigns its result to the outer `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`; return err). With WorkerThreads > 1 (group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)) these are unsynchronized writes to the same variables from multiple goroutines: a data race that can make group.Wait() return a nil or unrelated error and corrupt the reported count of indexed namespaces. This is now on the startup path, where a returned error makes the whole server fail to start, so use per-goroutine locals and an atomic counter.

Eager Init turns any search/DB failure into a fatal Grafana startup failure

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns an error if it fails. Init runs the lifecycle hook (the SQL backend opens the resource DB) and searchSupport.init, which synchronously rebuilds every search index with no timeout. Any failure — a temporarily unreachable resource DB, a single namespace failing to build, a bleve error — now aborts construction of the ResourceServer and therefore Grafana startup, whereas before the server was constructed and only the affected requests failed. Because Init is guarded by sync.Once and the constructed server is discarded on error, there is no retry path: a transient failure requires a process restart. Consider making init failure non-fatal (mark unhealthy instead of failing construction) or bounding the index build with a timeout.

Init error path leaks the cancel func, the DB pool, and the search watcher goroutine

When s.Init(ctx) returns an error, NewResourceServer returns nil but never calls the cancel func created at line 229 and never invokes s.lifecycle.Stop (which is what calls backend.Stop and closes the resource DB pool opened by lifecycle.Init). Additionally, searchSupport.init has already started its WatchWriteEvents consumer goroutine with context.Background() (search.go:202), which polls the SQL backend every 100ms and is not tied to the server context, so it keeps running forever against a server that was never returned. Clean up (cancel()/Stop) before returning nil, err.

Postgres variant of the storage-server integration test is skipped, hiding a startup regression

This test validates that the storage-server target starts and serves the instrumentation endpoint. Skipping it for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres (with a TODO saying it only fails in Drone) removes the only coverage for the storage target against Postgres exactly in the PR that makes initialization eager and therefore makes construction depend on the resource_api DB being reachable. If the test now fails because NewResourceServer can no longer be constructed with that configuration, that is the regression the PR should address rather than skip.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

At teardown this invokes remove() on a non-existent provider (typically a 404/WebApplicationException, which can fail the test teardown), and none of the 20+ `idp-alias-*` providers the test creates are ever deleted. They leak into the realm and can break later tests in the class that assume a clean IDP set or re-create the same aliases. It should use `idpRep.getAlias()` (or `"idp-alias-" + i`) in the cleanup.

Login-cache invalidation on update computes the 'original' state from an org-aware wrapper, so disabling an IDP of a disabled org is not invalidated

In update(), `original` is obtained via `getById(model.getInternalId())`, which returns `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...)` whose `isEnabled()` returns false when the linked organization is disabled (see line 141 and 436-443). However the login cache is populated from the raw `enabled` column (the delegate's `getForLogin`/`getAllStream` ignores organization enabled state), so an IDP linked to a currently-disabled organization is present in the cached login list while `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` evaluates to false for it. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` then hits the `!predicate(original) && !predicate(updated)` early-return at line 405 and skips invalidation when that IDP's own `enabled` flag is set to false, leaving a now-disabled IDP in the cached list returned by `getForLogin` (violating the method contract that it returns login-eligible IDPs). create()/remove() use raw (un-wrapped) models, so update() is inconsistent with them. The original state used for the login predicate should be the raw model (e.g. from `idpDelegate`), not the organization-aware wrapper.

The test removes `idp-alias-1`, which was created disabled (`enabled = (i % 2) == 0`), so it only exercises the negative branch of the newly added remove() logic (`registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` where the provider is not login-eligible and therefore must not invalidate the caches). No test removes an enabled, public IDP and asserts that the login caches ARE cleared, so the positive invalidation path added to remove() is untested; a regression there (or an NPE/pruning of the newly introduced `storedIdp` lookup) would go unnoticed.

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type, which is normally SUN, not BouncyCastle. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() was added to the public CryptoProvider SPI as an abstract method. Third-party implementations compiled against the previous version do not implement it, so ServiceLoader can instantiate them but CryptoIntegration.detectProvider's call to CryptoProvider::order throws AbstractMethodError, breaking all crypto initialization. Make order() a default method with a defined fallback order, or otherwise preserve compatibility with legacy providers.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384/ES512 tests do not use P-384/P-521 keys

The test class creates one default EC key pair (typically P-256) and reuses it for testES256, testES384 and testES512. The ES384 and ES512 cases therefore only exercise padding a P-256 signature to 96/132 bytes; they never exercise real P-384/P-521-sized r and s values, nor verify the produced ASN.1 DER against the key. A regression that mishandles full-size ES384/ES512 signatures could pass. Generate the matching curve key pair per algorithm, or use fixed vectors and verify the result.

detectProvider now sorts all discovered providers by order and returns the first, only logging the rest at debug. All existing built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) still return order 200, so when more than one is visible there is no unique winner and selection depends on ServiceLoader/JAR order. In a FIPS deployment this can silently select the non-FIPS provider, or at minimum construct/register both providers' global security state before ignoring one, defeating FIPS compliance. The previous code failed fast on multiple providers. The selection should fail on a tie for the highest order or the built-in providers need distinct orders.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client removal event breaks when V2 permissions are enabled

The new listener guard checks only Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, but management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If both features are enabled, ClientRemovedEvent reaches clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...), which ClientPermissionsV2 overrides to throw UnsupportedOperationException, so deleting a client can fail. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is skipped entirely and the deleted client's V2 permission resource/policies are never cleaned up. The guard needs to handle V2 explicitly (skip it or provide a no-op/cleanup implementation).

true_positives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The third argument to ResourceStore.findByName is the resource owner. V2 per-resource authorization resources are created with owner resourceServer.getClientId() in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (line 104), but this lookup passes server.getId(), which is the Keycloak client UUID (see AdminPermissionsSchema.isAdminPermissionClient). The lookup therefore misses the per-client resource and falls back to the 'Clients' all-resource, ignoring per-client grants/denials: per-client MANAGE/VIEW grants do not work, and a per-client negative permission can be bypassed by a global allow. The same owner mistake exists at line 244 for the 'Clients' all-resource lookup. Use the same owner as creation or the two-argument findByName.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the new Clients scopes/resources

Realms that already had the V2 admin-permissions client before this change will therefore never get the newly added Clients scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite) or the 'Clients' all-resource. Creating a client permission later fails in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource when those new scopes are not found ('No scopes found.'), and ClientPermissionsV2 can then fall back to a null resource and NPE in policyStore.findByResource. false_negatives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

Token exchange invokes this evaluator, so token exchange requests will return a 500 instead of a normal authorization decision. Implement the check or return a denial; the other overrides that throw UnsupportedOperationException are similarly reachable from management endpoints and should not leak 500s.

getResourceName does not handle the new Clients resource type

getResourceName only special-cases USERS. For the newly added CLIENTS resource type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is not set for resources created by getOrCreateResource. Client permission resources will therefore be shown with null/empty names instead of the client id or 'All clients' in APIs/UI. Add a CLIENTS branch analogous to the USERS branch.

requireView/requireViewClientScopes Javadoc incorrectly describes return values

The Javadoc for requireView() says 'Returns true if canView() returns true', but the method is void and throws ForbiddenException. The same wrong text is repeated for requireViewClientScopes() at line 101. Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Documented exit codes are not asserted in the CLI tests

The new feature-disabled test only asserts the error text, not that the command exits with the newly documented code 4. Likewise, `testWrongVersions` only checks the incompatibility message and does not assert that an incompatible result exits with the newly documented code 3. true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() accepts VIEW scope, so a view-only admin can create groups

canManage() (no group argument) returns true when the caller has any of VIEW or MANAGE on the all-groups resource, while canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires MANAGE. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls auth.groups().requireManage(), which uses this method, so an admin granted only VIEW on all groups can create top-level groups. The javadoc added to GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() repeats the VIEW-or-MANAGE rule, so both the implementation and the documentation should be corrected to require MANAGE.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource IDs instead of group IDs

The method collects groupResource.getId() (the generated authorization-resource UUID) into the returned set, and line 122 passes that same value to hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...). But group resources are created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource with name = the group id while the resource id is a generated UUID, and hasPermission resolves its argument via resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId). For a per-group resource the lookup therefore misses and evaluation falls back to the all-groups resource, so the set never contains real group ids. Callers use this set as a group-id filter: UsersResource.searchForUser puts it into the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute and UsersResource.getUsersCount and BruteForceUsersResource pass it to the user provider. Consequences: (1) per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions never restrict the database query, so pagination is applied to the unfiltered user list and users the caller can see can be missing from a page, and the count is not group-restricted; (2) when the caller has VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS on the all-groups resource, the set contains the all-groups resource UUID, which no group has, so user search and count return no users at all. The new tests only grant per-group member permissions and use first=-1/max=-1, so neither case is covered.

false_positives.candidate:
All-groups permission is ignored once any per-group resource exists

hasPermission only falls back to the all-groups resource when resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) returns null. As soon as a per-group resource exists for any scope, only that resource is evaluated and the all-groups resource is never consulted. Concrete case: an admin holds MANAGE on the all-groups resource and some per-group permission (for example VIEW_MEMBERS) was created for group G; canManage(G), canView(G) and canManageMembership(G) then look only at G's resource, find no MANAGE/VIEW, and deny the action even though the global permission grants it. requireManageMembers javadoc names the wrong method

The javadoc on requireManageMembers(GroupModel) says the ForbiddenException is thrown when canManageMembership(GroupModel) returns false, but the implementation checks canManageMembers(GroupModel). This documents the wrong permission required to call the method.

true_positives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Anchor allowance check is order-sensitive and removes the wrong occurrence

In `santizeAnchors` the `Matcher` is built over the original `value`, but inside the loop `value` is reassigned to a shorter string via `value.replaceFirst(...)`. `replaceFirst` removes the first occurrence of the English anchor text from the current string, not the occurrence the matcher is inspecting, and because positions are taken from the old string, matching is only correct when the translation contains the anchors in exactly the same order and count as the English source. A legitimate translation that keeps both anchors but reorders them is reported as "Didn't find anchor tag" (false positive, fails the build); conversely, if English has more anchors than the translation the extra `matcher.find()` never runs and a translation that dropped a required link is not reported (false negative). In `encodeTokenId`, concatenating a null raw ID produces the literal string `onrtac:null`, so multiple tokens can share the same `jti` rather than failing fast. true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

For an ID like `onrtac:<uuid>`, the grant shortcut occupies indices 4-6 (`ac`), but the matcher reads `substring(3, 5)` (`ta`) and returns false when that value equals the expected shortcut. true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:

For audit logs the column is a timestamp, so comparing it to an integer either raises a Postgres "operator does not exist: timestamp with time zone <= bigint" error or produces wrong ordering. `DateTimePaginator` deliberately overrides this method to convert the cursor value back with `datetime.fromtimestamp(value / multiplier)`; the optimized paginator must do the same (or reuse `DateTimePaginator`) for datetime-ordered querysets. The endpoint chooses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` vs `DateTimePaginator` from the client-supplied `optimized_pagination=true` query param, but the two paginators encode the cursor `value` differently: `DateTimePaginator` uses millisecond epoch values and converts them back with `datetime.fromtimestamp`, while `OptimizedCursorPaginator` stores/interprets the raw field value. Likewise a superuser who drops the param cannot resume a pagination session started with it. false_positives.candidate:
Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs

FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown. Both APIs were added in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs, q.shutdown raises AttributeError, which the broad except swallows, so blocked worker threads are never woken. Each worker.join(timeout=5.0) then waits the full 5 seconds, meaning shutdown takes 100 seconds with the default 20 queues and leaves the threads alive. Separately, if a worker ever hits the except queue.ShutDown clause, evaluating the missing attribute raises another AttributeError and kills that worker. Use an Event/sentinel-based shutdown compatible with the supported Python version.

Shared queue pool is permanently shut down and then reused

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and reuses it for every create_with_partitions call, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down all queues and workers. On a Kafka rebalance Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again with the same factory, so the new strategy gets an already shut-down pool. With queue shutdown available, put() raises ShutDown, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches it, marks the offset complete, and the background commit loop commits it, silently dropping messages. Without queue shutdown, the workers are gone and the offsets may never complete. The pool should be owned by the strategy or recreated for each strategy instance, not shut down from close() while the factory still holds it.

Queues are unbounded, so submit applies no backpressure

Each queue is created as queue.Queue() with the default maxsize of 0, which is infinite, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always enqueues immediately. poll() only emits a metric and never blocks or rejects based on queue depth. A single slow subscription can therefore grow its queue without bound while the consumer keeps polling and decoding messages, increasing memory use and accumulating an uncommitted Kafka backlog until the process is OOM-killed. This contradicts the class docstring's claim of natural backpressure; use a bounded queue and block or apply another explicit backpressure policy.

Failed work items are still marked offset-complete

OrderedQueueWorker.run has a finally block that unconditionally calls complete_offset(), including when result_processor raises and the exception is merely logged by the generic except. Once the offset is removed from outstanding, OffsetTracker will treat it as processed and the commit loop will commit past it, so the failed result is acknowledged to Kafka and will not be retried. This also contradicts the strategy docstring that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Failed offsets should remain outstanding or be sent through an explicit retry/DLQ path, not completed as if the work succeeded.

Shutdown stops workers before draining queued items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False), but each worker checks while not self.shutdown before calling get() again. A worker that finishes its current item therefore exits immediately, leaving any remaining items in the queue even though immediate=False was requested. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close also joins the commit thread before shutting the pool down, so work processed during shutdown is not committed. The net effect is that graceful shutdown abandons buffered results and relies on Kafka redelivery, contrary to the graceful-drain behavior implied by the code and docstrings.

Error-handling test is timing-dependent and asserts the wrong outcome

The test makes the first result processor call raise and the second succeed, then asserts that no offset was committed for the partition. In the implementation, OrderedQueueWorker completes the offset in its finally block even when processing raised, so both offsets become complete and the background commit loop should eventually commit the partition. The test only sleeps 0.2 seconds after processing finishes, while the commit loop wakes every 1 second, so it usually passes before the commit happens and will flake when setup or processing takes slightly longer. It therefore does not reliably verify the intended error semantics; it should either assert the actual expected commit behavior or the production code should keep failed offsets outstanding.

false_positives.candidate:
Changing span buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks existing Redis data during rollout

Span buffers are stored at `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id`. Before this change those keys are Redis sets; this diff starts writing them with `ZADD` and later calls `ZCARD`/`ZSCAN`/`ZUNIONSTORE` (`buffer.py` lines 197 and 434, plus `add-buffer.lua`). During a rolling deploy, any old set key touched by the new consumer, or any old consumer touching a new zset key, will get a `WRONGTYPE` error. Existing keys have a TTL up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600 seconds), so affected batches can fail and spans/segments can be lost or stuck until keys expire. There is no dual read/write path, versioned key prefix, or migration/flush step.

Span buffer hard-codes 1000-span cap and ignores SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans

Eviction is now `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...)` inside the Lua script, while the Python span-count check was removed from `_load_segment_data`. `SpansBuffer` still exposes `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) and passes nothing to the script, so any configured value is silently ignored and the actual limit is always 1000, which is also one lower than the default. Operators/tests cannot tune the cap, and the Python span-count safety check no longer matches the Lua behavior.

ZUNIONSTORE sums duplicate timestamp scores instead of preserving the latest

The script uses `zunionstore set_key, 2, set_key, span_key` (and the same for `parent_key`) without an `AGGREGATE` option. Redis's default is `SUM`, so if a span payload is present in both source sets its score becomes the sum of two `end_timestamp_precise` values rather than the max/latest timestamp. This occurs routinely with at-least-once duplicate/reprocessed spans: a duplicate child is re-added under its parent key and then merged into the destination where the first copy already exists. Since `ZPOPMIN` later uses the score to decide which spans to evict, duplicated spans can be moved to the wrong end of the ordering and be kept or evicted incorrectly. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` or otherwise define duplicate-score handling.

No test exercises the new ZPOPMIN eviction path

All buffer tests still use only a handful of spans, so the new >1000-span eviction path is completely untested. There is no coverage for the cap being enforced, eviction ordering by `end_timestamp_precise`, retention of a root/segment span, or cleanup/redirect behavior for evicted spans. A regression here silently drops span data, so a test with more than 1000 spans should verify the resulting segment contents and Redis key cleanup.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator and audit-log branch have no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new ~90-line paginator used by the audit-log endpoint, but no test instantiates it or calls the endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true`. Basic coverage would have caught both the datetime `TypeError` and the negative-offset `ValueError`. Add tests for first/next/prev pages, forged negative offsets, and the audit-log optimized path.

The loop that resolves parent redirects was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, removing the comment that documented the old limit. If a trace's span-buffer redirect chain is deeper than 1000, the loop stops at an intermediate span id, so the current span is attached to the wrong buffer and segments can be split or duplicated. This is an abrupt behavior change unrelated to the eviction work and has no test; either restore the old bound or justify and test the new one.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache has no invalidation and can override fresh allows

`Check` returns immediately from `permDenialCache` before consulting `permCache` or the DB, and `permDenialCache.Set` is called after any DB-backed denial. Nothing invalidates these entries when permissions are granted or when a new dashboard/folder is created. A denied check (for example, before a just-created dashboard's creator permission is visible, or before an admin grants a role) therefore keeps returning Allowed=false for the 30s shortCacheTTL even after the DB grants access. This also means a stale denial overrides a later-refreshed allow in permCache, which directly undermines the PR goal of making newly created resources accessible. Deny entries need invalidation, or must not override a fresh cached allow, and likely deserve a shorter TTL.

Denial cache key uses raw subject ID and omits identity type

The denial-cache key is built from the raw subject ID (`checkReq.UserUID`) before `GetUserIdentifiers` resolves the canonical UID, and it does not include the identity type. The permission cache, in contrast, is keyed by the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID`. The same user can therefore have separate denial entries for `user:123` and `user:<uid>`, so the denial cache is bypassed when the subject form changes. Conversely, identities such as `user:123`, `service-account:123`, or `anonymous:123` share the same denial key even though they can represent different principals; a denial for one can be served for another until TTL expiry. Resolve the subject first and include the identity type plus canonical UID, and escape or hash the key components.

No test that Check populates the denial cache

The new test for the denial cache only seeds `permDenialCache` manually; it does not exercise a normal denied `Check` and verify that the denial entry is written. A bug in the key used by `s.permDenialCache.Set` or a missed Set call would pass the current tests. Add a case with a denying fake permission store that asserts a second identical `Check` is served from the denial cache without incrementing `store.calls` and still returns Allowed=false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes `metadata` contains a `sender` dict with a `login` key. `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` only adds `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is set, and `test_basic_flow` asserts that pipeline-created integrations have metadata without `sender`. Any Integration whose metadata lacks `sender` (e.g. created by the pipeline itself, created by an older version, or whose metadata was overwritten by `build_integration`) will raise `KeyError` here, returning a 500 rather than the intended `github-integration-failed.html` error. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing value as a verification failure.

false_positives.candidate:
User/installer verification is skipped whenever the Integration row does not already exist

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch the new check that the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user matches the installer is reached only after `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` succeeds. When that lookup raises `Integration.DoesNotExist`, the code returns `pipeline.next_step()` immediately, and `build_integration` then creates the Integration. This is exactly the first-install path (it is also what happens whenever the GitHub `installation` webhook that populates `metadata["sender"]` has not been processed yet, since webhook delivery is not ordered relative to the browser redirect). Consequently the authenticated GitHub user is never compared to the installer on the primary flow; the check only runs on later re-install attempts. An attacker who starts an install with their own installation_id while the victim completes OAuth as a different GitHub account is not caught, which defeats the stated security fix. The verification needs to run (or fail closed) even when the Integration row is absent / the sender is not yet known.

Token exchange and user-info fetch are not guarded, so upstream failures produce a 500

`safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is outside the try/except; the except only wraps `safe_urlread`. `safe_urlopen` raises on connection errors and non-2xx responses, and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) can raise `ApiError` as well. Those exceptions propagate and render a 500, not the friendly `github-integration-failed.html` page, contradicting the PR's claim that an invalid/reused code or failed token exchange always shows that error. Wrap the exchange and the user-info call in error handling and return `error(...)` on failure.

test_installation_not_found no longer covers the 404 installation-not-found path

The test still stubs a 404 for `/app/installations/{id}`, but the requests it issues never reach `get_installation_info`/`build_integration`: the second GET uses a bogus `state` ("ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05") and the changed assertion now checks the generic "Invalid installation request." message emitted by OAuthLoginView's state-mismatch branch. The original assertion (`The GitHub installation could not be found.`) was removed, so the `ApiError` 404 → `IntegrationError` code path in `build_integration` is no longer tested by any test. Either keep a test that drives the pipeline to completion with a 404 or rename/repurpose this test and add coverage for the 404 branch.

Runtime _() on error_short prevents these messages from being extracted for translation

The refactor passes the user-facing strings as plain `error_short` arguments (`"GitHub installation pending deletion."`, `"Github installed on another Sentry organization."`, and the `"Invalid installation request."` default), then calls `_()` on the runtime variable inside `error()`. `gettext`/`makemessages` only extracts literals passed directly to `_()`, so these strings will no longer appear in the message catalog and will be shown untranslated (previously they were `_("...")` literals). Pass lazy literals at the call sites (or make the arguments default to `_()` literals) so they remain extractable.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check after acquiring the write lock causes duplicate manifest loads

After reading the cache under RLock and releasing it, the function takes the write lock at line 48 but never re-checks whether the cache was filled by another goroutine in the meantime. On a cold start (or any time the cache is nil in non-Dev env), N concurrent callers all observe `ret == nil` at line 45 and then queue on the write lock; each one runs the full read path (lines 51-67, including reading and JSON-decoding assets-manifest.json, and its error paths) and overwrites the cache. The final value is still correct, but N concurrent requests produce N serialized disk reads/parses instead of one, and every queued request is blocked for the whole duration of the I/O. This is the classic double-checked-locking omission: re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and return the cached value early.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: an incomplete double-checked locking pattern where the function checks the cache under a read lock, releases it, acquires a write lock, and fails to re-check if the cache was populated by another goroutine in the meantime.

false_positives.candidate:
No test exercises concurrent GetWebAssets calls

The PR's sole purpose is to eliminate a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache, but it adds no test. A race like this is only reliably caught by running concurrent GetWebAssets invocations under `go test -race`; without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce an unguarded read/write without CI noticing. Add a test that spawns multiple goroutines calling GetWebAssets against a temp manifest and asserts they all get a non-nil, consistent result (run with -race).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

On the Storage error-return path, Create calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ..., startStorage)` (line 45) and Update does the same (line 129) instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Conversely the DeleteCollection legacy goroutine records its result via `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` (line 166). As a result storage errors/latency are attributed to the legacy store and legacy-write errors to unified storage, making the per-backend error and latency metrics/dashboards wrong. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name as the resource `kind` metric label

In the Delete success path the storage duration is recorded with the object name passed as the `kind` argument: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` (line 106). The third parameter of `recordStorageDuration` is the resource kind, so every deleted object adds a new label value, exploding metric cardinality and mislabeling the series. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: passing `name` instead of `options.Kind` when recording metrics, which is inconsistent with other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes use the request context and get cancelled when the handler returns

Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection launch the legacy write in a goroutine that derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51 `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`; same pattern at lines 110, 135, 163). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which is immediately after the goroutine is spawned. The legacy backup write is therefore usually aborted with `context canceled` before it runs, so mode 3's safety-net write to legacy silently does not happen and the legacy-store metrics record spurious failures/timeouts. Detach the goroutine's context from the request (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` to keep values, or a fresh background context) so it survives handler completion.

Async legacy-write failures are never logged

The legacy-write goroutines capture the legacy error but only feed it to a metric and never log it (e.g. Create lines 55-56 `_, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...)` then `d.recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`; same in Delete, Update and DeleteCollection). The previous synchronous implementation logged these failures with `log.Error`. Now a failed legacy backup write is invisible in logs, so operators cannot diagnose why the legacy copy is missing. Log the error inside the goroutine (using a logger not tied to the soon-to-be-cancelled request context).

mode 3 integration tests race the asynchronous legacy write

The new mode 3 subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which after writing through the k8s API immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoint and asserts the same UIDs are present (line 529), and `getFromBothAPIs` does a legacy GET right after each k8s write. Mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, so these assertions race the background write and can fail intermittently (and will fail deterministically while the request-context cancellation bug exists). The test needs to wait/poll for the legacy copy to appear (e.g. `require.Eventually`) rather than asserting immediately.

Unit tests never assert the legacy (async) write and don't wait for the goroutine

TestMode3_Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection set up expectations on the legacy store but never verify the legacy write occurred (no `AssertCalled`/`AssertExpectations`) and never wait for the goroutine. Because the legacy write is fire-and-forget, the tests pass even if the legacy path never runs, so the defining behavior of mode 3 (dual write to legacy) is not actually tested. The goroutine can also still be invoking the shared `*mock.Mock` and metrics registry after the subtest returns, which can cause data races/flaky failures under `-race`. Wait for the goroutine (channel/WaitGroup) and assert the legacy call was made.

Under concurrency, two first-time requests from different new devices can both observe `count < deviceLimit` and both insert, so the number of tracked devices exceeds the configured `device_limit`. Because tagging now runs synchronously on the authentication path, this race is easy to trigger with parallel browser sessions. The limit needs to be enforced atomically (e.g. a single conditional insert that also checks the count, or serialization via a lock), otherwise the configured limit is only advisory.

Fallback locales are only loaded for controller requests

`translate` still only calls `load_locale(config.locale)` for the current locale, and the only place that calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is `ApplicationController#set_locale` (application_controller.rb:159). Because the patched `load_translations` forces explicit loading and `load_locale` is the only loader, any translation performed outside a web request (Sidekiq/background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, the console, or `I18n.with_locale` / `I18n.t(key, locale: x)` inside a request) will try the fallback chain (`SiteSetting.default_locale`, `:en`) without those locale files ever having been loaded. When the requested locale lacks a key, the fallback lookup then misses and the caller gets a missing translation/raw key instead of the site-default/English string. For example, a job running under `I18n.locale = 'de'` on a site whose default locale is `'fr'` never loads `fr`, so a missing German key cannot fall back to French. Ensure the whole fallback chain is loaded whenever a locale is loaded (e.g. make `load_locale`/`translate` call `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for each entry of `I18n.fallbacks[locale]`), not only from the controller before_filter.

`I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on every `I18n.translate`/`I18n.exists?` that reaches the backend (i.e. every translation not served from the translate accelerator's LRU cache), and this `[]` override calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` each time. It also means an early `I18n.t` (boot initializers, asset precompilation, rake tasks, console before the DB/Redis are available) now attempts to read site settings and can raise instead of simply returning a translation. Memoize the default locale / compute the chain once per locale and invalidate it on reload.

No tests for the new fallback behavior, which is now enabled in every environment

The PR changes translation resolution globally (fall back to the site default locale, then English) but adds no specs covering `FallbackLocaleList#[]`, the fallback ordering, or `ensure_loaded!`. Additionally, `I18n.fallbacks = FallbackLocaleList.new` runs in every environment, while the `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` lines that were removed only existed in production/profile/Cloud66, so fallbacks now also apply in test/development where they were previously unset. Tests that assert a missing key is returned verbatim, or that a given locale has no translation, will now silently receive the site-default/English string. Add tests for the new fallback chain and confirm the intended test-environment behavior.
