false_positives.candidate:
Unconditional visible assignment can hide groups on partial updates

`update` always executes `group.visible = params[:visible] == "true"`. A PATCH or PUT that omits `visible`—including the old PATCH membership-changes API that still routes to `update` because `resources :groups` accepts PATCH—now sets `visible` to false and saves. The old `update_patch` membership add/delete handling was also removed, so such requests no longer update memberships and can silently make the group invisible. Only assign `visible` when the parameter is present, and either support or explicitly reject the old PATCH contract.

Public members endpoint accepts unbounded and negative pagination values

`limit` and `offset` are taken directly from public query parameters and passed into `.limit(...).offset(...)`. A caller can request a very large limit, causing an unnecessarily large database result and JSON serialization, or pass negative values that can produce SQL errors/500 responses. Clamp `limit` to a sane maximum and enforce `offset >= 0`.

Public group member list truncates at 50 with no pagination

The backend now returns only one page of members (default limit 50), and the public group-members route never requests another page. This template simply iterates `members` and has no pagination controls. Groups with more than 50 members will silently show only the first 50, whereas non-automatic groups previously returned all members. Either add paging or explicitly fetch all members for the public view.

Removing the last member on the last page leaves an invalid offset

`removeMember` deletes the user and then calls `findMembers()` with the current offset. If the removed user was the only member on the current page (for example 51 members at offset 50), the new total becomes 50 but the request still uses offset 50, so the reload returns an empty page and the UI stays on an invalid blank page. Adjust the offset when it reaches or exceeds the new `user_count` after deletion.

Username input is not cleared after adding members or switching groups

`usernames` is state on the singleton admin group controller and is not reset after `addMembers` or when `setupController` switches to another group. After adding users to group A, selecting group B leaves the old usernames in the selector; clicking Add again can add those stale users to group B unintentionally. Clear the property after each add and when the model changes (the existing TODO acknowledges this).

Creating a group ignores the selected alias level

The client’s `Group.asJSON()` sends `alias_level` when creating a group, and the admin template exposes the alias selector for new groups, but `create` only assigns `name` and `visible`. A newly created group therefore silently loses the selected alias level and falls back to the database default. Assign `group.alias_level = params[:alias_level].to_i` when present.

Public members endpoint response shape is a breaking change

`/groups/:group_id/members.json` previously returned a JSON array of users; it now returns an object of the form `{members: [...], meta: {...}}`. The in-repo JavaScript client was updated, but any plugin, mobile app, or external consumer expecting the old array will break. If this endpoint is part of the public API, either maintain backward compatibility or introduce a versioned/new endpoint.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation triggers a DB write and double-counts blocked-email statistics

`EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and `should_block?` (app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 12-17) loads the matching record, increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and calls `record.save`. This means a simple `valid?`/`save` check now performs a database write. In `UsersController#create` the user is validated twice on the same request: `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), so a single signup attempt against a blocked (or even `do_nothing`) email increments `match_count` by 2 instead of 1. Match counts will be inflated unpredictably, defeating the purpose of these statistics for spotting spam campaigns, and read-only validation paths unexpectedly mutate the DB. The stat update should be decoupled from the pure predicate and triggered once per real block event (e.g., after a confirmed rejection), not on every validation invocation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same core problem: the predicate method `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (or `should_block_email?`) causes unexpected database side effects by updating statistics (`match_count` and `last_match_at`) during a read/check operation, and recommend decoupling the statistic updates from the check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and bypassable

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` compares the raw submitted email against the stored string with exact case. E-mail addresses are treated case-insensitively in practice, and nothing downcases the user's email when it is set/validated (`User.new_from_params` stores it verbatim). So an entry for `spam@bad.com` will not block a signup using `Spam@Bad.com` or `spam@BAD.com`, and imported/manually-entered records in mixed case won't match either — trivially bypassing the blocklist. Normalize on both sides: downcase/`Email.downcase` the value in `should_block?` (and ideally normalize the stored `email` in a `before_validation`/`before_save` so the unique index also behaves case-insensitively).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is case-sensitive, which allows users to bypass the blocklist by using a different casing for their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic counter update loses matches under concurrency

`should_block?` performs a read-modify-write: `record.match_count += 1; record.save`. Two concurrent requests matching the same blocked email both read count N and write N+1, losing one increment. Since these counters are the signal used to identify spam waves (exactly when many concurrent attempts happen), the undercounting is most severe in the scenario the data is meant to detect. Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now])` (or `increment_counter`) instead.

New validator spec does not cover the ported domain restrictions or the real lookup

The only new validator specs stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so they neither exercise the actual database lookup/scoping nor verify the end-to-end behavior (`user.valid?` returning false for a blocked email). More importantly, this PR moves the `email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` logic out of `User#email_validator` into `EmailValidator`, but no spec covers that moved logic (whitelist pass/fail, blacklist pass/fail). A regression in the relocated domain-restriction behavior would go undetected. Add specs covering the whitelist and blacklist branches (and ideally one integration spec that a blocked email makes a `User` invalid), plus a test for the new `errors`/`values` fields returned by `UsersController#create`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin omits -moz-box-align fallback

The new `align-items()` mixin emits `-webkit-box-align`, `-webkit-align-items`, `-ms-flex-align`, and `align-items`, but omits `-moz-box-align`. Since the new `flexbox()` and `inline-flex()` mixins explicitly fall back to `display: -moz-box`/`display: -moz-inline-box`, old Firefox versions will select the legacy box display but ignore the requested alignment. Add `-moz-box-align: $alignment;` for parity; the `-ms-align-items` declaration is not a recognized IE property and can be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate's primary focus is on the missing `-moz-box-align` fallback, it explicitly identifies the exact same issue as the golden comment in the last sentence: 'the `-ms-align-items` declaration is not a recognized IE property and can be removed', while also noting that `-ms-flex-align` is present.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex layout breaks right-aligned small-action button

Adding `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action` changes its children to flex items. The existing `.small-action button { float: right; }` rule (line 309) can no longer right-align a button that is a direct flex child because floats are ignored on flex items. Also, `.small-action-desc` is not given `flex-grow`, so it no longer spans the remaining row width; if the button is nested inside it, the internal float will no longer push the button to the full row’s right edge either. The undo/act action button will therefore sit next to the description instead of at the right side. Add `margin-left: auto` to the button or make `.small-action-desc` grow.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the `?` suffix and is never called

ActiveModel::Serializers decides whether to emit an attribute by calling `include_<attr>?`; every other predicate in this file (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_stats?`, `include_suspend_reason?`) uses the question mark. Because this method is defined as `include_website_name` without `?`, it is dead code: `website_name` is always serialized, including `website_name: null` for users with no website, and any conditional exclusion written here would silently do nothing. Rename it to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the primary issue described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the required `?` suffix needed by Rails serializers for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue about string concatenation, the core bug is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:
Domain comparison is asymmetric and can treat unrelated domains as equal

The path is appended only when the instance host ends with '.'+website_host (else branch) or when both hosts have the same label count > 2 and their labels after the first match (elsif). As a result, instance `example.com` with website `www.example.com` (2 vs 3 labels) falls into the else branch, fails `ends_with?('.www.example.com')`, and returns only `www.example.com`, while the reverse case (`forum.example.com` instance, `example.com` website) shows the path. The feature therefore works inconsistently. In addition, comparing all-but-the-first labels treats unrelated registrable domains under multi-label public suffixes as identical: `foo.co.uk` and `bar.co.uk` both reduce to `co.uk`, so the full path of one is shown as if it belonged to the other. Use a proper registrable-domain/subdomain comparison instead of label counting.

New specs miss the untrusted/anonymous leak and the elsif branch

The added examples only cover different domains and the equal/parent-domain cases. There is no example for a TL0 user with a website viewed by an anonymous guardian, so the `website_name` privacy leak is not caught, and the `untrusted_attributes` list at line 11 still omits `website_name`. The `elsif` branch (same label count, different subdomain, e.g. `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`) that the code comment describes is never exercised, nor is a user with a blank website (the `include_website_name` behavior). Add these cases so the serializer's inclusion and matching logic is verified.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check uses substring matching instead of exact origin equality

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) return;` accepts any origin that appears as a substring of the trusted URL, for example `http://forum.example` when `discourseUrl` is `http://forum.example.com`, or the same host on a different port. Such a page can send a `discourse-resize` message and control the iframe height. Compare `e.origin` against the normalized origin of `discourseUrl` exactly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the origin validation uses `indexOf` (substring matching) instead of an exact origin check, allowing malicious origins to bypass the check.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is a full referer URL instead of an origin

The resize script sends `parent.postMessage(..., '<%= request.referer %>')`. `targetOrigin` must be a serialized origin (scheme://host[:port]); a referer with a path (and query string, which ERB also HTML-escapes to `&` inside the script) does not match the parent origin. The browser therefore drops the message, so the iframe never receives the height and content is clipped to the initial iframe size. Build the target origin from `URI(request.referer).scheme`, host, and port (or use a controlled site setting), not the full URL.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: passing the full referrer URL as the targetOrigin in postMessage instead of just the origin (scheme+host+port), which causes the browser to drop the message and prevents iframe resizing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Imported feed/readability HTML is stored as raw HTML and rendered without sanitization

`TopicEmbed.import` sets `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, and `Post#cook` returns the raw string for that method, bypassing Markdown/sanitization. `Jobs::PollFeed` feeds arbitrary RSS/Atom content here (after `CGI.unescapeHTML`, which can turn escaped `<script>` into a real script tag), and `app/views/embed/best.html.erb:19` emits `raw post.cooked`. The readability path only filters tag/attribute names, not dangerous URL schemes, and line 13 interpolates the feed-provided URL unescaped into the raw post. A malicious or compromised feed can therefore inject script/event-handler HTML and execute it in the forum origin when the embed is viewed. Sanitize the HTML (and URL schemes/attributes) before storing it, or do not use the raw_html cook method for untrusted feed content.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment identifies two issues in TopicEmbed.import: a NoMethodError when contents is nil, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped URL interpolation. The candidate issue focuses on the XSS vulnerability in TopicEmbed.import, specifically noting that 'line 13 interpolates the feed-provided URL unescaped into the raw post' alongside broader HTML sanitization concerns. While it misses the nil NoMethodError part, it directly identifies the exact XSS vulnerability from unescaped URL interpolation mentioned in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid `end if` makes the embed template fail to compile

Line 6 closes the header `if` with `end if` and no condition. ERB compiles this to Ruby containing `end if`, which is a SyntaxError, so every request that renders `embed/best` will raise instead of displaying discussion highlights or the start-discussion link. It should just be `<%- end %>`. Controller specs do not render views by default, so this is not caught.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same syntax error in the ERB template: using `end if` instead of `end` to close an `if` block, which causes a Ruby SyntaxError when rendering.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed items without `content` raise NoMethodError and abort polling

`i.content.scrub` assumes every RSS/Atom item has a `content` field. Many valid feeds provide only `description` or `summary`, so `i.content` is nil and `nil.scrub` raises, aborting the entire poll and preventing all later items from importing. Use `i.content || i.description` (and handle nil) before scrubbing/unescaping.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: calling `i.content.scrub` will raise an error when `i.content` is nil (common in RSS feeds), and recommends falling back to `i.description`.

false_positives.candidate:
Guard tests pass without exercising the setting under test

The `feed_polling_url` test stubs only `feed_polling_url` to nil; it leaves `feed_polling_enabled?` at its default false, so `execute` short-circuits before the URL check. The `embed_by_username` test has the same issue. These tests would still pass if the corresponding condition were deleted. Stub all earlier guards true in each test, and only the condition under test false, to make the assertion meaningful.

URL absolutization corrupts protocol-relative URLs and misses path-relative URLs

Only root-relative links are rewritten, and protocol-relative URLs are corrupted: `//cdn.example.com/x` satisfies `start_with?('/')`, then `sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips both slashes, producing `http://article-host/cdn.example.com/x` instead of `http://cdn.example.com/x`. Path-relative URLs such as `foo/bar` are not absolutized at all. The same issue exists for `img[src]` below. Treat `//` separately and resolve relative URLs against the article URI.

Unvalidated `open(url)` allows command execution/file reads from Disqus links

`TopicEmbed.import_remote` calls `open(url)` before any URL validation. Ruby's `Kernel#open` treats a string beginning with `|` as a shell command and other strings as local file paths, so a malicious Disqus export can put e.g. `|touch /tmp/pwned` or `/etc/passwd` in a thread link; `lib/tasks/disqus.thor:148` now passes `t[:link]` directly to this method. Running the importer would execute the command or read the file. Validate that the URL is http/https and use an HTTP client (with redirect/size/timeout handling) instead of Kernel#open.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

New downsize overload silently shadows the 4-argument downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height)

`def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` (line 149) redefines the `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` method declared at line 145; in Ruby the later definition wins, so the 4-argument form is unreachable. Any caller passing explicit dimensions (e.g. `OptimizedImage.downsize(src, dst, 1024, 768)`) is now dispatched to the new method with `dimensions = 1024` and `opts = 768`; `optimize` then evaluates `opts[:allow_animation]` and raises `NoMethodError: undefined method '[]' for 768:Integer` instead of producing a `1024x768` instruction. Even when no exception is raised, `dimensions` is a bare Integer, yielding a broken `-resize` argument. true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client upload limit hard-coded to 10MB, ignoring max_image_size_kb/max_attachment_size_kb site settings

`validateUploadedFile` previously derived the limit from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`; it now always uses `10 * 1024` KB for both images and attachments. Attachments are not auto-downsized on the server, so sites configured with a smaller `max_attachment_size_kb` will now accept up to 10MB in the browser and only fail later with a less clear server error (or the setting is effectively bypassed). The same applies to images where an admin deliberately configured a limit below 10MB. In addition, the 413 handler at line 246 now reports `max_size_kb: 10MB` regardless of the web server's real limit, so the error message can be wrong. The limit should stay driven by the site settings (or a dedicated setting for the resize threshold).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: hardcoding the upload size limit to 10 * 1024 KB instead of using Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'] causes client-side validation and the 413 error handler to diverge from the actual site settings.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsizing an animated GIF keeps only the first frame when allow_animated_thumbnails is off

The controller's new resize path calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(..., allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)`. When that setting is false (the default), `optimize` selects `downsize_instructions`, whose command contains `#{from}[0]`, i.e. only the first frame of a multi-frame GIF. Because the downsized temp file replaces the upload, an animated GIF larger than `max_image_size_kb` is permanently stored as a static single-frame image, silently destroying the user's animation. The animated instruction set is only used when the setting is explicitly enabled. Animated uploads should either always go through the animated/`gifsicle` path or be exempted from automatic downsizing.

Downsize loop with at most five 80% steps cannot bring files more than ~3x the limit under the limit

Repeatedly applying `-resize 80%` five times yields only 0.8^5 ≈ 0.33 of the original, so a file more than roughly 3x `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` is still oversized after the loop and `Upload.create_for` then rejects it. The advertised feature (accept large images by shrinking them) therefore still fails for genuinely large uploads, e.g. a 10MB image on a 1MB limit. Each pass is also a separate lossy re-encode (no `-quality` specified), so intermediate steps degrade the image more than necessary. The required scale factor should be computed from `tempfile.size / limit` (or the loop should recompute a percentage from the current size) rather than using fixed 80% steps.

Resize loop runs ImageMagick on SVG uploads, which convert cannot faithfully handle

The guard only checks `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)`, and that helper's image list includes SVG, so an SVG larger than `max_image_size_kb` is fed to `OptimizedImage.downsize` → `convert`. `OptimizedImage.create_for` deliberately special-cases `.svg` (it copies the file instead of calling `resize`), showing that `convert` is not suitable for vector files. The result is either a rewritten/rasterized file different from what the user uploaded (data loss) or a failed `convert`; in the failure case the loop still spawns five pointless `convert` processes per upload before giving up. Exclude SVG (and any format that cannot round-trip through `convert`) from the resize loop.

No tests for the new automatic downsizing behavior or the OptimizedImage API refactor

The PR adds a multi-iteration in-place resize loop in `UploadsController#create_upload` and changes the public signatures of `OptimizedImage.resize/downsize/optimize`, but no specs were added or updated. Tests covering (a) an oversized image that must be shrunk, (b) a file that remains oversized after five attempts, (c) an animated GIF and an SVG upload, and (d) a call to `downsize` with explicit width/height would have caught the shadowed-method bug and the first-frame truncation. Please add model/controller specs for these paths.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes on missing TopicUser and bypasses TopicUser.change

`TopicUser.find_by(...)` returns nil whenever a logged-in user visits the unsubscribe URL without an existing topic_users row (for example a direct visit or a stale email link), and the next `tu.notification_level` call raises NoMethodError, returning a 500. Even when the row exists, assigning the level and calling `tu.save!` bypasses `TopicUser.change`, so `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` are not updated and the `notification_level_change` MessageBus event is not published, leaving the topic's notification reason stale. false_positives.candidate:
Explicit render in perform_show_response breaks canonical URL on topic pages

Adding `render :show` inside `perform_show_response` causes the normal `show` action to render before it executes `canonical_url` (line 87). `canonical_url` sets `@canonical_url` for the layout, so topic show pages will no longer emit the canonical link (or will use a stale one). Move the canonical URL assignment before `perform_show_response`, or render explicitly only from `unsubscribe`.

State-changing unsubscribe action is a GET without a CSRF/token check

`unsubscribe` changes the current user's notification level in response to a plain GET and is authorized only by the session cookie. A third-party page can therefore embed `/t/<slug>/<id>/unsubscribe` as an image/link and mute a logged-in user's topic (and email link scanners can trigger it too). Unsubscribe route name does not match the added template path

The route is declared at top level as `topicUnsubscribe`, so Ember's default template lookup is `templates/topic-unsubscribe.hbs`. The PR adds `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`, which is the path for a nested route named `topic.unsubscribe`, not for a top-level `topicUnsubscribe` route. As written the new URL has no template and will render blank or throw a template-not-found error. Either nest the route under the `topic` resource as `this.route('unsubscribe', { path: '/unsubscribe' })` or rename the added template to `topic-unsubscribe.hbs`.

Unsubscribe only downgrades watching/tracking users to regular

When the user's level is tracking or watching, the action sets it to regular instead of muted. Regular still sends notifications for replies and mentions, so the page text 'You will stop receiving notifications' is false and a mention/reply email can keep arriving after the user clicks the unsubscribe link. Set the level to muted when the intent is to stop notifications, or change the branch and copy to describe a downgrade.

No coverage for the new unsubscribe behavior

The spec change only adds `unsubscribe_url` to the builder options; it does not assert that the rendered body or HTML actually contains the per-topic unsubscribe URL. There are also no controller/route specs for `TopicsController#unsubscribe` (missing TopicUser, watching/tracking to regular/muted, slug redirect) or for the new Ember route. The nil crash and the notification-level behavior above would pass CI.

New locale interpolation makes unsubscribe_url mandatory for all add_unsubscribe_link emails

Any other mailer or plugin that uses `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without `unsubscribe_url` will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument and fail to send email. Provide a fallback to `user_preferences_url` or make the option explicitly required and update all callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`sed -i ''` is macOS-only, so the script silently fails to update .env on Linux

`sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD/macOS in-place invocation. With GNU sed (Linux), the empty `''` argument is not consumed as an in-place suffix, so the command errors out and the file is never modified, yet the script still prints "✅ Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL in $ENV_FILE to $TUNNEL_URL", leaving developers with a stale webhook URL while believing it was updated. Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"` or write to a temp file) and check the command's exit status before printing success. `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is also cwd-dependent and only correct when the script is run from `scripts/`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using the macOS/BSD-specific `sed -i ''` syntax, which fails on Linux systems using GNU sed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

Non-US users therefore see US-formatted dates (M/D/YY, 12-hour clock) in an otherwise translated UI. false_positives.candidate:
Cache status stays stale after deleting cached data

The deleteCacheMutation only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop; it never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. In the apps-installed calendar page `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` is rendered without an `onChanged` prop, so `onSuccess` is undefined. As a result the dropdown keeps showing "Cache Status / Last updated: …" and the "Delete cached data" entry after the rows were already deleted, until a full page reload. The sibling `disconnectMutation` in the same component does invalidate `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (and `viewer.apps.integrations`) in `onSettled`, so the omission looks accidental. Add the same invalidation to the deleteCache mutation.

Cache deletion always fails for credentials not owned by the session user (delegation/team credentials)

The authorization check is `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`, i.e. it only accepts credentials whose `userId` equals the logged in user. Team/service-account delegation credentials are not user-owned (they are stored with `userId = null` and belong to a team / DelegationCredential), and in-memory delegation credentials even have negative ids, so the query never matches and the mutation throws "Credential not found or access denied". The UI does not guard against this: `canDisconnect` is computed from `delegationCredentialId`, but `hasCache` only checks the integration type, so the "Delete cached data" item is rendered for delegation-connected Google calendars and then always fails with the generic "Error deleting cache" toast. Either authorize team/delegation ownership in the handler or hide the action when `delegationCredentialId` is set. Note also that for in-memory delegation credentials, cache lookups are keyed by `userId` (see `getCachedAvailability`), so a delete-by-`credentialId` would not clear those rows even if it succeeded.

Cache status reports expired cache rows as a live cache

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups over all CalendarCache rows for a credential without filtering on `expiresAt`. Expired rows are not removed from the table (availability reads just ignore rows with `expiresAt < now` and the row is only replaced on the next upsert), so a user whose Google cache expired weeks ago is shown "Cache Status — Last updated: <old date>" and offered "Delete cached data" even though the cache is effectively dead and the next availability request will miss. Add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` to the `where` clause so the indicator reflects a usable cache. Relatedly, the migration backfills `updatedAt = NOW()` for all pre-existing rows, so after deploy every legacy cache row will display the deploy timestamp as its "last updated" time rather than when it was actually written.

Unconditional bulk update of all SelectedCalendar rows on every cache refresh

`fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` now ends with `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, whose only effect is to bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` via the Prisma `@updatedAt` attribute (the data object is empty). This runs on every cache population, which is triggered by the Google push webhook — i.e. potentially many times per minute for busy calendars — and issues an UPDATE touching every SelectedCalendar row of the credential, adding write load and row-lock contention. The PR description itself notes that SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is not shown in the frontend (the UI uses CalendarCache.updatedAt), so this write has no consumer. Remove it, or make it conditional on an actual reader existing.

Cache-status query bypasses the CalendarCache factory and runs on every connectedCalendars call

The handler instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly instead of going through `CalendarCache.init()` (the factory that returns the mock when calendar-cache is disabled / not enabled for the user's teams). Consequence: every `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` request — including onboarding, apps pages, and users/orgs where the calendar-cache feature is off — performs an extra `groupBy` aggregate over CalendarCache, even though the mock exists specifically to avoid that work when the feature is disabled. Scope the query (e.g. only for Google credentials, and via the repository factory) so non-cache users don't pay for it.

Unrelated dev:cron change introduces an undeclared `tsx` dependency invoked via npx

Changing `dev:cron` from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts` is unrelated to calendar cache status/actions and means the script depends on `tsx`, which is not declared anywhere in this package's devDependencies. On a clean checkout `npx` will download `tsx` from the network at run time (failing in offline sandboxes/CI) and pins nothing, so different developers may run different versions. Either revert this line or add `tsx` as a devDependency and call it through the package manager (`yarn tsx`).

Removal of the `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` assertion drops type-checking of the hand-written where clause

`findMany` previously validated the hand-rolled `FindManyArgs` (whose `where` is a narrowed custom shape with e.g. `googleChannelId?: string | null | { not: null }`) against Prisma's generated `SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` via `satisfies`. The new code passes the raw object to `prisma.selectedCalendar.findMany` without that assertion, so a future edit to the custom `FindManyArgs` type can now silently produce a filter Prisma will reject at runtime instead of failing the build. This change is also unrelated to the feature. Restore the `satisfies` assertion (or explain why it had to go) so the type contract keeps being enforced.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end uses the slot start minute instead of the slot end minute

`const end` is computed from `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`, exactly the same value as `start`. For a 60-minute slot starting 12:00 when a fixed host's working hours end at 12:30, `end > workingHour.endTime` is `720 > 750`, so the slot is not rejected even though it ends at 13:00. This lets round-robin fixed hosts be booked outside their working hours. Compute `end` from `slotEndTime` (or compare timestamps) and reject slots whose end exceeds the working-hour end.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: calculating the `end` time using `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length date override comparison uses object identity

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two distinct Dayjs object references, so it is always false. If a date override with equal start and end is used to represent an unavailable day, that case is never detected; only slots before the override are rejected, and the slot at the override start can be treated as available. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare timestamps.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using the strict equality operator (`===`) to compare two `dayjs` objects (`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)`), which always evaluates to false due to reference comparison. Both suggest using `.isSame()` as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override short-circuits the busy-time check

When a slot falls inside a user's date override, `dateOverrideExist` is true and `checkIfIsAvailable` returns true before reaching the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom. A date override replaces working hours, not existing bookings/calendar busy time, so a fixed host with an override 10:00-14:00 and an existing booking 11:00-12:00 will still make the 11:00 round-robin slot pass. That can lead to double booking the fixed host. Only bypass the normal working-hours check for an override; the busy check must still run.

Working-hours check tests only the first matching day and ignores days with no hours

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true as soon as it sees the first entry whose `days` includes the slot's UTC day and the slot is outside that one interval. With split availability (09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00), a 13:30 slot is outside the first interval, so the host is marked unavailable even though the second interval contains it. Conversely, if no working-hour entry includes the slot's day, `find` returns undefined and the function falls through to the busy check, treating the fixed host as available on a day they do not work. The check should test whether the slot is inside any matching interval and reject it when no interval matches.

Date override date comparison mixes server-local and UTC dates

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` formats in the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime` is a `.utc()` Dayjs. On self-hosted servers not running in UTC, the shifted override date is compared to a UTC slot date, so date overrides can be missed or matched to the wrong day. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` (and end) for the date/range calculations so both sides use UTC.

Active date overrides are filtered by wall-clock date, not actual UTC/invitee date

`activeOverrides` compares `dayjs.utc(override.start)`—where `override.start` is the organizer's wall-clock date/time stored as UTC—against the invitee day boundaries. The new conversion below explicitly treats it as wall time by subtracting the organizer offset, but this filter does not. For example, with an organizer in UTC+14, an override at local D 01:00 is stored as D 01:00Z but actually occurs at D-1 11:00Z; when an invitee in UTC views day D-1, the stored value is outside that invitee day, so the override is ignored and normal working hours are used. Convert the override to actual UTC (or to the invitee timezone) before deciding whether it belongs to the invitee day.

No test covers the fixed-host round-robin date override behavior or the new availability branches

The only added test changes the invitee timezone for a personal event. It does not exercise the PR's main claim: a round-robin event with a fixed host whose date override should constrain available slots. There are also no tests for a fixed host with busy time inside an override, slots partially overlapping an override, or split working hours. These missing cases would have caught the early return that skips busy checks and the working-hours containment bugs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Read-modify-write of retryCount loses increments under overlapping cron runs

Both increment sites (the `else` branch here and the one at line 195) compute `reminder.retryCount + 1` in application code from the value returned by the earlier `findMany`. If two cron invocations overlap — plausible because the per-reminder loop awaits a `profile.findFirst` and `getBookerBaseUrl` call for every reminder, so a run can exceed the cron interval — both read the same retryCount and write the same value. Failures are then under-counted and a persistently failing reminder may never reach the `> 1` threshold, so it is retried indefinitely and the PR's retry cap never takes effect. Use Prisma's atomic `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency/race condition issue with `reminder.retryCount + 1` in both locations, and both recommend using Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` operation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount cleanup clause is not scoped to SMS/unscheduled reminders

The new deletion branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` inside the `OR` is not restricted by `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` or `scheduled: false`, unlike the pre-existing branch next to it. As written, any WorkflowReminder row (email, WhatsApp, or an already-scheduled reminder) whose retryCount is greater than 1 is hard-deleted on each cron run. Today only this handler increments retryCount, but the column lives on the shared model, so as soon as another scheduler writes retryCount — or a concurrent run manages to schedule a reminder after it has already been bumped twice — unrelated reminders are silently purged, and an already-scheduled reminder is deleted without cancelling its provider-side scheduled message (referenceId), leaving an orphaned SMS/email job that will still fire. The clause should be constrained to the same rows this handler owns, e.g. `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduled: false, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: the `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` condition in the `OR` clause for deletion is missing the `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, which causes non-SMS reminders (like email or WhatsApp) to be deleted.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders that cannot be attempted never increment retryCount and are retried forever

retryCount is only incremented when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy or throws. When `sendTo` is missing (e.g. an SMS_ATTENDEE reminder for a booking with no `smsReminderNumber`, or an SMS_NUMBER step with an empty `sendTo`) or the computed `message` is empty, the `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` guard simply skips the reminder. Those rows stay `scheduled: false` forever, are re-fetched on every cron run, and are skipped again — exactly the unbounded-rescheduling behavior this PR is meant to stop. A missing phone number is one of the common failure modes, so this path needs to bump retryCount (or delete the reminder) when the reminder cannot be attempted.

Unguarded update inside catch can abort the whole batch

The `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` added inside the catch block is not itself protected. If it throws (row deleted concurrently by the cleanup query, or a transient DB error), the exception escapes the `catch` and the `for` loop, so all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are left unprocessed and the endpoint returns a 500. Additionally, this catch also runs when `twilio.scheduleSMS` succeeded but the subsequent `update({ scheduled: true, referenceId })` threw; in that case retryCount is bumped even though a Twilio message is already scheduled, so the reminder is re-sent on the next run (duplicate SMS) and then eventually deleted while the Twilio job remains live. The increment should be guarded with its own try/catch and should not be applied when the failure occurred after a successful provider call.

New retryCount predicate has no supporting index

The `retryCount > 1` condition has no index, and mixing it in an `OR` with the indexed `(method, scheduledDate)` predicate means Postgres cannot satisfy the whole query from the existing composite index. WorkflowReminder is a high-volume table (one row per reminder per booking), so every cron invocation can fall back to a sequential scan of the whole table. Consider a partial index such as `CREATE INDEX ... ON "WorkflowReminder"(retryCount) WHERE retryCount > 0`, or restructuring the cleanup so the unindexed predicate is not part of the main scan.

Comment no longer describes the delete query

The comment says "delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date", but the query now also deletes unscheduled SMS (and, due to the unscoped OR branch, non-SMS) reminders that have exceeded the retry limit. The comment should be updated to reflect both deletion conditions so future readers understand that the cleanup is not limited to past-due reminders.

Generated Prisma artifacts for retryCount were not regenerated

The schema's `zod` and `kysely` generators write committed outputs (`packages/prisma/zod/*`, `packages/prisma/kysely/types.ts`). This PR adds `retryCount` to `WorkflowReminder` and the migration, but does not update those generated files, so the WorkflowReminder zod schema and the Kysely `WorkflowReminder` interface still lack the new column. Any code that validates a reminder via the generated zod schema will silently drop retryCount, and Kysely-typed queries cannot reference it; the repository's prisma-generate check will also fail or produce a dirty diff. Regenerate and commit the zod/kysely outputs alongside the schema change.

Removing `findMany` breaks existing consumers

This PR deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, but the diff updates no call sites. `InsightsBookingService` is exported and was previously responsible for executing the denormalized query; any consumer still calling `findMany` will fail TypeScript compilation or runtime. Either migrate every call site in this PR or keep a `findMany` wrapper that executes a raw query using `getBaseConditions()`.

Unparenthesized OR authorization condition can be miscombined by callers

When scope is `team` or `org` and no filter conditions are supplied, `getBaseConditions()` returns `authConditions` directly. For those scopes `authConditions` is a top-level `OR` such as `(team booking) OR (user booking)`. If a caller appends another predicate, e.g. `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" >= ...`, SQL precedence makes it `(team booking) OR ((user booking) AND date filter)`, so the extra predicate is applied only to one branch. The returned fragment should always be wrapped in parentheses, otherwise date/security predicates can be silently skipped for part of the dataset.

Composite `Prisma.Sql` expectations are not structurally equal to reduce-built fragments

The service builds org/team and combined-filter conditions through `reduce` using nested fragments like `Prisma.sql`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` and `Prisma.sql`(${acc}) AND (${condition})`. The expectations at lines 295, 332, and 429 are single flat `Prisma.sql` templates. `Prisma.Sql` equality is structural over its internal `strings` and `values`, not based on the rendered SQL text, so a nested fragment built with `reduce` will not deep-equal a flat template even when the SQL renders identically. These assertions will fail; compare rendered SQL or execute the query instead of using `toEqual` on `Prisma.Sql` objects.

Exact SQL array order depends on unordered repository results

The expected SQL hard-codes the order of `teamIds` and user IDs inside `ANY([...])`. `teamIds` comes from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId` and user IDs come from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`; neither call specifies an `orderBy`. If Postgres returns those rows in a different order, the `ANY` arrays differ even though the authorization semantics are identical, and the exact `Prisma.sql` comparison fails intermittently. Sort the IDs before asserting or compare semantically.

No database execution coverage for org/team `ANY` conditions

The only test that actually executes the generated conditions against Postgres uses `scope: "user"`. The org/team authorization paths, which are the only places that emit `ANY(${array})`, are only compared as `Prisma.sql` strings and never run against the database. A real parameter-binding/type-inference problem in those paths (for example around array parameters) would therefore pass the test suite while failing in production. Add a `$queryRaw` execution test for at least one org/team scope.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync-mode token schema does not pass through provider token fields and fabricates a refresh token

[z.string().toString()] evaluates to the literal key '[object Object]' (and the second computed key overwrites the first), so minimumTokenResponseSchema only validates access_token and strips all other fields because z.object is not passthrough. The code then invents refresh_token: 'refresh_token' when it is absent (lines 25-27). Use a passthrough schema and preserve existing refresh tokens.

FOR UPDATE`), or store codes as individual rows and delete by id/`deleteMany`.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding non-default getShortcut breaks existing grant provider implementations

`OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` now has a new abstract `getShortcut()` method. Any custom grant factory compiled against an older Keycloak does not implement it. `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls `getShortcut()` for every registered OAuth2 grant factory during server startup, so such an extension will throw `AbstractMethodError` and prevent startup. Make this a default method with a safe fallback, or explicitly tolerate providers that do not implement it.

Decoder hard-codes 2-character shortcuts but the factory contract does not

The decoder assumes the encoded prefix is exactly 6 characters and splits it into three fixed 2-character fields. The grant field comes from `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()`, whose contract does not enforce a 2-character value (its Javadoc even says 'usually like 3-letters'). A custom grant returning e.g. `foo` will be encoded successfully as `onrtfoo:<id>`, but `getTokenContextFromTokenId` will then reject it because the prefix is 7 characters. Enforce the length at registration or make the decoder length-aware; otherwise Keycloak can issue tokens that it cannot parse itself.

validateToken unconditionally tags recreated tokens as refresh-token grant

`validateToken` recreates an access token from an existing `oldToken`, and this new line always stores `refresh_token` in `Constants.GRANT_TYPE`. This method is used outside the refresh flow as well (legacy token exchange uses it while validating the subject token and producing the exchanged access token), so those exchanged tokens get the refresh shortcut `rt` instead of the actual token-exchange grant. The grant type should be set by the calling flow, as `StandardTokenExchangeProvider` does, or only set to refresh in the refresh-specific path.

After this change getCredential() can return a credential supplied by user storage. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client removal event breaks when V2 permissions are enabled

The new listener guard checks only Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, but management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If both features are enabled, ClientRemovedEvent reaches clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...), which ClientPermissionsV2 overrides to throw UnsupportedOperationException, so deleting a client can fail. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is skipped entirely and the deleted client's V2 permission resource/policies are never cleaned up. The guard needs to handle V2 explicitly (skip it or provide a no-op/cleanup implementation).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same feature-flag mismatch: the cleanup listener checks only V1, so enabling V2 without V1 skips cleanup and leaves orphaned permissions. Its additional exception scenario and broader fix suggestions do not negate this direct match.

The third argument to ResourceStore.findByName is the resource owner. V2 per-resource authorization resources are created with owner resourceServer.getClientId() in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (line 104), but this lookup passes server.getId(), which is the Keycloak client UUID (see AdminPermissionsSchema.isAdminPermissionClient). The lookup therefore misses the per-client resource and falls back to the 'Clients' all-resource, ignoring per-client grants/denials: per-client MANAGE/VIEW grants do not work, and a per-client negative permission can be bypassed by a global allow. The same owner mistake exists at line 244 for the 'Clients' all-resource lookup. Use the same owner as creation or the two-argument findByName.

Token exchange invokes this evaluator, so token exchange requests will return a 500 instead of a normal authorization decision. true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JVM default KeyStore provider

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type, which is normally SUN, not BouncyCastle. The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning the BouncyCastle security provider, and callers may use the returned provider to resolve BC-specific algorithms or to obtain a provider name. Returning SUN silently gives such callers the wrong provider. Since this minimal authz-client provider has no BouncyCastle dependency, it should return null or throw UnsupportedOperationException rather than return an unrelated provider.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JVM default KeyStore provider rather than the BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() was added to the public CryptoProvider SPI as an abstract method. Third-party implementations compiled against the previous version do not implement it, so ServiceLoader can instantiate them but CryptoIntegration.detectProvider's call to CryptoProvider::order throws AbstractMethodError, breaking all crypto initialization. Make order() a default method with a defined fallback order, or otherwise preserve compatibility with legacy providers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not implement it. The candidate adds details about the resulting AbstractMethodError and a possible fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Provider selection is nondeterministic when highest order is tied

detectProvider now sorts all discovered providers by order and returns the first, only logging the rest at debug. All existing built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) still return order 200, so when more than one is visible there is no unique winner and selection depends on ServiceLoader/JAR order. In a FIPS deployment this can silently select the non-FIPS provider, or at minimum construct/register both providers' global security state before ignoring one, defeating FIPS compliance. The previous code failed fast on multiple providers. The selection should fail on a tie for the highest order or the built-in providers need distinct orders.

ES384/ES512 tests do not use P-384/P-521 keys

The test class creates one default EC key pair (typically P-256) and reuses it for testES256, testES384 and testES512. The ES384 and ES512 cases therefore only exercise padding a P-256 signature to 96/132 bytes; they never exercise real P-384/P-521-sized r and s values, nor verify the produced ASN.1 DER against the key. A regression that mishandles full-size ES384/ES512 signatures could pass. Generate the matching curve key pair per algorithm, or use fixed vectors and verify the result.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount now returns null where it previously always returned a count

This method previously never returned null (it either produced a count or threw), so callers had no reason to treat the Long as nullable. With the change, a deleted cached group yields null, which will throw NPE for any caller that auto-unboxes the value (comparisons, arithmetic, or passing it to a primitive parameter) and silently drops the count from serialized representations. The nullability should be documented/handled explicitly, and the callers of GroupModel#getSubGroupsCount audited for unboxing assumptions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify getSubGroupsCount() returning null despite its non-null expectation, potentially causing NPEs in callers. The candidate does not explicitly cite the Javadoc contract, but describes the same underlying issue and consequence.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the assertion can miss the exception it is looking for

The reader thread is started and never joined: the main thread deletes the 100 groups, sets deletedAll, and immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty (line 157). Any read request that is still in flight when the last group is deleted - precisely the window in which the NPE occurs - can add its exception to the list after the assertion has already run, so the test can pass even though the bug is present and is inherently racy. In addition, if a remove() call throws before deletedAll is set, this non-daemon thread loops forever, continuing to issue admin requests into subsequent tests and potentially hanging the JVM. The loop should be wrapped in try/finally, the flag set in the finally block, and the thread joined (with a timeout) before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the reader thread is not joined before deletedAll is set and caughtExceptions is asserted, allowing an in-flight read to record an exception after the assertion. The candidate's additional cleanup concern does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrent-deletion NPE is still reachable through the other getSubGroupsStream overloads

The fix only makes getSubGroupsCount() tolerate modelSupplier.get() returning null. The neighbouring overrides getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) (line 256), getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) (line 262) and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) (line 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` and dereference the result without a null check. When a CachedGroup is read while its row has been deleted concurrently - the exact scenario this PR targets - the delegate returned by modelSupplier is null, so calling these methods on the cached adapter (which is what the paginated/filtered subgroup endpoints do) still throws NPE. The fix is therefore incomplete unless the same null handling is applied there (or the model is fetched and null-checked in one place).

Test never requests subgroup counts, so the method changed by this PR may not be exercised

The reader calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)`, which only fills in search/first/max/briefRepresentation. Subgroup counts are populated only when the request opts into them (the subGroupCount request parameter that leads to GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount), and with briefRepresentation=true and no such flag the server never calls GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount() - the method this PR modifies. If so, the test would pass on the unfixed code and provides no regression coverage. The read request should explicitly ask for subgroup counts (e.g. the overload with the subGroupCount parameter) so getSubGroupsCount() is on the request path.

Unthrottled reader loop hammers the server for the whole duration of the deletions

The background loop has no delay/backoff and repeatedly issues `groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` admin requests as fast as the client can go while 100 groups are deleted sequentially. On CI this generates a large burst of concurrent requests (each building a list of up to 100 groups) that can starve the server, cause timeouts and make the test flaky. Add a small sleep/backoff or cap the number of iterations.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset "advanced" branch raises instead of paginating

When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `start_offset = cursor.offset` and then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django `QuerySet` slicing explicitly rejects a negative start (`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so the comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false and this branch raises a 500 for any cursor carrying a negative offset. Even if the ORM allowed it, negative slicing returns rows from the end of the queryset, which is not the intended "reverse pagination" semantics. Handle negative offsets by clamping/validating (as `OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, and `MergingOffsetPaginator` do with `BadPaginationError`) rather than by slicing with a negative index.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses negative slice offsets on a Django QuerySet, which rejects negative slicing and raises an exception. The differing exception type does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime fields

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key()` reads the raw model attribute and passes it to `math.floor()` / `math.ceil()`. The audit log endpoint calls this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, "datetime")` is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. Unlike `DateTimePaginator`, this class has no `multiplier` / `strftime("%s.%f")` conversion. Because `build_cursor` calls `key(results[-1])` even on the very first page, every request that reaches this paginator returns HTTP 500, so the optimized branch can never serve a result.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: get_item_key passes a datetime field to math.floor/ceil when the audit logs endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", causing a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns an int where a datetime is required

`value_from_cursor()` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (an integer/timestamp number). `BasePaginator.build_queryset()` then interpolates that value into a raw `WHERE` clause on the ordered column (`... WHERE audit_log_entry.datetime <= %s`). For audit logs the column is a timestamp, so comparing it to an integer either raises a Postgres "operator does not exist: timestamp with time zone <= bigint" error or produces wrong ordering. `DateTimePaginator` deliberately overrides this method to convert the cursor value back with `datetime.fromtimestamp(value / multiplier)`; the optimized paginator must do the same (or reuse `DateTimePaginator`) for datetime-ordered querysets. Any request carrying a cursor (page 2+) will fail or paginate incorrectly.

enable_advanced_features kwarg is not accepted by Endpoint.paginate

`self.paginate(...)` is `Endpoint.paginate`, whose signature is `(request, queryset, order_by, paginator_cls, on_results, default_per_page, max_per_page, max_hits, count_hits, known_hits, cursor)`. It has no `enable_advanced_features` parameter and does not forward arbitrary kwargs to the paginator constructor (it instantiates `paginator_cls(queryset, order_by=..., on_results=..., max_limit=...)`). Passing `enable_advanced_features=True` therefore raises `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'`, so a superuser/global-access user requesting `?optimized_pagination=true` gets a 500 instead of an optimized page. If a constructor option is needed it must be threaded through `paginate` explicitly.

Switching paginator class by query param breaks cursor continuity

The endpoint chooses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` vs `DateTimePaginator` from the client-supplied `optimized_pagination=true` query param, but the two paginators encode the cursor `value` differently: `DateTimePaginator` uses millisecond epoch values and converts them back with `datetime.fromtimestamp`, while `OptimizedCursorPaginator` stores/interprets the raw field value. The `next`/`prev` cursor links generated by `paginate` do not include `optimized_pagination=true`, so a client that follows a next link silently falls back to `DateTimePaginator` with a cursor produced under different semantics, yielding wrong pages or SQL errors. For all valid (non-negative) cursors it is a no-op, so it does not add the advertised negative-offset capability; it only turns a previously-erroring malformed cursor (negative offset on a forward cursor) into a silent first-page response. That masks client/API bugs and is inconsistent with the other paginators that raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. The added comment says negative offsets are allowed for "advanced pagination scenarios", but the diff only adds a comment—`self.offset = int(offset)` is unchanged. false_positives.candidate:
Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs

FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown. Both APIs were added in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs, q.shutdown raises AttributeError, which the broad except swallows, so blocked worker threads are never woken. Each worker.join(timeout=5.0) then waits the full 5 seconds, meaning shutdown takes 100 seconds with the default 20 queues and leaves the threads alive. Separately, if a worker ever hits the except queue.ShutDown clause, evaluating the missing attribute raises another AttributeError and kills that worker. Use an Event/sentinel-based shutdown compatible with the supported Python version.

Shared queue pool is permanently shut down and then reused

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and reuses it for every create_with_partitions call, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down all queues and workers. On a Kafka rebalance Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again with the same factory, so the new strategy gets an already shut-down pool. With queue shutdown available, put() raises ShutDown, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches it, marks the offset complete, and the background commit loop commits it, silently dropping messages. Without queue shutdown, the workers are gone and the offsets may never complete. The pool should be owned by the strategy or recreated for each strategy instance, not shut down from close() while the factory still holds it.

Queues are unbounded, so submit applies no backpressure

Each queue is created as queue.Queue() with the default maxsize of 0, which is infinite, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always enqueues immediately. poll() only emits a metric and never blocks or rejects based on queue depth. A single slow subscription can therefore grow its queue without bound while the consumer keeps polling and decoding messages, increasing memory use and accumulating an uncommitted Kafka backlog until the process is OOM-killed. This contradicts the class docstring's claim of natural backpressure; use a bounded queue and block or apply another explicit backpressure policy.

Failed work items are still marked offset-complete

OrderedQueueWorker.run has a finally block that unconditionally calls complete_offset(), including when result_processor raises and the exception is merely logged by the generic except. Once the offset is removed from outstanding, OffsetTracker will treat it as processed and the commit loop will commit past it, so the failed result is acknowledged to Kafka and will not be retried. This also contradicts the strategy docstring that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Failed offsets should remain outstanding or be sent through an explicit retry/DLQ path, not completed as if the work succeeded.

Shutdown stops workers before draining queued items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False), but each worker checks while not self.shutdown before calling get() again. A worker that finishes its current item therefore exits immediately, leaving any remaining items in the queue even though immediate=False was requested. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close also joins the commit thread before shutting the pool down, so work processed during shutdown is not committed. The net effect is that graceful shutdown abandons buffered results and relies on Kafka redelivery, contrary to the graceful-drain behavior implied by the code and docstrings.

Error-handling test is timing-dependent and asserts the wrong outcome

The test makes the first result processor call raise and the second succeed, then asserts that no offset was committed for the partition. In the implementation, OrderedQueueWorker completes the offset in its finally block even when processing raised, so both offsets become complete and the background commit loop should eventually commit the partition. The test only sleeps 0.2 seconds after processing finishes, while the commit loop wakes every 1 second, so it usually passes before the commit happens and will flake when setup or processing takes slightly longer. It therefore does not reliably verify the intended error semantics; it should either assert the actual expected commit behavior or the production code should keep failed offsets outstanding.
