Changing span buffer keys from sets to sorted sets breaks existing Redis data during rollout

Span buffers are stored at `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id`. Before this change those keys are Redis sets; this diff starts writing them with `ZADD` and later calls `ZCARD`/`ZSCAN`/`ZUNIONSTORE` (`buffer.py` lines 197 and 434, plus `add-buffer.lua`). During a rolling deploy, any old set key touched by the new consumer, or any old consumer touching a new zset key, will get a `WRONGTYPE` error. Existing keys have a TTL up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600 seconds), so affected batches can fail and spans/segments can be lost or stuck until keys expire. There is no dual read/write path, versioned key prefix, or migration/flush step.

Span buffer hard-codes 1000-span cap and ignores SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans

Eviction is now `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...)` inside the Lua script, while the Python span-count check was removed from `_load_segment_data`. `SpansBuffer` still exposes `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) and passes nothing to the script, so any configured value is silently ignored and the actual limit is always 1000, which is also one lower than the default. Operators/tests cannot tune the cap, and the Python span-count safety check no longer matches the Lua behavior.

ZUNIONSTORE sums duplicate timestamp scores instead of preserving the latest

The script uses `zunionstore set_key, 2, set_key, span_key` (and the same for `parent_key`) without an `AGGREGATE` option. Redis's default is `SUM`, so if a span payload is present in both source sets its score becomes the sum of two `end_timestamp_precise` values rather than the max/latest timestamp. This occurs routinely with at-least-once duplicate/reprocessed spans: a duplicate child is re-added under its parent key and then merged into the destination where the first copy already exists. Since `ZPOPMIN` later uses the score to decide which spans to evict, duplicated spans can be moved to the wrong end of the ordering and be kept or evicted incorrectly. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` or otherwise define duplicate-score handling.

No test exercises the new ZPOPMIN eviction path

All buffer tests still use only a handful of spans, so the new >1000-span eviction path is completely untested. There is no coverage for the cap being enforced, eviction ordering by `end_timestamp_precise`, retention of a root/segment span, or cleanup/redirect behavior for evicted spans. A regression here silently drops span data, so a test with more than 1000 spans should verify the resulting segment contents and Redis key cleanup.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator and audit-log branch have no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new ~90-line paginator used by the audit-log endpoint, but no test instantiates it or calls the endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true`. Basic coverage would have caught both the datetime `TypeError` and the negative-offset `ValueError`. Add tests for first/next/prev pages, forged negative offsets, and the audit-log optimized path.

This is an abrupt behavior change unrelated to the eviction work and has no test; either restore the old bound or justify and test the new one.

`self.request` is a `rest_framework.request.Request`, whose `GET` attribute is a read-only property. `self.request.GET = QueryDict("")` and the later assignments at lines 79, 83, 87, 97, and 100 raise `AttributeError: can't set attribute`, so the new helper tests never run. Build the query string through `RequestFactory().get("/", data=...)` or set the underlying `_request.GET` instead.

Discover eligibility uses a naive substring of request.GET instead of the actual query

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True for any raw request query containing `event.type:error`, so it also matches negated or mixed queries such as `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. It also ignores the actual `query` argument passed to `_get_event_stats`; dashboard split calls with derived `errors_only_query`/`transactions_only_query` are judged against the original request query instead. This can apply `upsampled_count()` to transaction rows where `sample_weight` is absent, or skip upsampling for an error-only derived query, producing incorrect counts.

Cache key uses Python hash and can collide across project sets

The eligibility cache key is `error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}`. Different project sets can produce the same Python hash, so a cached allowlist result for one set can be reused for another set in the same organization, causing `upsampled_count()` to run for non-allowlisted projects and inflating counts. Use the serialized sorted project IDs (or a cryptographic digest) as the key instead.

Internal upsampled_count function is exposed to user queries

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction does not set `private=True`, unlike neighboring internal functions such as `count_if`. User-supplied queries can therefore request `yAxis=upsampled_count()` directly, bypassing the allowlist/dataset/query checks in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and obtaining sample-weighted counts for arbitrary projects. Mark it private if it is only intended to be emitted internally.

Top-events ordering and equations still use unsampled count()

Only `timeseries_columns` is transformed to `upsampled_count()`; `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` and `equations=self.get_equation_list(...)` still use raw `count()`. For topEvents requests, the top-N groups are selected and ranked by unsampled counts while the returned series shows upsampled counts, and equations containing `count()` remain unsampled. Apply the transform to orderby/equations or reject those combinations.

Upsampling transform applied even when the discover query uses the metrics layer

The endpoint can route a discover query through the metrics layer via `use_metrics_layer` (line 311), but `upsampled_count` was only registered in `DiscoverDataset`. The transform at line 296 is applied based solely on dataset/request and does not check `forceMetricsLayer` or the `organizations:use-metrics-layer` feature, so in that configuration the generated metrics-layer query can reference an unknown `upsampled_count()` function. Gate the transform on the metrics-layer setting or register the function there.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache has no invalidation and can override fresh allows

`Check` returns immediately from `permDenialCache` before consulting `permCache` or the DB, and `permDenialCache.Set` is called after any DB-backed denial. Nothing invalidates these entries when permissions are granted or when a new dashboard/folder is created. A denied check (for example, before a just-created dashboard's creator permission is visible, or before an admin grants a role) therefore keeps returning Allowed=false for the 30s shortCacheTTL even after the DB grants access. This also means a stale denial overrides a later-refreshed allow in permCache, which directly undermines the PR goal of making newly created resources accessible. Deny entries need invalidation, or must not override a fresh cached allow, and likely deserve a shorter TTL.

Denial cache key uses raw subject ID and omits identity type

The denial-cache key is built from the raw subject ID (`checkReq.UserUID`) before `GetUserIdentifiers` resolves the canonical UID, and it does not include the identity type. The permission cache, in contrast, is keyed by the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID`. The same user can therefore have separate denial entries for `user:123` and `user:<uid>`, so the denial cache is bypassed when the subject form changes. Conversely, identities such as `user:123`, `service-account:123`, or `anonymous:123` share the same denial key even though they can represent different principals; a denial for one can be served for another until TTL expiry. Resolve the subject first and include the identity type plus canonical UID, and escape or hash the key components.

No test that Check populates the denial cache

The new test for the denial cache only seeds `permDenialCache` manually; it does not exercise a normal denied `Check` and verify that the denial entry is written. A bug in the key used by `s.permDenialCache.Set` or a missed Set call would pass the current tests. Add a case with a denying fake permission store that asserts a second identical `Check` is served from the denial cache without incrementing `store.calls` and still returns Allowed=false.

The final value is still correct, but N concurrent requests produce N serialized disk reads/parses instead of one, and every queued request is blocked for the whole duration of the I/O. This is the classic double-checked-locking omission: re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and return the cached value early.

The ruler-based equivalent gates these on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule`, which is also true for Grafana-managed recording rules, and Grafana recording rules can be paused and exported. In the new list view (where only the prom-based ability is available) the Export item therefore disappears for Grafana recording rules, and Pause would be reported unsupported (currently masked by the separate `rulerRule` guard in AlertRuleMenu). Use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule` for the actions that apply to recording rules, and keep `alertingRule` only for Silence.

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader.GrafanaRuleListItem` built the view link with `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })`, where `returnTo = createReturnTo()`. The new component uses `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` without the `returnTo` query parameter. The rule view page uses `returnTo` to render its back link to the page the user came from (e.g. a filtered/paginated list); without it users are sent to the default destination instead of the list they navigated from. Restore the `returnTo` parameter (the AlertRuleMenu export item still relies on this mechanism).

Comment and variable name still describe ruler-rule preloading that was removed

The ruler prefetch (`alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)`) was removed from `useGrafanaGroupsGenerator`, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX..." and the local variable is still called `cacheAndRulerPreload`. Both now describe behaviour that no longer exists and will mislead future readers into thinking ruler rules are still fetched here; update the comment and rename the variable (e.g. `cachePreload`).

No test covers Delete/Silence in the prom-only list; the new test asserts the broken behaviour

The new "should render correct menu actions" test grants AlertingRuleDelete and per-folder delete permissions but then asserts `expect(menuItems.length).toBe(4)` (Silence, Copy link, Duplicate, Export), i.e. it locks in the fact that Delete is missing from the prom-only list view; it also never clicks Silence even though the drawer cannot render without a ruler rule. Additionally, `RulesTable.test.tsx` mocks `useRulerRuleAbilities`/`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` wholesale, so the `(ruler ability) || (prom ability)` combination logic is never exercised with real hooks, and the newly added `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`/`useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` have no direct unit tests for provisioned rules or folder-loading states. Add at least one test that grants delete/silence and verifies the actions actually work in the prom-only list.

Interpolation before querySupportsSplitting bypasses the $__range guard

runSplitQuery applies template variables to every target at line 299 before partitioning with querySupportsSplitting. applyTemplateVariables resolves $__range against the full request range and removes the token, so isQueryWithRangeVariable in querySupportsSplitting no longer detects these queries and they are split. Each time chunk then keeps the full-range duration (for example rate({...}[$__range]) becomes rate({...}[2d]) in every 1-day chunk), producing overlapping or double-counted results; these queries were previously left unsplit specifically to avoid that. Check the range variable on the raw expression before interpolation, or carry the original expression through to the guard.

Targets are interpolated twice on the shard-splitting path

runShardSplitQuery maps every target through applyTemplateVariables here, and then each shard group calls runSplitQuery, which applies applyTemplateVariables again (querySplitting.ts:299). Template interpolation is not idempotent: a literal escaped dollar such as $$__range becomes $__range after the first pass and is substituted on the second, and variable values containing $ are re-expanded. The new test expecting 5 applyTemplateVariables calls (one initial plus four shard groups) asserts this double interpolation. Pass already-interpolated targets to the nested splitting call or add an option to skip interpolation there.

Empty-after-interpolation targets are not filtered out

The expr filter runs before applyTemplateVariables. A query whose whole expression is a variable (for example $query) passes the filter even when interpolation produces an empty string, so runSplitQuery can execute datasource.runQuery with an empty expr. On the shard path the same ordering in shardQuerySplitting.ts:50 lets such an empty target reach groupTargetsByQueryType; when it is later passed to runSplitQuery it is filtered out and can leave the grouped request list empty, causing the Math.max/undefined access in runSplitGroupedQueries to fail. Filter again after mapping, as the old shard code did, or map before filtering.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert device limiting is not atomic and allows exceeding the limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` first calls `CountDevices` and, only if `count < deviceLimit`, runs a separate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. The count and the insert are independent statements with no transaction, lock, or conditional insert. Under concurrency, two first-time requests from different new devices can both observe `count < deviceLimit` and both insert, so the number of tracked devices exceeds the configured `device_limit`. Because tagging now runs synchronously on the authentication path, this race is easy to trigger with parallel browser sessions. The limit needs to be enforced atomically (e.g. a single conditional insert that also checks the count, or serialization via a lock), otherwise the configured limit is only advisory.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same count-then-insert race: concurrent requests can pass the device count check and insert devices beyond the configured limit. Both recommend atomic enforcement or locking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero affected rows is conflated with 'device limit reached', producing false limit errors

`updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever the UPDATE affects 0 rows. Zero rows means 'no row matched the WHERE clause', which also happens for legitimate cases that are not a limit breach: (a) a device that already exists but has not been updated in the last 30 days is excluded from `CountDevices` but its old `updated_at` is outside the `BETWEEN now-30d AND now+1m` window, so it can never be re-activated while the store is at capacity and is incorrectly reported as 'limit reached'; (b) on MySQL, `RowsAffected` reports *changed* rows, so if client_ip/user_agent are unchanged and `updated_at` is truncated to the same value the row matches but 0 rows are reported, yielding a false limit error. The error means 'could not refresh this device', not specifically 'limit reached', so callers and users are misled.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: updateDevice incorrectly treats zero affected rows as ErrDeviceLimitReached, even though zero rows can indicate no matching device or a device outside the update time window. The candidate's additional MySQL example does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed because the local cache is populated before the DB write succeeds

In `tagDeviceUI` the device's cache key is written (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`, line 87) *before* `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs (line 93). With the new `return err` at line 147, `ErrDeviceLimitReached` now propagates through `TagDevice` into `Anonymous.Authenticate`, which returns `nil, err` and fails the request. But the cache entry set on line 87 is never removed on failure. On the next request from the same device (within the 29-minute cache TTL) `tagDeviceUI` hits the cache and returns nil without touching the DB, so `Authenticate` succeeds. Net effect: the limit only fails the very first request per device per 29 minutes and is trivially bypassed by reloading the page; furthermore, an expired device that `updateDevice` refuses to update still reaches the app on retry without ever being recorded, so it never counts toward the limit. The cache must only be populated after a successful write, and `ErrDeviceLimitReached` must not be masked by a cache hit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the cache entry after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit for the 29-minute cache lifetime.

false_positives.candidate:
Device-limit rejection is returned as a raw error and surfaces as an internal server error

When `TagDevice` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, `Authenticate` returns `nil, err`. That error is a plain `fmt.Errorf` with no HTTP status mapping, so the authn middleware has no way to translate it and the client over the limit receives an internal-server (500) response rather than a defined status such as 403/429. The raw 'device limit reached' string is also exposed. A dedicated typed/status error should be returned so the caller can respond with a meaningful status and message.

Anonymous authentication now performs a synchronous DB call using the request context

The previous implementation tagged the device in a detached goroutine (`context.Background()` with a 2-minute timeout and a panic recovery). The new code calls `TagDevice(ctx, ...)` inline in `Authenticate` with the inbound request context. This adds a DB round-trip (a count plus an upsert) to the anonymous auth path, makes tagging fail if the inbound request context is cancelled or short-lived, and removes the panic recovery so a panic in tagging now propagates into authentication. If synchronous enforcement is required, at least keep panic recovery and use a bounded/detached context rather than the raw request context.

Provider signature changed without regenerating wire_gen.go

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` changed its dependency from `anonstore.AnonStore` to `db.DB`, and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an extra `int64` argument for which there is no wire provider. `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` is registered through Grafana's wire dependency graph, and `pkg/server/wire_gen.go` is generated but committed. That file is not part of this PR, so it still calls the old signature and the build will fail to compile unless `wire_gen.go` (and any wire set referencing `ProvideAnonDBStore`) is regenerated.

No test covers the primary enforcement path or the cache-driven bypass

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a brand-new device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached` a single time; it does not assert that an existing, in-window device can still be successfully re-tagged while the store is at capacity (the main reason for `updateDevice`), nor does it exercise the end-to-end rejection through `Anonymous.Authenticate`. `impl_test.go` only runs with the default limit of 0. As a result, neither the retry-after-error bypass (cache set before write, see impl.go) nor the false-limit cases in `updateDevice` are caught by the tests.

Frontend type allows undefined but backend always sends 0

`anonymousDeviceLimit` is typed `number | undefined` here (and defaulted to `undefined` in `GrafanaBootConfig`), but the backend DTO field `FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit int64` has no `omitempty`, so the JSON always contains the key and it is `0` when the feature is unlimited. Consumers that test `=== undefined` to detect 'not configured' will never match; they must treat `0` (or `<= 0`) as unlimited. Either make the DTO field a pointer with `omitempty` or type it as `number` and document that 0 means unlimited.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded for controller requests

`translate` still only calls `load_locale(config.locale)` for the current locale, and the only place that calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is `ApplicationController#set_locale` (application_controller.rb:159). Because the patched `load_translations` forces explicit loading and `load_locale` is the only loader, any translation performed outside a web request (Sidekiq/background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, the console, or `I18n.with_locale` / `I18n.t(key, locale: x)` inside a request) will try the fallback chain (`SiteSetting.default_locale`, `:en`) without those locale files ever having been loaded. When the requested locale lacks a key, the fallback lookup then misses and the caller gets a missing translation/raw key instead of the site-default/English string. For example, a job running under `I18n.locale = 'de'` on a site whose default locale is `'fr'` never loads `fr`, so a missing German key cannot fall back to French. Ensure the whole fallback chain is loaded whenever a locale is loaded (e.g. make `load_locale`/`translate` call `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for each entry of `I18n.fallbacks[locale]`), not only from the controller before_filter.

Fallback chain recomputes a SiteSetting lookup on the translation hot path

`I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on every `I18n.translate`/`I18n.exists?` that reaches the backend (i.e. every translation not served from the translate accelerator's LRU cache), and this `[]` override calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` each time. That turns a previously pure in-memory fallback-list lookup into a site-setting lookup on the hot translation path and, via `set_locale`, once per request. It also means an early `I18n.t` (boot initializers, asset precompilation, rake tasks, console before the DB/Redis are available) now attempts to read site settings and can raise instead of simply returning a translation. Memoize the default locale / compute the chain once per locale and invalidate it on reload.

No tests for the new fallback behavior, which is now enabled in every environment

The PR changes translation resolution globally (fall back to the site default locale, then English) but adds no specs covering `FallbackLocaleList#[]`, the fallback ordering, or `ensure_loaded!`. Additionally, `I18n.fallbacks = FallbackLocaleList.new` runs in every environment, while the `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` lines that were removed only existed in production/profile/Cloud66, so fallbacks now also apply in test/development where they were previously unset. Tests that assert a missing key is returned verbatim, or that a given locale has no translation, will now silently receive the site-default/English string. Add tests for the new fallback chain and confirm the intended test-environment behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Unconditional visible assignment can hide groups on partial updates

`update` always executes `group.visible = params[:visible] == "true"`. A PATCH or PUT that omits `visible`—including the old PATCH membership-changes API that still routes to `update` because `resources :groups` accepts PATCH—now sets `visible` to false and saves. The old `update_patch` membership add/delete handling was also removed, so such requests no longer update memberships and can silently make the group invisible. Only assign `visible` when the parameter is present, and either support or explicitly reject the old PATCH contract.

Public members endpoint accepts unbounded and negative pagination values

`limit` and `offset` are taken directly from public query parameters and passed into `.limit(...).offset(...)`. A caller can request a very large limit, causing an unnecessarily large database result and JSON serialization, or pass negative values that can produce SQL errors/500 responses. Clamp `limit` to a sane maximum and enforce `offset >= 0`.

Public group member list truncates at 50 with no pagination

The backend now returns only one page of members (default limit 50), and the public group-members route never requests another page. This template simply iterates `members` and has no pagination controls. Groups with more than 50 members will silently show only the first 50, whereas non-automatic groups previously returned all members. Either add paging or explicitly fetch all members for the public view.

Removing the last member on the last page leaves an invalid offset

`removeMember` deletes the user and then calls `findMembers()` with the current offset. If the removed user was the only member on the current page (for example 51 members at offset 50), the new total becomes 50 but the request still uses offset 50, so the reload returns an empty page and the UI stays on an invalid blank page. Adjust the offset when it reaches or exceeds the new `user_count` after deletion.

`usernames` is state on the singleton admin group controller and is not reset after `addMembers` or when `setupController` switches to another group. After adding users to group A, selecting group B leaves the old usernames in the selector; clicking Add again can add those stale users to group B unintentionally. Clear the property after each add and when the model changes (the existing TODO acknowledges this).

Creating a group ignores the selected alias level

The client’s `Group.asJSON()` sends `alias_level` when creating a group, and the admin template exposes the alias selector for new groups, but `create` only assigns `name` and `visible`. A newly created group therefore silently loses the selected alias level and falls back to the database default. Assign `group.alias_level = params[:alias_level].to_i` when present.

Public members endpoint response shape is a breaking change

`/groups/:group_id/members.json` previously returned a JSON array of users; it now returns an object of the form `{members: [...], meta: {...}}`. The in-repo JavaScript client was updated, but any plugin, mobile app, or external consumer expecting the old array will break. If this endpoint is part of the public API, either maintain backward compatibility or introduce a versioned/new endpoint.

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation triggers a DB write and double-counts blocked-email statistics

`EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and `should_block?` (app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 12-17) loads the matching record, increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and calls `record.save`. This means a simple `valid?`/`save` check now performs a database write. In `UsersController#create` the user is validated twice on the same request: `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), so a single signup attempt against a blocked (or even `do_nothing`) email increments `match_count` by 2 instead of 1. Match counts will be inflated unpredictably, defeating the purpose of these statistics for spotting spam campaigns, and read-only validation paths unexpectedly mutate the DB. The stat update should be decoupled from the pure predicate and triggered once per real block event (e.g., after a confirmed rejection), not on every validation invocation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: the blocked-email predicate updates statistics and writes to the database during what should be a read-only check. The candidate adds a double-counting example rather than emphasizing race conditions, but the core concern matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and bypassable

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` compares the raw submitted email against the stored string with exact case. E-mail addresses are treated case-insensitively in practice, and nothing downcases the user's email when it is set/validated (`User.new_from_params` stores it verbatim). So an entry for `spam@bad.com` will not block a signup using `Spam@Bad.com` or `spam@BAD.com`, and imported/manually-entered records in mixed case won't match either — trivially bypassing the blocklist. Normalize on both sides: downcase/`Email.downcase` the value in `should_block?` (and ideally normalize the stored `email` in a `before_validation`/`before_save` so the unique index also behaves case-insensitively).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, allowing blocked users to bypass the blocklist by changing the capitalization of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic counter update loses matches under concurrency

`should_block?` performs a read-modify-write: `record.match_count += 1; record.save`. Two concurrent requests matching the same blocked email both read count N and write N+1, losing one increment. Since these counters are the signal used to identify spam waves (exactly when many concurrent attempts happen), the undercounting is most severe in the scenario the data is meant to detect. Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now])` (or `increment_counter`) instead.

The only new validator specs stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so they neither exercise the actual database lookup/scoping nor verify the end-to-end behavior (`user.valid?` returning false for a blocked email). More importantly, this PR moves the `email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` logic out of `User#email_validator` into `EmailValidator`, but no spec covers that moved logic (whitelist pass/fail, blacklist pass/fail). A regression in the relocated domain-restriction behavior would go undetected. Add specs covering the whitelist and blacklist branches (and ideally one integration spec that a blocked email makes a `User` invalid), plus a test for the new `errors`/`values` fields returned by `UsersController#create`.

The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. The same applies to images where an admin deliberately configured a limit below 10MB. In addition, the 413 handler at line 246 now reports `max_size_kb: 10MB` regardless of the web server's real limit, so the error message can be wrong. The controller's new resize path calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(..., allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)`. When that setting is false (the default), `optimize` selects `downsize_instructions`, whose command contains `#{from}[0]`, i.e. only the first frame of a multi-frame GIF. Because the downsized temp file replaces the upload, an animated GIF larger than `max_image_size_kb` is permanently stored as a static single-frame image, silently destroying the user's animation. The animated instruction set is only used when the setting is explicitly enabled. Animated uploads should either always go through the animated/`gifsicle` path or be exempted from automatic downsizing.

Repeatedly applying `-resize 80%` five times yields only 0.8^5 ≈ 0.33 of the original, so a file more than roughly 3x `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` is still oversized after the loop and `Upload.create_for` then rejects it. The advertised feature (accept large images by shrinking them) therefore still fails for genuinely large uploads, e.g. a 10MB image on a 1MB limit. Each pass is also a separate lossy re-encode (no `-quality` specified), so intermediate steps degrade the image more than necessary. The required scale factor should be computed from `tempfile.size / limit` (or the loop should recompute a percentage from the current size) rather than using fixed 80% steps.

The guard only checks `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)`, and that helper's image list includes SVG, so an SVG larger than `max_image_size_kb` is fed to `OptimizedImage.downsize` → `convert`. `OptimizedImage.create_for` deliberately special-cases `.svg` (it copies the file instead of calling `resize`), showing that `convert` is not suitable for vector files. For a 60-minute slot starting 12:00 when a fixed host's working hours end at 12:30, `end > workingHour.endTime` is `720 > 750`, so the slot is not rejected even though it ends at 13:00. If a date override with equal start and end is used to represent an unavailable day, that case is never detected; only slots before the override are rejected, and the slot at the override start can be treated as available. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: strict equality compares distinct Dayjs object references rather than date values, making the comparison false. Both recommend using .isSame() instead.

false_positives.candidate:

When a slot falls inside a user's date override, `dateOverrideExist` is true and `checkIfIsAvailable` returns true before reaching the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom. A date override replaces working hours, not existing bookings/calendar busy time, so a fixed host with an override 10:00-14:00 and an existing booking 11:00-12:00 will still make the 11:00 round-robin slot pass. That can lead to double booking the fixed host. Only bypass the normal working-hours check for an override; the busy check must still run.

Date override check accepts slots only partially inside the override

The containment test rejects a slot only when it ends at/before the override start or when it starts after the override end. It never checks that the slot end is within the override end (or that the slot start is at/after the override start). For an override 10:00-11:00, a 60-minute slot 09:30-10:30 or 10:30-11:30 falls through, sets `dateOverrideExist`, and returns true. In round-robin events, aggregate slots generated from another host can therefore be accepted for a fixed host even though they are only partially within the fixed host's override. Require the whole slot to be inside the override.

Working-hours check tests only the first matching day and ignores days with no hours

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true as soon as it sees the first entry whose `days` includes the slot's UTC day and the slot is outside that one interval. With split availability (09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00), a 13:30 slot is outside the first interval, so the host is marked unavailable even though the second interval contains it. Conversely, if no working-hour entry includes the slot's day, `find` returns undefined and the function falls through to the busy check, treating the fixed host as available on a day they do not work. Date override date comparison mixes server-local and UTC dates

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` formats in the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime` is a `.utc()` Dayjs. On self-hosted servers not running in UTC, the shifted override date is compared to a UTC slot date, so date overrides can be missed or matched to the wrong day. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` (and end) for the date/range calculations so both sides use UTC.

`activeOverrides` compares `dayjs.utc(override.start)`—where `override.start` is the organizer's wall-clock date/time stored as UTC—against the invitee day boundaries. The new conversion below explicitly treats it as wall time by subtracting the organizer offset, but this filter does not. For example, with an organizer in UTC+14, an override at local D 01:00 is stored as D 01:00Z but actually occurs at D-1 11:00Z; when an invitee in UTC views day D-1, the stored value is outside that invitee day, so the override is ignored and normal working hours are used. Convert the override to actual UTC (or to the invitee timezone) before deciding whether it belongs to the invitee day.

The only added test changes the invitee timezone for a personal event. It does not exercise the PR's main claim: a round-robin event with a fixed host whose date override should constrain available slots. There are also no tests for a fixed host with busy time inside an override, slots partially overlapping an override, or split working hours. These missing cases would have caught the early return that skips busy checks and the working-hours containment bugs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Both increment sites (the `else` branch here and the one at line 195) compute `reminder.retryCount + 1` in application code from the value returned by the earlier `findMany`. If two cron invocations overlap — plausible because the per-reminder loop awaits a `profile.findFirst` and `getBookerBaseUrl` call for every reminder, so a run can exceed the cron interval — both read the same retryCount and write the same value. Failures are then under-counted and a persistently failing reminder may never reach the `> 1` threshold, so it is retried indefinitely and the PR's retry cap never takes effect. Use Prisma's atomic `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` instead.

This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

retryCount cleanup clause is not scoped to SMS/unscheduled reminders

The new deletion branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` inside the `OR` is not restricted by `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` or `scheduled: false`, unlike the pre-existing branch next to it. As written, any WorkflowReminder row (email, WhatsApp, or an already-scheduled reminder) whose retryCount is greater than 1 is hard-deleted on each cron run. Today only this handler increments retryCount, but the column lives on the shared model, so as soon as another scheduler writes retryCount — or a concurrent run manages to schedule a reminder after it has already been bumped twice — unrelated reminders are silently purged, and an already-scheduled reminder is deleted without cancelling its provider-side scheduled message (referenceId), leaving an orphaned SMS/email job that will still fire. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing SMS-method filter on the retryCount > 1 OR deletion branch, which causes non-SMS reminders such as Email and WhatsApp to be deleted. Its additional concerns about scheduled reminders do not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders that cannot be attempted never increment retryCount and are retried forever

retryCount is only incremented when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy or throws. When `sendTo` is missing (e.g. an SMS_ATTENDEE reminder for a booking with no `smsReminderNumber`, or an SMS_NUMBER step with an empty `sendTo`) or the computed `message` is empty, the `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` guard simply skips the reminder. Those rows stay `scheduled: false` forever, are re-fetched on every cron run, and are skipped again — exactly the unbounded-rescheduling behavior this PR is meant to stop. A missing phone number is one of the common failure modes, so this path needs to bump retryCount (or delete the reminder) when the reminder cannot be attempted.

The `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` added inside the catch block is not itself protected. If it throws (row deleted concurrently by the cleanup query, or a transient DB error), the exception escapes the `catch` and the `for` loop, so all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are left unprocessed and the endpoint returns a 500. Additionally, this catch also runs when `twilio.scheduleSMS` succeeded but the subsequent `update({ scheduled: true, referenceId })` threw; in that case retryCount is bumped even though a Twilio message is already scheduled, so the reminder is re-sent on the next run (duplicate SMS) and then eventually deleted while the Twilio job remains live. The `retryCount > 1` condition has no index, and mixing it in an `OR` with the indexed `(method, scheduledDate)` predicate means Postgres cannot satisfy the whole query from the existing composite index. WorkflowReminder is a high-volume table (one row per reminder per booking), so every cron invocation can fall back to a sequential scan of the whole table. The comment says "delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date", but the query now also deletes unscheduled SMS (and, due to the unscoped OR branch, non-SMS) reminders that have exceeded the retry limit. The comment should be updated to reflect both deletion conditions so future readers understand that the cleanup is not limited to past-due reminders.

The schema's `zod` and `kysely` generators write committed outputs (`packages/prisma/zod/*`, `packages/prisma/kysely/types.ts`). This PR adds `retryCount` to `WorkflowReminder` and the migration, but does not update those generated files, so the WorkflowReminder zod schema and the Kysely `WorkflowReminder` interface still lack the new column. Any code that validates a reminder via the generated zod schema will silently drop retryCount, and Kysely-typed queries cannot reference it; the repository's prisma-generate check will also fail or produce a dirty diff. When scope is `team` or `org` and no filter conditions are supplied, `getBaseConditions()` returns `authConditions` directly. For those scopes `authConditions` is a top-level `OR` such as `(team booking) OR (user booking)`. If a caller appends another predicate, e.g. `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" >= ...`, SQL precedence makes it `(team booking) OR ((user booking) AND date filter)`, so the extra predicate is applied only to one branch. The returned fragment should always be wrapped in parentheses, otherwise date/security predicates can be silently skipped for part of the dataset.

The service builds org/team and combined-filter conditions through `reduce` using nested fragments like `Prisma.sql`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` and `Prisma.sql`(${acc}) AND (${condition})`. The expectations at lines 295, 332, and 429 are single flat `Prisma.sql` templates. `Prisma.Sql` equality is structural over its internal `strings` and `values`, not based on the rendered SQL text, so a nested fragment built with `reduce` will not deep-equal a flat template even when the SQL renders identically. These assertions will fail; compare rendered SQL or execute the query instead of using `toEqual` on `Prisma.Sql` objects.

The expected SQL hard-codes the order of `teamIds` and user IDs inside `ANY([...])`. `teamIds` comes from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId` and user IDs come from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`; neither call specifies an `orderBy`. If Postgres returns those rows in a different order, the `ANY` arrays differ even though the authorization semantics are identical, and the exact `Prisma.sql` comparison fails intermittently. Sort the IDs before asserting or compare semantically.

No database execution coverage for org/team `ANY` conditions

The only test that actually executes the generated conditions against Postgres uses `scope: "user"`. The org/team authorization paths, which are the only places that emit `ANY(${array})`, are only compared as `Prisma.sql` strings and never run against the database. A real parameter-binding/type-inference problem in those paths (for example around array parameters) would therefore pass the test suite while failing in production. Add a `$queryRaw` execution test for at least one org/team scope.

Worse, two concurrent requests with *different* codes each write back a list derived from the same original snapshot, so the last write wins and the code consumed by the other request is silently restored and becomes reusable. FOR UPDATE`), or store codes as individual rows and delete by id/`deleteMany`.

The decoder assumes the encoded prefix is exactly 6 characters and splits it into three fixed 2-character fields. The grant field comes from `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()`, whose contract does not enforce a 2-character value (its Javadoc even says 'usually like 3-letters'). A custom grant returning e.g. `foo` will be encoded successfully as `onrtfoo:<id>`, but `getTokenContextFromTokenId` will then reject it because the prefix is 7 characters. Enforce the length at registration or make the decoder length-aware; otherwise Keycloak can issue tokens that it cannot parse itself.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same mismatch: the Javadoc says shortcuts are 'usually like 3-letters', but the code actually uses 2-letter shortcuts. The golden comment treats this as a documentation inaccuracy. The candidate goes further and calls it a functional bug in the decoder, but it explicitly cites the same Javadoc versus 2-char discrepancy. That makes it the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Incorrect-grant test passes on NPE instead of testing the intended failure

The test's `before` method constructs the factory but never sets a `KeycloakSessionFactory`. Looking up an unknown shortcut such as `ac` therefore calls `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)` on null and throws NPE. The test catches any `RuntimeException`, so it passes without ever verifying the intended `IllegalArgumentException` for an unknown grant shortcut. Initialize the factory dependency and assert the exception type/message.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the test catches a generic RuntimeException when it should check for the specific IllegalArgumentException. The candidate adds that an NPE is what actually gets caught, but its core point and fix are the same: assert the specific exception type.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding non-default getShortcut breaks existing grant provider implementations

`OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` now has a new abstract `getShortcut()` method. Any custom grant factory compiled against an older Keycloak does not implement it. `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls `getShortcut()` for every registered OAuth2 grant factory during server startup, so such an extension will throw `AbstractMethodError` and prevent startup. Make this a default method with a safe fallback, or explicitly tolerate providers that do not implement it.

validateToken unconditionally tags recreated tokens as refresh-token grant

`validateToken` recreates an access token from an existing `oldToken`, and this new line always stores `refresh_token` in `Constants.GRANT_TYPE`. This method is used outside the refresh flow as well (legacy token exchange uses it while validating the subject token and producing the exchanged access token), so those exchanged tokens get the refresh shortcut `rt` instead of the actual token-exchange grant. The grant type should be set by the calling flow, as `StandardTokenExchangeProvider` does, or only set to refresh in the refresh-specific path.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rebuilt federated recovery credential loses the stored credential id

getCredentials() rebuilds the recovery-code credential with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...) but never copies myUser.recoveryCodes.getId(). The reconstructed object therefore has a different (newly generated or null) id than the credential originally stored by updateCredential(). Any caller that identifies the credential by id—account REST deletion or the all-codes-used removal in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator—cannot address the stored credential. Set the id on the reconstructed model from myUser.recoveryCodes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel is rebuilt without copying the id from myUser.recoveryCodes. Both also say this breaks removal by id in the authenticator flow. It is the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery-code creation reads the wrong credential input field

CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential builds the UserCredentialModel as new UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson), which stores the JSON in getValue() and leaves getChallengeResponse() null. This update path reads input.getChallengeResponse() as the credential data, so the federated recovery-code credential is persisted with null credentialData. A later getCredentials() call cannot reconstruct a usable RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel from that data, so the new test will fail when rendering or validating the recovery-code form. Read the value from the UserCredentialModel (or populate challengeResponse in the helper consistently).

All-codes-used removal does not remove federated credentials

After this change getCredential() can return a credential supplied by user storage. When such a credential reports all codes used, this branch calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...), which only removes credentials from Keycloak's local credential store; it does not remove a federated credential from user storage. The exhausted recovery credential therefore remains visible to isConfiguredFor()/getCredential(), and the recovery-code form can still be selected for a credential that has no usable codes (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean may even call get() on an empty next-code Optional). Removal/disablement needs to go through the federated-aware credential-updater API (for example disableCredentialType) or be delegated explicitly to the user-storage provider.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

false_positives.candidate:
Exit code 4 changes meaning from recreate-required to feature-disabled

This PR changes `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` from 4 to 3 and assigns 4 to the new `FEATURE_DISABLED` result. Exit code 4 was the actual value emitted by the previous implementation, so any existing automation that used the real binary contract (rather than the older documentation) will now interpret a disabled-preview-feature result as “recreate upgrade required” and may proceed to shut down the deployment instead of treating the command as unavailable. Since the documentation explicitly calls the exit code the stable scripting interface, avoid reusing the existing numeric code for a new condition or ensure all consumers are updated in the same change.

Documented exit codes are not asserted in the CLI tests

The new feature-disabled test only asserts the error text, not that the command exits with the newly documented code 4. Likewise, `testWrongVersions` only checks the incompatibility message and does not assert that an incompatible result exits with the newly documented code 3. Since the PR changes `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` from 4 to 3 and introduces `FEATURE_DISABLED = 4`, a regression in the exit-code contract would pass these tests even though automation relies on those codes. Add `assertEquals(4, result.exitCode())` for the disabled-feature case and `assertEquals(3, result.exitCode())` for the incompatible-version cases, covering both `metadata` and `check` subcommands where applicable.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client removal event breaks when V2 permissions are enabled

The new listener guard checks only Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, but management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If both features are enabled, ClientRemovedEvent reaches clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...), which ClientPermissionsV2 overrides to throw UnsupportedOperationException, so deleting a client can fail. If only V2 is enabled, the listener is skipped entirely and the deleted client's V2 permission resource/policies are never cleaned up. The guard needs to handle V2 explicitly (skip it or provide a no-op/cleanup implementation).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same root problem: the listener is guarded by the V1 flag instead of V2. It says that when only V2 is enabled, cleanup is skipped and permissions are left orphaned, which is exactly the golden issue. The candidate also raises an extra case (both flags enabled causing an exception), but that does not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-specific resources are looked up with the wrong owner id

The third argument to ResourceStore.findByName is the resource owner. V2 per-resource authorization resources are created with owner resourceServer.getClientId() in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (line 104), but this lookup passes server.getId(), which is the Keycloak client UUID (see AdminPermissionsSchema.isAdminPermissionClient). The lookup therefore misses the per-client resource and falls back to the 'Clients' all-resource, ignoring per-client grants/denials: per-client MANAGE/VIEW grants do not work, and a per-client negative permission can be bypassed by a global allow. The same owner mistake exists at line 244 for the 'Clients' all-resource lookup. Use the same owner as creation or the two-argument findByName.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The per-client resource lookup passes server.getId() as the owner, but creation uses resourceServer.getClientId(), so the lookup misses the resource and falls back to the all-clients resource.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the new Clients scopes/resources

init() returns as soon as realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. Realms that already had the V2 admin-permissions client before this change will therefore never get the newly added Clients scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite) or the 'Clients' all-resource. Creating a client permission later fails in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource when those new scopes are not found ('No scopes found.'), and ClientPermissionsV2 can then fall back to a null resource and NPE in policyStore.findByResource. Initialization needs to be idempotent and upgrade an existing admin-permissions resource server by adding missing scopes/resources.

canExchangeTo now throws UnsupportedOperationException under V2

With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException. Token exchange invokes this evaluator, so token exchange requests will return a 500 instead of a normal authorization decision. Implement the check or return a denial; the other overrides that throw UnsupportedOperationException are similarly reachable from management endpoints and should not leak 500s.

getResourceName does not handle the new Clients resource type

getResourceName only special-cases USERS. For the newly added CLIENTS resource type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is not set for resources created by getOrCreateResource. Client permission resources will therefore be shown with null/empty names instead of the client id or 'All clients' in APIs/UI. Add a CLIENTS branch analogous to the USERS branch.

requireView/requireViewClientScopes Javadoc incorrectly describes return values

The Javadoc for requireView() says 'Returns true if canView() returns true', but the method is void and throws ForbiddenException. The same wrong text is repeated for requireViewClientScopes() at line 101. This contradicts the actual contract and will mislead implementors; document both as throwing ForbiddenException when the corresponding can* check is false.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JVM default KeyStore provider

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type, which is normally SUN, not BouncyCastle. The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning the BouncyCastle security provider, and callers may use the returned provider to resolve BC-specific algorithms or to obtain a provider name. Returning SUN silently gives such callers the wrong provider. Since this minimal authz-client provider has no BouncyCastle dependency, it should return null or throw UnsupportedOperationException rather than return an unrelated provider.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider instead of BouncyCastle.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() was added to the public CryptoProvider SPI as an abstract method. Third-party implementations compiled against the previous version do not implement it, so ServiceLoader can instantiate them but CryptoIntegration.detectProvider's call to CryptoProvider::order throws AbstractMethodError, breaking all crypto initialization. Make order() a default method with a defined fallback order, or otherwise preserve compatibility with legacy providers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider breaks backward compatibility with existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Provider selection is nondeterministic when highest order is tied

detectProvider now sorts all discovered providers by order and returns the first, only logging the rest at debug. All existing built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) still return order 200, so when more than one is visible there is no unique winner and selection depends on ServiceLoader/JAR order. In a FIPS deployment this can silently select the non-FIPS provider, or at minimum construct/register both providers' global security state before ignoring one, defeating FIPS compliance. The previous code failed fast on multiple providers. The selection should fail on a tie for the highest order or the built-in providers need distinct orders.

ES384/ES512 tests do not use P-384/P-521 keys

The test class creates one default EC key pair (typically P-256) and reuses it for testES256, testES384 and testES512. The ES384 and ES512 cases therefore only exercise padding a P-256 signature to 96/132 bytes; they never exercise real P-384/P-521-sized r and s values, nor verify the produced ASN.1 DER against the key. A regression that mishandles full-size ES384/ES512 signatures could pass. Generate the matching curve key pair per algorithm, or use fixed vectors and verify the result.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount now returns null where it previously always returned a count

This method previously never returned null (it either produced a count or threw), so callers had no reason to treat the Long as nullable. With the change, a deleted cached group yields null, which will throw NPE for any caller that auto-unboxes the value (comparisons, arithmetic, or passing it to a primitive parameter) and silently drops the count from serialized representations. The nullability should be documented/handled explicitly, and the callers of GroupModel#getSubGroupsCount audited for unboxing assumptions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same issue: getSubGroupsCount now returns null, which breaks the non-null expectation callers rely on and can cause NPEs. The candidate does not cite the Javadoc contract explicitly, but it makes the same point by saying the method previously never returned null and callers relied on that.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the assertion can miss the exception it is looking for

The reader thread is started and never joined: the main thread deletes the 100 groups, sets deletedAll, and immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty (line 157). Any read request that is still in flight when the last group is deleted - precisely the window in which the NPE occurs - can add its exception to the list after the assertion has already run, so the test can pass even though the bug is present and is inherently racy. In addition, if a remove() call throws before deletedAll is set, this non-daemon thread loops forever, continuing to issue admin requests into subsequent tests and potentially hanging the JVM. The loop should be wrapped in try/finally, the flag set in the finally block, and the thread joined (with a timeout) before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem: the reader thread is never joined, so the assertion that runs right after deletedAll is set can miss exceptions added later, which makes the test racy. The candidate also raises extra points, but they do not change that the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrent-deletion NPE is still reachable through the other getSubGroupsStream overloads

The fix only makes getSubGroupsCount() tolerate modelSupplier.get() returning null. The neighbouring overrides getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) (line 256), getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) (line 262) and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) (line 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` and dereference the result without a null check. When a CachedGroup is read while its row has been deleted concurrently - the exact scenario this PR targets - the delegate returned by modelSupplier is null, so calling these methods on the cached adapter (which is what the paginated/filtered subgroup endpoints do) still throws NPE. The fix is therefore incomplete unless the same null handling is applied there (or the model is fetched and null-checked in one place).

Test never requests subgroup counts, so the method changed by this PR may not be exercised

The reader calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)`, which only fills in search/first/max/briefRepresentation. Subgroup counts are populated only when the request opts into them (the subGroupCount request parameter that leads to GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount), and with briefRepresentation=true and no such flag the server never calls GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount() - the method this PR modifies. If so, the test would pass on the unfixed code and provides no regression coverage. The read request should explicitly ask for subgroup counts (e.g. the overload with the subGroupCount parameter) so getSubGroupsCount() is on the request path.

Unthrottled reader loop hammers the server for the whole duration of the deletions

The background loop has no delay/backoff and repeatedly issues `groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` admin requests as fast as the client can go while 100 groups are deleted sequentially. On CI this generates a large burst of concurrent requests (each building a list of up to 100 groups) that can starve the server, cause timeouts and make the test flaky. Add a small sleep/backoff or cap the number of iterations.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to undefined isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation

UsernameForm.authenticate calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but UsernameForm, UsernamePasswordForm, and AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator do not define a no-argument method with that name. The only method added by this PR is UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel). This is a compile error, so the services module cannot build. The call should pass context.getUser() or use a correctly defined passkeys-enabled helper.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: UsernameForm.authenticate calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, while the method requires a UserModel parameter. The candidate also notes this causes a compile error and suggests passing the user.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Conditional passkeys are no longer rendered when the user is unidentified

isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) returns false when user is null (line 161), but fillContextForm() is now gated on this helper both in authenticate() at line 115 and in the error challenge override at line 137. Before this change, authenticate() filled conditional WebAuthn when context.getUser() was null and challenge(error, field) explicitly filled only when context.getUser() == null. On the first username/password page, after a username-only submission, and after a failed password while the user is still unidentified, fillContextForm() is therefore not called, so the WebAuthn challenge, RP ID, and ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI attributes are absent. Discoverable passkeys will not auto-fill/one-tap and the webauth form is missing, breaking first-login passkey flows and tests that expect //form[@id='webauth'] on those pages. The fill condition must remain true for passkeys-enabled realms even when no user is identified, while also running for known re-authenticating users.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. isConditionalPasskeysEnabled returns false when the user is null, so fillContextForm is skipped on the initial login page and conditional passkey login breaks. The candidate also covers the error challenge path, but its core issue is identical to the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset "advanced" branch raises instead of paginating

When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `start_offset = cursor.offset` and then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django `QuerySet` slicing explicitly rejects a negative start (`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so the comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false and this branch raises a 500 for any cursor carrying a negative offset. Even if the ORM allowed it, negative slicing returns rows from the end of the queryset, which is not the intended "reverse pagination" semantics. Handle negative offsets by clamping/validating (as `OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, and `MergingOffsetPaginator` do with `BadPaginationError`) rather than by slicing with a negative index.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the optimized/advanced paginator slices a Django queryset with a negative offset, which Django does not support, so it raises an error. The exception types differ (AssertionError vs ValueError) depending on Django version, but the underlying issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime fields

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key()` reads the raw model attribute and passes it to `math.floor()` / `math.ceil()`. The audit log endpoint calls this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `getattr(item, "datetime")` is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. Unlike `DateTimePaginator`, this class has no `multiplier` / `strftime("%s.%f")` conversion. Because `build_cursor` calls `key(results[-1])` even on the very first page, every request that reaches this paginator returns HTTP 500, so the optimized branch can never serve a result.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on the datetime value when the audit logs endpoint orders by -datetime, which raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns an int where a datetime is required

`value_from_cursor()` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (an integer/timestamp number). `BasePaginator.build_queryset()` then interpolates that value into a raw `WHERE` clause on the ordered column (`... WHERE audit_log_entry.datetime <= %s`). For audit logs the column is a timestamp, so comparing it to an integer either raises a Postgres "operator does not exist: timestamp with time zone <= bigint" error or produces wrong ordering. `DateTimePaginator` deliberately overrides this method to convert the cursor value back with `datetime.fromtimestamp(value / multiplier)`; the optimized paginator must do the same (or reuse `DateTimePaginator`) for datetime-ordered querysets. Any request carrying a cursor (page 2+) will fail or paginate incorrectly.

enable_advanced_features kwarg is not accepted by Endpoint.paginate

`self.paginate(...)` is `Endpoint.paginate`, whose signature is `(request, queryset, order_by, paginator_cls, on_results, default_per_page, max_per_page, max_hits, count_hits, known_hits, cursor)`. It has no `enable_advanced_features` parameter and does not forward arbitrary kwargs to the paginator constructor (it instantiates `paginator_cls(queryset, order_by=..., on_results=..., max_limit=...)`). Passing `enable_advanced_features=True` therefore raises `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'`, so a superuser/global-access user requesting `?optimized_pagination=true` gets a 500 instead of an optimized page. If a constructor option is needed it must be threaded through `paginate` explicitly.

Switching paginator class by query param breaks cursor continuity

The endpoint chooses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` vs `DateTimePaginator` from the client-supplied `optimized_pagination=true` query param, but the two paginators encode the cursor `value` differently: `DateTimePaginator` uses millisecond epoch values and converts them back with `datetime.fromtimestamp`, while `OptimizedCursorPaginator` stores/interprets the raw field value. The `next`/`prev` cursor links generated by `paginate` do not include `optimized_pagination=true`, so a client that follows a next link silently falls back to `DateTimePaginator` with a cursor produced under different semantics, yielding wrong pages or SQL errors. Likewise a superuser who drops the param cannot resume a pagination session started with it. Cursor values must be interchangeable across the paginators (or the chosen paginator must be encoded in the cursor/links) before letting a request parameter switch implementations.

Negative-offset clamping in BasePaginator silently changes malformed-cursor behavior

For forward cursors (`is_prev` false) this changes `queryset[offset:stop]` to `queryset[max(0, offset):...]`, and for `is_prev` it assigns `offset` unchanged. For all valid (non-negative) cursors it is a no-op, so it does not add the advertised negative-offset capability; it only turns a previously-erroring malformed cursor (negative offset on a forward cursor) into a silent first-page response. That masks client/API bugs and is inconsistent with the other paginators that raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. Either reject negative offsets explicitly or document that they are clamped.

Comment claims negative offsets are supported but no support was added

The added comment says negative offsets are allowed for "advanced pagination scenarios", but the diff only adds a comment—`self.offset = int(offset)` is unchanged. Moreover negative offsets are not actually usable: `OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `MergingOffsetPaginator`, and `CombinedQuerysetPaginator` explicitly raise `BadPaginationError` for negative offsets, and `BasePaginator`'s `is_prev` path still slices with the negative start (which Django rejects). The comment documents behavior that does not exist and will mislead future callers.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the new endpoint branch

The PR adds a new paginator class and a new conditional code path in the audit log endpoint but no tests. Because `OptimizedCursorPaginator` diverges from `BasePaginator`/`DateTimePaginator` in `get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor`, a single test paging an audit-log queryset with `optimized_pagination=true` would have caught the `math.floor(datetime)` crash, the integer-vs-timestamp `WHERE` clause, and the unaccepted `enable_advanced_features` kwarg. Add coverage for the first page, next page, previous page, cursors with non-zero values, and negative/invalid cursor offsets.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No longer serialized: concurrent BuildIndex for the same key races and leaks the losing index

Removing the function-wide cacheMu means two BuildIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource can now run simultaneously (e.g. two Search RPCs that both miss the cache for a key, which is exactly the case the TODO in getOrCreateIndex warns about). Both build a full index, both assign to b.cache[key], and the index that loses the assignment is never closed, leaking file handles/disk (bleve file-backed indexes) or memory. The old coarse lock at least serialized the two builds; if per-key concurrency is now intended, add per-key single-flight and close the replaced index before overwriting the cache entry.
