false_positives.candidate:
Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs

FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown. Both APIs were added in Python 3.13. On the Python versions Sentry currently runs, q.shutdown raises AttributeError, which the broad except swallows, so blocked worker threads are never woken. Each worker.join(timeout=5.0) then waits the full 5 seconds, meaning shutdown takes 100 seconds with the default 20 queues and leaves the threads alive. Separately, if a worker ever hits the except queue.ShutDown clause, evaluating the missing attribute raises another AttributeError and kills that worker. Use an Event/sentinel-based shutdown compatible with the supported Python version.

Shared queue pool is permanently shut down and then reused

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and reuses it for every create_with_partitions call, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which permanently shuts down all queues and workers. On a Kafka rebalance Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions again with the same factory, so the new strategy gets an already shut-down pool. With queue shutdown available, put() raises ShutDown, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches it, marks the offset complete, and the background commit loop commits it, silently dropping messages. Without queue shutdown, the workers are gone and the offsets may never complete. The pool should be owned by the strategy or recreated for each strategy instance, not shut down from close() while the factory still holds it.

Queues are unbounded, so submit applies no backpressure

Each queue is created as queue.Queue() with the default maxsize of 0, which is infinite, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always enqueues immediately. poll() only emits a metric and never blocks or rejects based on queue depth. A single slow subscription can therefore grow its queue without bound while the consumer keeps polling and decoding messages, increasing memory use and accumulating an uncommitted Kafka backlog until the process is OOM-killed. This contradicts the class docstring's claim of natural backpressure; use a bounded queue and block or apply another explicit backpressure policy.

Failed work items are still marked offset-complete

OrderedQueueWorker.run has a finally block that unconditionally calls complete_offset(), including when result_processor raises and the exception is merely logged by the generic except. Once the offset is removed from outstanding, OffsetTracker will treat it as processed and the commit loop will commit past it, so the failed result is acknowledged to Kafka and will not be retried. This also contradicts the strategy docstring that offsets are committed only after successful processing. Failed offsets should remain outstanding or be sent through an explicit retry/DLQ path, not completed as if the work succeeded.

Shutdown stops workers before draining queued items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False), but each worker checks while not self.shutdown before calling get() again. A worker that finishes its current item therefore exits immediately, leaving any remaining items in the queue even though immediate=False was requested. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close also joins the commit thread before shutting the pool down, so work processed during shutdown is not committed. The net effect is that graceful shutdown abandons buffered results and relies on Kafka redelivery, contrary to the graceful-drain behavior implied by the code and docstrings.

Before this change those keys are Redis sets; this diff starts writing them with `ZADD` and later calls `ZCARD`/`ZSCAN`/`ZUNIONSTORE` (`buffer.py` lines 197 and 434, plus `add-buffer.lua`). During a rolling deploy, any old set key touched by the new consumer, or any old consumer touching a new zset key, will get a `WRONGTYPE` error. Existing keys have a TTL up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600 seconds), so affected batches can fail and spans/segments can be lost or stuck until keys expire. There is no dual read/write path, versioned key prefix, or migration/flush step.

Eviction is now `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...)` inside the Lua script, while the Python span-count check was removed from `_load_segment_data`. `SpansBuffer` still exposes `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) and passes nothing to the script, so any configured value is silently ignored and the actual limit is always 1000, which is also one lower than the default. Operators/tests cannot tune the cap, and the Python span-count safety check no longer matches the Lua behavior.

ZUNIONSTORE sums duplicate timestamp scores instead of preserving the latest

The script uses `zunionstore set_key, 2, set_key, span_key` (and the same for `parent_key`) without an `AGGREGATE` option. Redis's default is `SUM`, so if a span payload is present in both source sets its score becomes the sum of two `end_timestamp_precise` values rather than the max/latest timestamp. This occurs routinely with at-least-once duplicate/reprocessed spans: a duplicate child is re-added under its parent key and then merged into the destination where the first copy already exists. Since `ZPOPMIN` later uses the score to decide which spans to evict, duplicated spans can be moved to the wrong end of the ordering and be kept or evicted incorrectly. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` or otherwise define duplicate-score handling.

No test exercises the new ZPOPMIN eviction path

There is no coverage for the cap being enforced, eviction ordering by `end_timestamp_precise`, retention of a root/segment span, or cleanup/redirect behavior for evicted spans. A regression here silently drops span data, so a test with more than 1000 spans should verify the resulting segment contents and Redis key cleanup.

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new ~90-line paginator used by the audit-log endpoint, but no test instantiates it or calls the endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true`. If a trace's span-buffer redirect chain is deeper than 1000, the loop stops at an intermediate span id, so the current span is attached to the wrong buffer and segments can be split or duplicated. This is an abrupt behavior change unrelated to the eviction work and has no test; either restore the old bound or justify and test the new one.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key uses raw subject ID and omits identity type

The denial-cache key is built from the raw subject ID (`checkReq.UserUID`) before `GetUserIdentifiers` resolves the canonical UID, and it does not include the identity type. The permission cache, in contrast, is keyed by the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID`. The same user can therefore have separate denial entries for `user:123` and `user:<uid>`, so the denial cache is bypassed when the subject form changes. Conversely, identities such as `user:123`, `service-account:123`, or `anonymous:123` share the same denial key even though they can represent different principals; a denial for one can be served for another until TTL expiry. Resolve the subject first and include the identity type plus canonical UID, and escape or hash the key components.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment is about ambiguous concatenation with underscores causing key collisions. The candidate's main point is different: the key uses the raw ID and omits the identity type, which also produces collisions and wrong denial hits. It does mention escaping or hashing key components, but only in passing. Both describe denial-cache key collisions leading to incorrect permission results, so this is a partial overlap with a different root cause.

A denied check (for example, before a just-created dashboard's creator permission is visible, or before an admin grants a role) therefore keeps returning Allowed=false for the 30s shortCacheTTL even after the DB grants access. This also means a stale denial overrides a later-refreshed allow in permCache, which directly undermines the PR goal of making newly created resources accessible. Deny entries need invalidation, or must not override a fresh cached allow, and likely deserve a shorter TTL.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check after acquiring the write lock causes duplicate manifest loads

After reading the cache under RLock and releasing it, the function takes the write lock at line 48 but never re-checks whether the cache was filled by another goroutine in the meantime. On a cold start (or any time the cache is nil in non-Dev env), N concurrent callers all observe `ret == nil` at line 45 and then queue on the write lock; each one runs the full read path (lines 51-67, including reading and JSON-decoding assets-manifest.json, and its error paths) and overwrites the cache. The final value is still correct, but N concurrent requests produce N serialized disk reads/parses instead of one, and every queued request is blocked for the whole duration of the I/O. This is the classic double-checked-locking omission: re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and return the cached value early.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, so the double-checked locking pattern is incomplete and concurrent callers each repopulate the cache.

No test exercises concurrent GetWebAssets calls

A race like this is only reliably caught by running concurrent GetWebAssets invocations under `go test -race`; without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce an unguarded read/write without CI noticing. Add a test that spawns multiple goroutines calling GetWebAssets against a temp manifest and asserts they all get a non-nil, consistent result (run with -race).

The new test expecting 5 applyTemplateVariables calls (one initial plus four shard groups) asserts this double interpolation. The expr filter runs before applyTemplateVariables. A query whose whole expression is a variable (for example $query) passes the filter even when interpolation produces an empty string, so runSplitQuery can execute datasource.runQuery with an empty expr. On the shard path the same ordering in shardQuerySplitting.ts:50 lets such an empty target reach groupTargetsByQueryType; when it is later passed to runSplitQuery it is filtered out and can leave the grouped request list empty, causing the Math.max/undefined access in runSplitGroupedQueries to fail. true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

Count-then-insert device limiting is not atomic and allows exceeding the limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` first calls `CountDevices` and, only if `count < deviceLimit`, runs a separate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. The count and the insert are independent statements with no transaction, lock, or conditional insert. Under concurrency, two first-time requests from different new devices can both observe `count < deviceLimit` and both insert, so the number of tracked devices exceeds the configured `device_limit`. Because tagging now runs synchronously on the authentication path, this race is easy to trigger with parallel browser sessions. The limit needs to be enforced atomically (e.g. a single conditional insert that also checks the count, or serialization via a lock), otherwise the configured limit is only advisory.

This adds a DB round-trip (a count plus an upsert) to the anonymous auth path, makes tagging fail if the inbound request context is cancelled or short-lived, and removes the panic recovery so a panic in tagging now propagates into authentication. If synchronous enforcement is required, at least keep panic recovery and use a bounded/detached context rather than the raw request context.

The golden comment's specific concern is that authentication now fails entirely when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. The candidate covers related consequences of the synchronous call: added latency, request-context cancellation, and lost panic recovery. It never mentions authentication failing because of the device-limit error. The error means 'could not refresh this device', not specifically 'limit reached', so callers and users are misled.

The candidate covers the time-window case and adds a MySQL changed-rows case, but the core issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. true_positives.matched_candidate:

In `tagDeviceUI` the device's cache key is written (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`, line 87) *before* `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs (line 93). With the new `return err` at line 147, `ErrDeviceLimitReached` now propagates through `TagDevice` into `Anonymous.Authenticate`, which returns `nil, err` and fails the request. But the cache entry set on line 87 is never removed on failure. On the next request from the same device (within the 29-minute cache TTL) `tagDeviceUI` hits the cache and returns nil without touching the DB, so `Authenticate` succeeds. Net effect: the limit only fails the very first request per device per 29 minutes and is trivially bypassed by reloading the page; furthermore, an expired device that `updateDevice` refuses to update still reaches the app on retry without ever being recorded, so it never counts toward the limit. The cache must only be populated after a successful write, and `ErrDeviceLimitReached` must not be masked by a cache hit.

The raw 'device limit reached' string is also exposed. A dedicated typed/status error should be returned so the caller can respond with a meaningful status and message.

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` changed its dependency from `anonstore.AnonStore` to `db.DB`, and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an extra `int64` argument for which there is no wire provider. `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` is registered through Grafana's wire dependency graph, and `pkg/server/wire_gen.go` is generated but committed. `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a brand-new device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached` a single time; it does not assert that an existing, in-window device can still be successfully re-tagged while the store is at capacity (the main reason for `updateDevice`), nor does it exercise the end-to-end rejection through `Anonymous.Authenticate`. `impl_test.go` only runs with the default limit of 0. false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded for controller requests

`translate` still only calls `load_locale(config.locale)` for the current locale, and the only place that calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` is `ApplicationController#set_locale` (application_controller.rb:159). Because the patched `load_translations` forces explicit loading and `load_locale` is the only loader, any translation performed outside a web request (Sidekiq/background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, the console, or `I18n.with_locale` / `I18n.t(key, locale: x)` inside a request) will try the fallback chain (`SiteSetting.default_locale`, `:en`) without those locale files ever having been loaded. When the requested locale lacks a key, the fallback lookup then misses and the caller gets a missing translation/raw key instead of the site-default/English string. For example, a job running under `I18n.locale = 'de'` on a site whose default locale is `'fr'` never loads `fr`, so a missing German key cannot fall back to French. Ensure the whole fallback chain is loaded whenever a locale is loaded (e.g. make `load_locale`/`translate` call `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for each entry of `I18n.fallbacks[locale]`), not only from the controller before_filter.

Fallback chain recomputes a SiteSetting lookup on the translation hot path

`I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` on every `I18n.translate`/`I18n.exists?` that reaches the backend (i.e. every translation not served from the translate accelerator's LRU cache), and this `[]` override calls `SiteSetting.default_locale` each time. That turns a previously pure in-memory fallback-list lookup into a site-setting lookup on the hot translation path and, via `set_locale`, once per request. It also means an early `I18n.t` (boot initializers, asset precompilation, rake tasks, console before the DB/Redis are available) now attempts to read site settings and can raise instead of simply returning a translation. Memoize the default locale / compute the chain once per locale and invalidate it on reload.

No tests for the new fallback behavior, which is now enabled in every environment

The PR changes translation resolution globally (fall back to the site default locale, then English) but adds no specs covering `FallbackLocaleList#[]`, the fallback ordering, or `ensure_loaded!`. Additionally, `I18n.fallbacks = FallbackLocaleList.new` runs in every environment, while the `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` lines that were removed only existed in production/profile/Cloud66, so fallbacks now also apply in test/development where they were previously unset. Tests that assert a missing key is returned verbatim, or that a given locale has no translation, will now silently receive the site-default/English string. Add tests for the new fallback chain and confirm the intended test-environment behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Unconditional visible assignment can hide groups on partial updates

`update` always executes `group.visible = params[:visible] == "true"`. A PATCH or PUT that omits `visible`—including the old PATCH membership-changes API that still routes to `update` because `resources :groups` accepts PATCH—now sets `visible` to false and saves. The old `update_patch` membership add/delete handling was also removed, so such requests no longer update memberships and can silently make the group invisible. Only assign `visible` when the parameter is present, and either support or explicitly reject the old PATCH contract.

Public members endpoint accepts unbounded and negative pagination values

`limit` and `offset` are taken directly from public query parameters and passed into `.limit(...).offset(...)`. A caller can request a very large limit, causing an unnecessarily large database result and JSON serialization, or pass negative values that can produce SQL errors/500 responses. Clamp `limit` to a sane maximum and enforce `offset >= 0`.

Public group member list truncates at 50 with no pagination

The backend now returns only one page of members (default limit 50), and the public group-members route never requests another page. This template simply iterates `members` and has no pagination controls. Groups with more than 50 members will silently show only the first 50, whereas non-automatic groups previously returned all members. Either add paging or explicitly fetch all members for the public view.

Removing the last member on the last page leaves an invalid offset

`removeMember` deletes the user and then calls `findMembers()` with the current offset. If the removed user was the only member on the current page (for example 51 members at offset 50), the new total becomes 50 but the request still uses offset 50, so the reload returns an empty page and the UI stays on an invalid blank page. Adjust the offset when it reaches or exceeds the new `user_count` after deletion.

Username input is not cleared after adding members or switching groups

`usernames` is state on the singleton admin group controller and is not reset after `addMembers` or when `setupController` switches to another group. After adding users to group A, selecting group B leaves the old usernames in the selector; clicking Add again can add those stale users to group B unintentionally. Clear the property after each add and when the model changes (the existing TODO acknowledges this).

Creating a group ignores the selected alias level

The client’s `Group.asJSON()` sends `alias_level` when creating a group, and the admin template exposes the alias selector for new groups, but `create` only assigns `name` and `visible`. A newly created group therefore silently loses the selected alias level and falls back to the database default. Assign `group.alias_level = params[:alias_level].to_i` when present.

Public members endpoint response shape is a breaking change

`/groups/:group_id/members.json` previously returned a JSON array of users; it now returns an object of the form `{members: [...], meta: {...}}`. The in-repo JavaScript client was updated, but any plugin, mobile app, or external consumer expecting the old array will break. If this endpoint is part of the public API, either maintain backward compatibility or introduce a versioned/new endpoint.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation triggers a DB write and double-counts blocked-email statistics

`EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and `should_block?` (app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 12-17) loads the matching record, increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and calls `record.save`. This means a simple `valid?`/`save` check now performs a database write. In `UsersController#create` the user is validated twice on the same request: `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), so a single signup attempt against a blocked (or even `do_nothing`) email increments `match_count` by 2 instead of 1. Match counts will be inflated unpredictably, defeating the purpose of these statistics for spotting spam campaigns, and read-only validation paths unexpectedly mutate the DB. The stat update should be decoupled from the pure predicate and triggered once per real block event (e.g., after a confirmed rejection), not on every validation invocation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the should_block? predicate has a side effect, updating match statistics during what should be a read-only check. The candidate also covers the double-counting consequence and recommends decoupling the update from the check, which is the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and bypassable

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` compares the raw submitted email against the stored string with exact case. E-mail addresses are treated case-insensitively in practice, and nothing downcases the user's email when it is set/validated (`User.new_from_params` stores it verbatim). So an entry for `spam@bad.com` will not block a signup using `Spam@Bad.com` or `spam@BAD.com`, and imported/manually-entered records in mixed case won't match either — trivially bypassing the blocklist. Normalize on both sides: downcase/`Email.downcase` the value in `should_block?` (and ideally normalize the stored `email` in a `before_validation`/`before_save` so the unique index also behaves case-insensitively).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same flaw: the email lookup in should_block? is case-sensitive, so someone can get past the blocklist by changing the letter case of a blocked address.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic counter update loses matches under concurrency

`should_block?` performs a read-modify-write: `record.match_count += 1; record.save`. Two concurrent requests matching the same blocked email both read count N and write N+1, losing one increment. Since these counters are the signal used to identify spam waves (exactly when many concurrent attempts happen), the undercounting is most severe in the scenario the data is meant to detect. Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now])` (or `increment_counter`) instead.

New validator spec does not cover the ported domain restrictions or the real lookup

The only new validator specs stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so they neither exercise the actual database lookup/scoping nor verify the end-to-end behavior (`user.valid?` returning false for a blocked email). More importantly, this PR moves the `email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` logic out of `User#email_validator` into `EmailValidator`, but no spec covers that moved logic (whitelist pass/fail, blacklist pass/fail). A regression in the relocated domain-restriction behavior would go undetected. Add specs covering the whitelist and blacklist branches (and ideally one integration spec that a blocked email makes a `User` invalid), plus a test for the new `errors`/`values` fields returned by `UsersController#create`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The new `align-items()` mixin emits `-webkit-box-align`, `-webkit-align-items`, `-ms-flex-align`, and `align-items`, but omits `-moz-box-align`. Adding `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action` changes its children to flex items. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

include_website_name is missing the `?` suffix and is never called

ActiveModel::Serializers decides whether to emit an attribute by calling `include_<attr>?`; every other predicate in this file (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_stats?`, `include_suspend_reason?`) uses the question mark. Because this method is defined as `include_website_name` without `?`, it is dead code: `website_name` is always serialized, including `website_name: null` for users with no website, and any conditional exclusion written here would silently do nothing. Rename it to `include_website_name?`.

The golden comment also mentions string mutation from '.' <<, which the candidate does not cover, but the primary issue matches.

Domain comparison is asymmetric and can treat unrelated domains as equal

The path is appended only when the instance host ends with '.'+website_host (else branch) or when both hosts have the same label count > 2 and their labels after the first match (elsif). As a result, instance `example.com` with website `www.example.com` (2 vs 3 labels) falls into the else branch, fails `ends_with?('.www.example.com')`, and returns only `www.example.com`, while the reverse case (`forum.example.com` instance, `example.com` website) shows the path. The feature therefore works inconsistently. In addition, comparing all-but-the-first labels treats unrelated registrable domains under multi-label public suffixes as identical: `foo.co.uk` and `bar.co.uk` both reduce to `co.uk`, so the full path of one is shown as if it belonged to the other. The browser therefore drops the message, so the iframe never receives the height and content is clipped to the initial iframe size. The readability path only filters tag/attribute names, not dangerous URL schemes, and line 13 interpolates the feed-provided URL unescaped into the raw post. A malicious or compromised feed can therefore inject script/event-handler HTML and execute it in the forum origin when the embed is viewed. The candidate explicitly notes that line 13 interpolates the feed-provided URL unescaped into the raw post, as part of its broader XSS concern. That covers the XSS half of the golden comment. Guard tests pass without exercising the setting under test

The `feed_polling_url` test stubs only `feed_polling_url` to nil; it leaves `feed_polling_enabled?` at its default false, so `execute` short-circuits before the URL check. `validateUploadedFile` previously derived the limit from `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`; it now always uses `10 * 1024` KB for both images and attachments. Attachments are not auto-downsized on the server, so sites configured with a smaller `max_attachment_size_kb` will now accept up to 10MB in the browser and only fail later with a less clear server error (or the setting is effectively bypassed). The same applies to images where an admin deliberately configured a limit below 10MB. In addition, the 413 handler at line 246 now reports `max_size_kb: 10MB` regardless of the web server's real limit, so the error message can be wrong. The limit should stay driven by the site settings (or a dedicated setting for the resize threshold).

false_positives.candidate:
Downsizing an animated GIF keeps only the first frame when allow_animated_thumbnails is off

The controller's new resize path calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(..., allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)`. When that setting is false (the default), `optimize` selects `downsize_instructions`, whose command contains `#{from}[0]`, i.e. only the first frame of a multi-frame GIF. Because the downsized temp file replaces the upload, an animated GIF larger than `max_image_size_kb` is permanently stored as a static single-frame image, silently destroying the user's animation. The animated instruction set is only used when the setting is explicitly enabled. Animated uploads should either always go through the animated/`gifsicle` path or be exempted from automatic downsizing.

Downsize loop with at most five 80% steps cannot bring files more than ~3x the limit under the limit

Repeatedly applying `-resize 80%` five times yields only 0.8^5 ≈ 0.33 of the original, so a file more than roughly 3x `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` is still oversized after the loop and `Upload.create_for` then rejects it. The advertised feature (accept large images by shrinking them) therefore still fails for genuinely large uploads, e.g. a 10MB image on a 1MB limit. Each pass is also a separate lossy re-encode (no `-quality` specified), so intermediate steps degrade the image more than necessary. true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so a code can be used twice or resurrected

The new backup-code login branch decrypts `user.backupCodes` into an array, nulls the matched entry (`backupCodes[index] = null`) and then writes the whole re-encrypted array back with `prisma.user.update`. This is a read-modify-write with no transaction or conditional update. Two login requests that arrive concurrently with the same code both match it and both return success, so the "each backup code can be used exactly once" guarantee advertised in `backup_code_instructions` is not enforced. Worse, two concurrent requests with *different* codes each write back a list derived from the same original snapshot, so the last write wins and the code consumed by the other request is silently restored and becomes reusable. Because an attacker typically does not need parallelism, this is not trivially exploitable, but the single-use property of a security credential must hold under concurrency. Suggested fix: perform the removal atomically (e.g. a `updateMany` guarded on the exact previous encrypted value, or a transaction with a row lock / `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), or store codes as individual rows and delete by id/`deleteMany`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue as the golden comment. Backup codes are consumed through a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent logins with the same code can both succeed, which breaks the one-time-use guarantee.

false_positives.candidate:
onEnable is only fired from the backup-codes Close button, so dismissing the dialog otherwise leaves 2FA state stale

Before this change `onEnable()` was called as soon as the enable API returned 200. Now enablement is only reported to the parent from the `backup-codes-close` button (`resetState(); onEnable();`). The dialog is controlled by the parent and Radix closes it on Escape (and on other dismissal paths) via `onOpenChange`, none of which call `onEnable` or `resetState`. Consequence: a user who enables 2FA and closes the dialog with Escape gets a server state where 2FA is enabled, while the settings page still shows the toggle as unchecked; if they retry, `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup` answers `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` and they get a generic "something went wrong" error. The internal `step` also stays on `DisplayBackupCodes`, so re-opening the modal later shows the old backup-code screen instead of the password step. `onEnable` should be invoked (and state reset) whenever the dialog is dismissed after a successful enable, not only from one button.

missing_backup_codes message tells users to generate codes in settings, which is impossible

The new `missing_backup_codes` string reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." but no such setting exists: backup codes are only produced by `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup`, which returns `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` for any user who already has 2FA on, and there is no UI to regenerate them. Every user who enabled 2FA before this migration (`backupCodes` is `NULL`) and then clicks "Lost access" will follow the advice, find nothing, and be stuck. Either provide a regenerate-codes entry point in the 2FA settings section or change the text to describe what the user can actually do (e.g. disable and re-enable 2FA).

No test covers logging in with a backup code or its single-use behaviour

The PR's core security behaviours are untested. The added assertions only verify that the download produces a file named `cal-backup-codes.txt`, that the copy button shows a toast, and that Close works (`// TODO: check file content`, `// TODO: check clipboard content`), and a `// TODO: add more backup code tests` is left behind. Nothing exercises: logging in via "Lost access" with a real code, rejection of a wrong code, the fact that a consumed code cannot be reused (the guarantee the UI copy makes), or disabling 2FA with a backup code. Since the consumption logic lives in `next-auth-options.ts` and is exactly the part that can silently regress (including the concurrency issue above), at least a happy-path login-with-backup-code test and a reuse-rejection test should be added before merge.

New `required` on the password field blocks disabling 2FA for accounts with no password

`required` was added to the password `PasswordField`. The field is rendered whenever the caller doesn't pass `disablePassword` (the default), and the API deliberately treats the password as optional: `disable.ts` only verifies it `if (user.password && user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL)`. Accounts that have 2FA enabled but no password (e.g. a user who set up 2FA while using CAL credentials and later signed in with Google, which nulls `password`, or SAML/Google accounts with 2FA) can legitimately disable 2FA server-side, but the browser now refuses to submit the form with an empty required field, so they are blocked in the UI. The client-side constraint should mirror the server rule (e.g. only mark it required when the account actually has a password).

Third-party identity-provider guard makes backup codes unusable for OAuth accounts with 2FA

The existing guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw new Error(ErrorCode.ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled)` runs before the new backup-code branch. A user with a GOOGLE/SAML identity provider who has 2FA enabled necessarily submits a backup code with an empty `totpCode`, so they always hit this error and can never use their backup codes, even though `loginWithTotp` routes such users through the 2FA login page. Either the guard should also accept a supplied `backupCode`, or the limitation should be made explicit (and the UI should not offer a path that can never succeed) — as written, the feature silently does not apply to that group of 2FA users.

Preserve `result.credentialId` for video results.

Location updates create calendar references without calendar linkage

`updateLocation` now builds references from `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` does not populate either field (it returns only appName/type/success/uid/updatedEvent/originalEvent/calError/calWarnings). Every location edit therefore creates calendar references with null `credentialId` and `externalCalendarId`, so later cancellation/reschedule can target the wrong calendar or all credentials. Populate these fields in updateEvent or derive them from the destination calendar.

Reschedule merge deletes only the first old calendar event

The PR now supports multiple calendar references, but the `newBookingId` merge branch still uses `booking.references.find(...)` and deletes only one old calendar event. Collective bookings can have references for several hosts, so old events for all but the first host remain on their calendars after a reschedule/merge. Iterate over all calendar references when deleting old events.

Google insert patches hangout link with undefined calendarId

The insert call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || 'primary'`, but the subsequent hangout-link patch uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the fallback. When no destination calendar matches the credential, the event is created on primary but the patch is sent with an undefined calendarId, so the hangout link/description is not patched and the unawaited call can reject. Use the same fallback for both calls.

Collective co-host calendars are dropped when organizer has no destination calendar

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor organizer has a destination calendar. The later `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is then a no-op, so destination calendars collected from co-hosts are discarded. A collective host with a calendar will not get an event if the organizer has none. Initialize to `[]` before pushing.

Office365 createEvent always uses the first destination calendar

EventManager calls createEvent once per destination credential, but Office365's createEvent reads `event.destinationCalendar[0]` and uses that calendar for every call. With two Office365 hosts, both calls create the event on the first host's calendar (or fail for the second credential), so additional hosts never get the event and the first can get duplicates. Select the destination belonging to the current credential (pass credentialId/externalId) instead of index 0.

Lark createEvent always uses the first destination calendar

Lark's createEvent derives the calendar id from `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. EventManager invokes the service for each destination credential, so a second Lark host's event is created against the first host's calendar id, likely failing due to permissions or writing into the wrong calendar. Use the destination matching the current credential rather than the first array entry.

CalDAV createEvent filters all calendars by the first destination

BaseCalendarService.createEvent filters calendars using only `event.destinationCalendar[0].externalId`. When a collective booking has multiple CalDAV destinations, every invocation filters to that first calendar, so other hosts' calendars never receive an event and the first calendar can receive duplicates. Select the destination for the current credential or pass the target externalId into createEvent.

Recurring collective cancellation ignores non-organizer credentials

The outer loop now iterates every calendar reference, but the recurring cancellation branch still builds its work from `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` and picks the first calendar reference per updated booking. Co-hosts' credentials are not in the organizer's `credentials`, and their per-reference ids are ignored, so recurring collective bookings leave calendar events on co-host calendars. Delete using each reference's own credential/external id.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach makes reschedule cancellations fire-and-forget and defeats the try/catch

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` is used inside a `try { ... } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }`. `forEach` discards the promises returned by the async callback, so the surrounding try/catch can never observe a failure from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`, and those failures become unhandled promise rejections (fatal by default in Node >= 15). `Reschedule` also resolves and returns `true` (and sends the reschedule email) before the external calendar/video events are actually deleted; in a serverless handler the process may be frozen at that point, leaving the old event on the organizer's calendar even though the booking is marked CANCELLED. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` or a `for...of` loop inside the try block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. An async forEach is used for calendar/video deletions, the promises are never awaited, and so the surrounding try/catch is defeated and rejections go unhandled. Both recommend Promise.all with map or a for...of loop.

false_positives.candidate:
async forEach makes reschedule cancellations fire-and-forget and defeats the try/catch

Same defect as in the vital reschedule file: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` returns immediately because `forEach` ignores the promises returned by the async callback. The outer `try/catch` around the loop therefore no longer catches errors from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`, those errors surface as unhandled rejections, and the function resolves before the calendar/video deletions complete, so the old event may remain on the user's calendar after a reschedule. Replace the `forEach` with `await Promise.all(...map(...))` or a `for...of` loop with `await`.

requestReschedule deletions are started asynchronously and never awaited

The `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` block in the `requestReschedule` mutation discards every returned promise. Before this change the callback was synchronous, so the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls were at least initiated synchronously in the handler; now they are deferred until after the surrounding synchronous code runs (i.e. potentially after `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` and after the mutation returns), and no failure from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` is observed or logged (unhandled rejection, fatal by default in Node). The old calendar/video event for the rescheduled booking can silently survive. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` or a `for...of` loop with `await`.

`!calendar` early return skips cleanIntegrationKeys and sends raw credentials to the client

In `getConnectedCalendars`, when `getCalendar` returns null the function returns `{ integration, credentialId }` with the raw `integration` object. `integration` comes from `getApps(credentials)`, i.e. the app object that carries `credentials` (including the user's OAuth `key`) and `credential` — see how this same object is used at lines 27-30 of this file. The other two return paths correctly call `cleanIntegrationKeys(integration)` precisely to avoid leaking credentials to the client (there is even a comment "Don't leak credentials to the client"), but this path returns them verbatim, so any credential whose calendar implementation is missing/keyless will ship the user's secrets to the browser via the connectedCalendars endpoint. Pre-existing, but it is inside the function this PR modifies; the return should also be `{ integration: cleanIntegrationKeys(integration), credentialId }`.

getCalendar is called for non-calendar-variant apps and its promise is dropped

In `getCalendarCredentials`, `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` runs for every credential, but the result is only kept when `app.variant === "calendar"`; for other variants the promise is created and discarded. Now that `getCalendar` is async this is (a) a wasted dynamic `import()` of the app's calendar module for every non-calendar-variant app on every call, and (b) a floating promise whose rejection (e.g. the lazy import failing, or `calendarType.split` on a malformed credential type) becomes an unhandled rejection. Move the `getCalendar` call inside the `app.variant === "calendar"` branch.

Commented-out example points at a non-existent path

The template comment `// example: import("./example"),` references `./example`, but the example app directory in this package is `_example` (the previous comment was `// import * as example from "./_example";`). A developer copying/uncommenting this template will get a module-resolution error. It should read `// example: import("./_example"),`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
